title: Installation
description: How to get a Zig master build, and why this guide needs one.
text: This guide uses Zig master , not a tagged release. Each night, CI compiles and runs each snippet on this site against a new master build. The nightly run keeps the snippets correct. But a stable release cannot compile some of these examples. The full procedure 1. Download Zig master │ ▼ 2. Put zig on PATH │ ▼ 3. Run zig version │ ▼ 4. Install a matching ZLS │ ▼ 5. Write hello world Only steps 1 and 2 are different on each platform. The other steps are the same on all platforms. Step 5 is hello world, the next chapter. title: An HTML Parser
description: A format with no parse errors, because the first browsers made that decision.
text: Each parser in this guide until now can refuse its input. The HTTP request parser rejects a header that has no colon. The language parser reports UnexpectedToken. When a parser refuses, it tells you that the input is not what it claims to be. An HTML parser cannot refuse. No HTML document fails to parse, and this rule is intentional. The specification defines the exact tree for each possible byte sequence. This includes sequences that no author would write intentionally. The reason is historical, and it explains most of the strange parts of this parser: Before anybody wrote a standard, the web already had millions of pages. Most of these pages had errors in their markup. All of them looked correct in the browsers that people used. A new browser that rejected these pages would look broken. Thus the standard describes what the old browsers already did, and their error recovery too. "Be lenient" became a written rule. The program What just happened The input has four things that would be errors in XML. The parser made a sensible tree from all four. The first has no end tag , and it did not swallow the second . The two paragraphs are siblings in the tree. HTML says that a start tag closes an open . A paragraph cannot contain a paragraph, thus the parser closes the first one for you. The real specification has a table of these rules for list items, table cells and about a dozen more elements. is complete without an end tag. It is a void element . A void element can never have children. Thus the parser adds it to the tree, but does not push it onto the stack of open elements. If

title: Hello World
description: Your first Zig program, and the reason that main now takes an argument.
headings: Why !void, and when to remove the !
text: This is the shortest Zig program that prints text. It is almost the same as the first program in each older Zig tutorial. It still compiles on current master: The four lines have two separate parts: the call that prints, and the signature of main. You can change one part and keep the other part. A Run button on this site means that the browser sandbox can run the snippet. The Run button does not tell you which shape to prefer. When to use std.debug.print std.debug.print needs no preparation and returns void. Thus you have no value to pass to other code and no error to handle. Use std.debug.print for lines that you will delete later. For example, use it to check that a loop runs, or to print a struct while you build a feature. You can use it as much as you like while you work. Do not use std.debug.print for the output of a program. The first time that you use a shell, you will see the reason: stdout carries the data that a different program reads when you pipe this program into it. stderr carries the text for the person who runs the program. The greeting above goes to stderr . Thus, if you redirect the program into a file, the file stays empty. To check, run zig run hello.zig out.txt. The greeting prints to your terminal, and the program writes zero bytes to out.txt. The standard streams chapter shows the two streams side by side. There is a second reason. std.debug.print ends in catch return. If the write fails, the output is lost and the program does not know about the failure. For a temporary line, this behaviour is acceptable. For software that you ship, it is not accept

title: An Append-Only Record Store
description: Never modify written data. A delete is a record that you add.
text: The simplest database is a file that you only append to. To write a record, seek to the end and write. The write does not touch the data that is already on disk. This rule seems to be a limitation, but it gives three benefits together: A write that crashes in the middle leaves a partial record at the end. All the data before the partial record does not change. Two readers can read while a writer appends, because the bytes that they read never change. The full history stays in the file. Thus the file can answer the question "what did this look like on Tuesday". The rule also causes two problems, and each log-structured store must solve them. This chapter is about those two problems. The program What the program did The program wrote alice two times, and the read gives the second value. No code updated the first record. The reader scans forward and keeps the last record for each key. Thus "update" means "append a newer record". The old value is still in the file. The old value can be a useful audit log. It can also be a leak, if the old value was a secret. The program deleted bob with a new record. The store never modifies the file, thus it also cannot remove data. The store must write a removal as a new record. That record is a tombstone , and all log-structured databases have tombstones: LSM trees, Kafka topics, Git. For the same reason, a delete in such a store makes the file larger. The value for carol contained a and a newline, and the value stayed correct. The separator causes this problem. title: Everything Is Bytes
description: A type is not a property of the bytes. A type is an agreement about how to read the bytes.
text: A computer stores one kind of thing: numbers from 0 to 255. One of these numbers is a byte . Letters do not have a separate place in memory. Decimals, dates and pictures do not have a separate place either. All of them are bytes. Then how does the machine know that one byte is the letter A and another byte is the number 65? The machine does not know. The two are the same byte. The difference is the type . A type is an agreement about how to read a sequence of bytes: how many bytes go together, and what the pattern means. The agreement is in your program, not in the memory. If you change the agreement, the same bytes have a different meaning. Many things that look strange later have this cause. For example, the operating system sees a file and an image as the same thing. Also, a network can send numbers and receive text. The program Press Run . The program runs in your browser. The build for this site compiled and ran the same file before this page went on the site. What just happened 'A' printed as 65. In Zig, 'A' does not make a letter. 'A' is a different way to write the number 65, and a person can read it more easily. You can use one in place of the other: letter == 65 is true. @sizeOf gave the number of bytes that each type uses. A u8 is one byte, and a u32 is four bytes. The Point in the program is two bytes, because it holds two u8 fields next to each other. @sizeOf answers a physical question: if you ask for a million of these values, how much memory do you ask for? The u32 that holds 1 printed as 1 0 0 0. The value has four bytes, and the useful byte is first. This

That one byte is the classic C buffer overflow. It does not need a bad pointer or malicious input. title: A Lexer
description: The lexer changes characters into tokens. It looks one character ahead and never moves back in the source.
text: A compiler is a short pipeline of programs. Each program takes the output of the program before it, and knows almost nothing about the other programs. This section builds that pipeline. The first stage changes characters into words. Source code comes in as bytes. let total = 0; is fourteen bytes. Nothing in the bytes says that let is a keyword, or that total is one name and not five letters. The stage that makes these decisions is the lexer , and its work is called lexing . When lexing is a separate pass, each later stage is easier to write. The parser never sees a space and never counts a digit. The parser also never checks if an identifier starts with a keyword. The program What just happened The whitespace is gone. The parser in the next chapter never sees a space, a tab or a newline. The lexer reads these characters and makes no token for them, thus each later stage is simpler. The line number stays, and each token holds it. An error message without a line number is almost useless, and the lexer is the last stage that knows the line. total became one token, not five. The scan is greedy: it takes as many characters as it can. When a letter starts a word, the scan continues to take letters and digits until it finds a different character. Because of this one rule, total3 is one identifier. 3total is a number and then an identifier, and the parser correctly rejects it. A keyword is an identifier that the lexer finds in the keyword table. The scanner does not try to match let first. It scans the full word, and then it searches the table for the word. Only this order works. I

title: cat
description: A loop around one fixed buffer. For this reason, cat can copy a file that is larger than memory.
text: cat copies its input to its output. That is the full specification, and it is a good place to start. Each program that moves bytes has the same loop: 1. Keep a fixed buffer. 2. Read into a part of the buffer. 3. Write exactly that part. 4. Do the steps again. The loop never asks how large is the input? It never needs to know. A program with this loop copies a four-byte file and a four-gigabyte file with the same code and the same memory. At no time does the program hold more than one full buffer. The program What just happened The buffer is four bytes, and the program still copied 44. The small buffer shows that the size of the buffer does not change the correctness. The size controls only the quantity of memory and the number of syscalls. Real cat reads 128 KB at a time. Each read is a trip into the kernel, and fewer trips are faster. A smaller buffer still gives the correct output. The read returns the bytes that it has, which can be fewer than you asked for. readSliceShort fills the buffer up to its size and tells you how many bytes it actually got. A common bug in programs like this one is to think that the buffer is now full. Then you write the full buffer, with the old bytes from the last read, and the output contains garbage. The bug appears only under load, because only under load does a read return fewer bytes. A write can also be partial. Thus the loop calls writeAll, not a single write. End of input is a read that returns zero bytes. The end of a file is not a problem, so the reader does not report it as an error. The loop stops when a read returns nothing. Check

title: Parse an HTTP Request
description: A request line, some headers, a blank line. The blank line is the difficult part.
text:
An HTTP request is text. A request is small, and you can read it aloud: POST /submit?id=7 HTTP/1.1 Host: example.com Content-Length: 13 name=ada&ok=1 A request has a request line, some headers, a blank line, and a body. That is the full format, and you can implement it without a library. The difficult part is the blank line. The purpose of the blank line seems simple, but it is not. HTTP gives no length at the start . A server that reads from a socket cannot know how many bytes are in this request. Thus the server cannot ask for that number of bytes. The server must read until the header section ends. After that, Content-Length tells the server the size of the body. This is the framing problem from the networking section. The HTTP solution is a delimiter: 

. The program What the program did The parse is a split, then a split, then a loop. The parser does these steps: 1. Find the blank line, to separate the head from the body. 2. Split the head on 
. 3. Use the first line as the request line. 4. Read each of the other lines as name: value. The parser needs no state machine and no buffering, because the full request is already in memory. The parser found Content-Type, but the client sent content-type. Header names are case-insensitive, and the parser must handle this from the start. curl sends Host, HTTP/2 clients use lowercase for all names, and a hand-written client sends the text that its author typed. A parser that compares names exactly works with the client that you used for the test. It fails with the other clients. The parser removes whitespace after the col

title: A Stylesheet and the Cascade
description: To match a rule is easy. The cascade is the decision about which match wins.
text: A stylesheet is a list of rules. A rule is a selector and some declarations. The parser is simple: split on {, then split on ;, then split on :. The difficult part is this: several rules match the same element, and the rules give different values . Something must decide which rule wins. That decision is the cascade, the C in CSS. The rule The cascade makes two comparisons, in this order: 1. Specificity. How precisely does the selector describe the element? 2. Source order. If the specificity is equal, the later rule wins. The cascade has no other comparisons. When CSS seems unpredictable, the cause is usually a wrong idea about specificity. The program What just happened got color: crimson. Each rule in the sheet matched the element, and four of the rules set a colour: black, orange, red and crimson. urgent won, because an id beats any number of classes. That is specificity. The same element got margin: 8, from p.warning. Three rules set a margin. Two of them are the plain p, with a specificity of 0,0,1. p.warning has 0,1,1, and it beats both. The class component makes the decision. The plain got margin: 4, from the last rule. Two rules with the same selector p set a margin. The specificity is equal, thus the source order makes the decision, and the later rule wins. This is the reason for the advice "put your overrides at the bottom". Specificity is three numbers, not one. The output shows the three numbers separately: 0,1,1 for p.warning and 1,0,0 for urgent. The cascade compares them from left to right, as you compare version numbers. Thus any id beats any number of class

title: Run Tests
description: Tests are part of the language.
headings: Leak detection is on by default
text: A test block is part of the Zig language. You do not import a test framework, register the test or add annotations to the test. Run the tests zig test file.zig just this file zig build test the test step of a build.zig zig test file.zig --test-filter "name" The tests in a file run only in these conditions: The file is the test root. The test root can get to the file through @import. If no module imports a file, the tests in that file never run. Thus, if a test does not fail when you expect it to fail, make sure that some module imports its file. The assertion helpers Helper Use --- --- expect(bool) general condition expectEqual(a, b) prints both values on failure expectEqualStrings string comparison with a readable diff expectEqualSlices(T, a, b) slice comparison expectError(err, expr) asserts a specific error Use expectEqual instead of expect(a == b). When expectEqual fails, it tells you the actual values. Leak detection is on by default std.testing.allocator makes the test fail if the test does not free all the memory that it allocated. You do not have to turn on this check or run a separate tool. Each test that allocates memory is also a leak test: const buf = try std.testing.allocator.alloc(u8, 10); defer std.testing.allocator.free(buf); // omit this and the test fails Skip a test return error.SkipZigTest marks a test as skipped, not as failed. Use it for a test that applies only to some targets. Where to put the tests Put the tests in the same file as the code that they test. The standard library does this. title: Two Writers, One File
description: What a lost update looks like, and the lock that prevents it.
text: To increment a counter in a file, you need three operations, not one: 1. Read the value. 2. Add one. 3. Write the value back. There is a gap between the read and the write. During that gap, the value on disk is stale, and a different writer can read it. Two writers, each with 200 increments, must give 400. They will not. The program This program has no Run button. It needs real threads and a real filesystem. Thus the build makes the program for the host and runs it there. The program also has no pinned output. That is unusual on this site, and the chapter explains the reason. This is one run on the computer that built this page: two threads, 200 increments each without a lock: 183, expected 400 updates lost: true with a lock: 400, expected 400 updates lost: false What the program did More than half of the increments disappeared. The program did not crash, report an error or write a log line. The file contains a number that is too small, and no part of the system saw the problem. Each lost update was the same sequence: one thread read 91, the other thread read 91, and both threads wrote 92. If you run the program again, you get a different number. Because the result changes, races are expensive to fix. You can bisect a bug that occurs again in the same way. This bug gives a different value each time. It disappears under a debugger, because the timing changes. It is worst on the computer with the most cores, and that computer is usually production. The value changes on each run. title: Numbers Have a Size
description: A u8 counts to 255 and stops. You decide what happens next.
text: In Python or JavaScript, a number is only a number. You add one to the number and you get one more. You can do that again and again, with no limit. At the level of the machine, a number is a fixed number of bytes. A fixed number of bytes can hold only a fixed number of different patterns. One byte has 256 patterns. No person selected this limit. The limit comes from a simple count: eight switches have 256 possible settings, and no 257th setting. Thus a u8 counts from 0 to 255. What occurs after 255? A language can do one of three things, and many well-known bugs come from the difference between them: The value wraps to 0. The program stops. The operation reports that the result did not fit, and lets you decide. Zig makes you write which one you want. The program What just happened The names describe the storage. u8 is an u nsigned 8 -bit integer: eight switches, no sign, thus 0 to 255. i8 has the same eight switches, but it uses one pattern for the sign. Thus i8 goes up only to 127, but it goes down to -128. u32 has thirty-two switches, thus it counts past four billion. After you see a few of these names, you can read the range directly from the name. Zig also has u1 to u65535, if you need an unusual size. 255 +% 1 gave 0. The value wrapped. This result is not a bug, because +% is a different operator from +. With the %, you tell the compiler: "I know that this can overflow, and I want the value to wrap". Hash functions and checksums need exactly this behaviour. std.math.add returned Overflow instead of a number. The return type of std.math.add says that the answer can be a

title: Tokenize a Command Line
description: Change "ls -la /tmp" into the argv that a shell needs, and copy nothing.
text: A shell reads a line and must change it into two things: a program to run, and a list of arguments for that program. execve takes an array of strings. Thus the line must become an array before the shell can do anything. This chapter looks like the cut chapter, but the rule is the opposite. cut splits a record on a delimiter, and two delimiters in a row mean an empty field. A command line splits on separation , and two spaces in a row mean nothing. ls -la is two arguments, not four. The rule is different because the meaning is different. In a data format, the delimiter is structure. On a command line, the delimiter is whitespace. The program What just happened " spaced out " gave exactly two arguments. Whitespace at the start, at the end and in runs needs no extra code, because the loop has two phases: 1. Skip the whitespace. 2. Take all the bytes that are not whitespace. Neither phase can make an empty token. Thus the code has no empty tokens to handle. Compare this loop with the cut chapter. In that chapter, a loop that collapsed runs of delimiters was the bug. Both chapters split a line of text. cut must keep the empty fields, and the tokenizer must remove them, because the two inputs mean different things. An empty line and a line of only whitespace gave zero arguments. A shell needs this result. When you press Enter on an empty line, the shell must do nothing. It must not try to run a program with an empty name. The loop handles this case without a special check at the top, and the code for that is short. The program copied nothing. Each argument is a slice of the line.

title: A Parser
description: One function for each precedence level. Each function calls the function for the next tighter level.
text: The lexer made a flat list. 1 + 2 3 is five tokens in a row, and a row has no shape. Nothing in the row tells you which operation occurs first. The job of the parser is to find the shape, and the shape is a tree. In the tree for 1 + 2 3, the + is at the top, because the + is the last operation. The right operand of the + is all of 2 3. A tree runs from the deepest node to the top, thus the deepest node runs first. This means that precedence is depth . This fact gives a more useful view of the problem. You do not need a rule that says binds tighter than +. You need to be deeper in the tree. It is possible to write a parser that puts deeper, and that parser never reads a table. The method Write one function for each precedence level, with the loosest level first. Each function gets its operands from the function for the next tighter level. comparison - sum ( " product ( "+" "-" product ) product - unary ( " " "/" unary ) unary - "-" unary primary primary - number name "(" comparison ")" sum cannot see a . sum asks product for each operand. product reads each multiplication and returns a complete subtree. Thus the multiplication is inside the operand of the addition, and that is exactly the meaning of "binds tighter". The call chain is the precedence table. This method is called recursive descent . Most production compilers use it, because the code is easy to read. The program What just happened 1 + 2 3 became (+ 1 ( 2 3)) , and (1 + 2) 3 became ( (+ 1 2) 3). A simple left-to-right order uses the same five tokens as the first case, but it makes a completely different tree. Par

title: wc
description: To count words, count each time that the input goes into a word.
text:
To count bytes is trivial. To count lines is almost as easy: add one for each 
. Words are more difficult, because a word is not a single byte in the input. A word is a pattern between bytes. If you try to count words directly, you need rules for many usual cases: Two spaces between words. A space at the start. A tab in place of a space. A line that ends without a newline. If you handle each case as a special case, the code becomes complex, and soon one case is wrong. Instead, count transitions . Keep one bit that tells if the program is inside a word now. Each time that bit changes from false to true, a word starts. The difficult cases need no special code. A run of twelve spaces sets the bit to false twelve times, and false is already false. This one bit and the rule that changes it are a state machine , and a very small one. The program What just happened Each sample tests one of the cases above. "hello world
" and " hello world 
" both give 2 words. The byte counts are different, 12 and 18, but the word count is the same. No code has a special case for whitespace at the start or for repeated whitespace. The transition never occurs two times in sequence, because the bit is already set. "no newline at the end" reports 0 lines and 5 words. This is correct. wc counts newline characters . Thus if the last line of a file has no terminator, the file has one line fewer than you count with your eyes. Real wc does exactly this. If wc reports "0 lines" for a file that clearly has text in it, the file has no newline at the end. The empty input gives three zeroes without special

title: An HTTP Server
description: The parser from the last chapter, with a socket in front of the parser.
headings: The next chapters in this section
text: The parser takes bytes and returns a request. A server is the parser, plus a source for the bytes and a destination for the answer. This chapter has little new code, because the parser is already complete. The program This program has no Run button. The program binds a listening socket, and the browser sandbox has no sockets. Thus the build makes the program for the host and runs the program there. CI runs the program on each change. The program serves two real requests over a real port, and CI checks what the client received. Without the Run button, the verification is the same. GET / HTTP/1.1 200 OK Content-Type: text/html Content-Length: 15 Connection: close hello GET /nope HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found Content-Type: text/plain Content-Length: 10 Connection: close not found What the program did The server reads until it finds a blank line. The server does not read a fixed number of bytes, and it does not read only one line. A loop reads lines until the collected bytes contain \r\n\r\n. This is the framing rule from the last chapter, and here the rule is important in practice. The bytes now come slowly from a socket, and the server cannot know how many bytes will come. Content-Length on the response has a purpose. Without the header, the client cannot know that the body ended. Thus the client waits, and the request seems to stop. The alternative is to close the connection. Then the end of the stream marks the end of the body. Connection: close tells the client about this choice, and the client in this program uses it. title: Layout
description: The parent gives each child its width. The children add up to the height of the parent.
headings: Why height: 100% does not do what people expect
text: After two chapters, the program has a tree of nodes and a way to ask how each node must look. Neither of them tells where each node goes. Layout is the stage that changes the tree into rectangles with positions. The earlier stages parse text. Layout is the first stage of a browser that calculates geometry. The algorithm is not symmetric: Width goes down. A block fills the width that it gets. Thus a parent can decide the widths of its children before it knows anything about them. Height goes up. A block is as tall as its contents. Thus a parent cannot know its height until the layout of each child is complete. One pass goes down for the widths, and one pass goes up for the heights. Many surprises in CSS sizes come from this difference. The program What just happened The widths become smaller at each level: 400, then 380, then 360. The viewport gives 400. page has a padding of 10 on each side, thus its content is 380. .box is inside page, and it has a margin of 5 and a padding of 5. These use 20 more, thus the children of .box get 360. The pass did not look at a child at any point. The heights add up from the bottom. The two paragraphs inside .box are 20 each, thus .box is 40. page contains these boxes: an h1 that is 40 tall the .box, which is 40 tall, with a margin of 5 and a padding of 5 on each side a footer that is 20 tall 40 plus 60 plus 20 is 120. No part of the program can know this number before the layout of the children. The h1 has an explicit height of 40, and it kept that height. Its text is 20 tall. title: An Index Over the Log
description: A second structure, made from the first, that you must now keep in agreement with the first.
text: A read of one key from the append-only store reads the full file. The read must do this. The newest record for a key can be the last record in the file. Thus a scan cannot stop early, because then the answer can be stale. An index solves that problem. People usually describe an index as a thing that makes lookups fast, but that description hides what an index is. An index is a second data structure . A program builds it from the first, and it holds no data of its own. It maps a key to the location of the record. The rest of this chapter comes from those two facts. The program What the program did The read became 16 bytes, not 528 bytes. The answer is the same, and the index went directly to offset 307. That offset is in the second half of the file. The demo shows this case intentionally. The program wrote each key two times. Thus the newest record is far from the first record, and a scan cannot know that it is complete until it gets to the end. The index holds offsets, not values. It has 16 entries for 32 records. The index answers "where", and the log still answers "what". Because the index stores only offsets, an index over a terabyte of records can fit in memory. You can build the index again from the log. build reads the file one time and makes the full index again. The index is derived data, and the log is the source of truth. This has three results: A corrupt index is an inconvenience, not a loss of data. You can delete an index to get the space back. To add a new index to a database that exists, you need one full scan. The index also contains tombstones. If the index

title: Memory Is Numbered
description: An address is an ordinary number, and a pointer is a variable that holds an address.
text: Memory is one long row of boxes, and each box holds one byte. The boxes have numbers, in order from one end. The number of a box is its address . Think of a street. Each house has a number, and the numbers are in order. If you know the number, you can go to the house. A house number is not a house. You can write a house number on a piece of paper, and give the paper to a different person. That person can go to the same house and paint the door. The paint goes on the real house, not on the paper. The piece of paper is a pointer . A pointer is a variable, and its value is an address. All the other facts about pointers come from this fact. The program Your numbers will not be the same as the numbers below. They also change if you press Run two times, or if you open this page tomorrow. This is correct. The loader decides the position of a program in memory when the program loads, not when you write the program. The spacing between the addresses does not change. What just happened Four u32 values printed at offsets 0, 4, 8 and 12. The values are four bytes apart, because a u32 is four bytes wide. An array puts its elements directly next to each other, with no gap. Thus the machine does not search for row[2]. The machine calculates the address of row[0] plus two times four, and goes directly to that address. To find element 999,999 of a large array, the machine does the same arithmetic as for element 0. Not all data structures have this property. @intFromPtr did nothing. @intFromPtr does no work and makes no new information. A pointer is already a number. With @intFromPtr, you te

title: The Read-Eval-Print Loop
description: Four steps and two ways to stop. Programmers often get the stop wrong.
text: Read a line. Find what the line means. Print the result. Return to the start. Each shell, each database prompt and each language REPL runs this loop, and the loop is four lines of code. The end of the loop is less obvious. The loop can end in two ways, and the two ways are completely different. A loop that handles only one of them has a bug, and you can easily miss that bug before a release. The two ways are: The user asks the loop to stop: the user types quit. The input stops. On a terminal, the user presses Ctrl-D. In a pipeline, the input reaches the end of the file. This occurs each time a person writes echo "help" yourshell. A loop that looks only for quit runs forever at the first end of input. The read continues to return an empty result, and an empty result is not quit. The program What just happened Two sessions, two exits. The first session ended on quit and printed (bye). The second session came to the end of its input and printed (end of input). Both are normal ends, and neither is an error. The code paths are different. The empty line did nothing and did not stop the loop. When a user presses Enter at a blank prompt, that is not a command and not an error. A REPL that uses either of these two meanings annoys the user quickly. An unknown command printed a message, and the loop continued. This is the difference between a REPL and a batch program. A batch program usually stops when it gets bad input. A REPL that exits on a typo is not usable. The input is the same in both cases. The correct behavior depends on one question: does a person wait at the prompt? This p

title: A Tree-Walking Interpreter
description: To evaluate a node, evaluate its children and then combine the results.
text: After two stages, the source is a tree. In this chapter, the tree runs. The code for this stage is smaller than the parser. To evaluate (+ 1 ( 2 3)), start at the top. The node is a +, thus evaluate its two children and add them. The left child is 1, and its value is 1. The right child is a , thus evaluate its two children and multiply them. There is no third rule. The function calls itself one time for each child, thus the recursion has the same shape as the tree. The recursion stops at numbers and names. This is a tree-walking interpreter . Most languages start this way, and some languages never needed anything more. Two kinds of node The grammar already separates expressions from statements, and the interpreter keeps the same split: eval takes a node and returns an i64. Expressions produce values. exec takes a node and returns nothing. Statements produce effects. Because the two functions are separate, you can never use a statement as a value: exec has nothing to return. The grammar does not let print appear inside an expression. Thus no code has to check for a print in an expression at run time. The program What just happened while in the interpreted language is while in the interpreter. Look at the .@"while" case. The case is a Zig loop, and the body of the loop calls exec. The interpreted language gets its loop from Zig, the language of the interpreter. The same is true for if, and for recursion when the next chapter adds functions. This property defines a tree-walking interpreter. It is also the main limit of a tree-walking interpreter: it can only give the control f

title: grep
description: Search is a loop over start positions, and the exit code is the answer.
text: grep prints the lines that contain a pattern. This chapter builds two parts of grep by hand: the search, and the exit code. The exit code is also a feature, and people often forget it. The obvious substring search is two nested loops: 1. Go to the first position. 2. Compare the bytes one by one, until the pattern ends. 3. If the pattern ended, that is a match. 4. If a byte is different, stop and go to the next start position. In the worst case, the search is O(n×m). The worst case needs input like aaaaaaaaab with the pattern aaab, and a normal line of text does not look like that. There are faster algorithms, for example Boyer-Moore. Here, they are less important than you possibly expect, because the simple search is fast enough on a line of text. The program What just happened The program did three searches, and the third search found nothing. Look at the output: exit 1. The program printed no error and nothing on stderr. Only the exit status changed. With the exit status, other programs can use grep. If you think only about the search, you do not think of this design. A shell must ask "does this file contain the pattern?", and the shell does not need the output. The shell asks with if grep -q pattern file; then. For this to work, "found nothing" must be a result that grep can report , not a failure. grep uses three values: 0 when it found a match. 1 when it found no match. 2 for a real error, for example a file that does not exist. One small integer carries all three results, as Talk to the Operating System describes. The program counted to get the line number. The search

title: Serve Files Safely
description: Decode first, then check. The opposite order is the bug.
text: A static file server has four steps of logic: 1. Take the request target. 2. Open that file under the document root. 3. Read the file. 4. Send the file. A static file server is also a common way to give your /etc/passwd to an attacker. The cause is a one-line mistake in the order of the steps. The target comes percent-encoded. %20 is a space, and %2e is a full stop. Thus a check on the string /%2e%2e/%2e%2e/etc/passwd finds no .. at all. A moment later, the string decodes to /../../etc/passwd. Decode first, then check. A guard that runs before the decode examines a string that is different from the string that the filesystem gets. The program What the program did The guard refused three traversal attempts, and one attempt used percent-encoding. The three attempts are: The plain /../etc/passwd. The hidden /static/../../etc/passwd. The encoded /%2e%2e/%2e%2e/etc/passwd. The third attempt is the one that gets through servers in production. The guard refuses it here for one reason: percentDecode runs before any code looks for ... Reject, and do not normalise. You can change a/../b into b. But then you must maintain a path normaliser. A path normaliser is a second thing that you must make exactly correct, and path normalisers have their own history of bugs. A rule that refuses each .. component is one rule with no edge cases. No legitimate URL contains a .. component, because the browser resolves .. before it sends the URL. The guard also refused the nul byte. /safe.txt%00.png decodes to a name that contains a zero byte. Code after the guard can use the name as a C string. That

title: Paint
description: A rectangle of memory, filled from back to front. The last write wins.
headings: Why this order and not another
text: Layout made rectangles with positions. The paint stage fills them in. It is the simplest stage in the pipeline. The canvas is a rectangle of memory. Each box writes its colour into the cells that it covers. The painter visits the parents first, then the children in document order. Thus a box that the painter paints later covers the previous contents. The painter does not use a depth buffer or a visibility test. It does not clip a box against the boxes that are already on the canvas. This method is the painter's algorithm . A painter on a canvas paints the later layers over the earlier layers, and this algorithm does the same. It is the correct choice here, because the order is already known. The document tells which element is in front of which element. The program What just happened The program made three fills and wrote three runs of text, in order. You can see the order in the picture. 1. page filled its area with -. 2. h1 filled a part of that area with =. 3. .box filled a lower part with o. 4. The program wrote the text over the fills. The paragraphs have no background rule, thus they did not fill. Each step wrote over the step before it, and nothing did a check first. The canvas is an array. A real framebuffer has four bytes for each pixel, not one character. The fill loop writes RGBA instead of a letter. The remainder of the structure is the same. The pixel buffers chapter builds the full version. Clipping is a bounds check. Each write tests if the cell is inside the canvas. The check stops a box that is off the edge, so that the box cannot write outside the buffer.

title: A Write-Ahead Log
description: Write down what you will do, then do it. Recovery is a replay of the note.
headings: What this program cannot show you
text: The last chapter ended on a problem that it could not solve: two files that must agree, and a crash between the two writes. This problem is not specific to files. It occurs with each change that is not one indivisible action. The answer is old and simple. All databases, all journalling filesystems and most message queues use it. Write down what you will do, then do it. If the power fails before you finish, the note is still there when the program starts again. Then you do the change again. That note is a write-ahead log . Recovery is a read of the note. The program What the program did A clean shutdown replayed all four records. The program built the in-memory store again from the log alone. The log is the database. The in-memory store is a fast cache of the log. The crash lost the record that was in the middle of a write, and nothing else. To simulate a power failure, the program truncated the log. This left a last line with no newline. The replay stopped there, and the first three records were correct. c is absent, and that is correct: that write did not complete, thus it did not occur. A WAL works because of this property. When the process stops, you can find a partial record at the end of an append-only file. A record is complete only after the program writes its terminator. The data before the partial record does not change, because no write touched that data. The checksum found the corrupted byte, and the replay stopped. The newline framing cannot see this problem. The record has its terminator, but its content is incorrect. Only the checksum sees the problem. The sto

title: The Stack
description: Where local variables live, and why a pointer to a local is not safe after the call returns.
text: The last chapter said that each value has an address. This chapter answers the next question: who decides the address, and for how long is the address valid? For a local variable, the machine decides, and the method costs very little. The machine keeps one number: the position where the used part of memory ends now. A function call moves that mark forward, to make space for the local variables of the call. A return moves the mark back. To make space costs one addition, and to give the space back costs one subtraction. Thus you do not have to plan for the cost of a function call. The region that a call gets is its frame , and the sequence of frames is the stack . A stack of plates is similar in one way only: the plate that you put down last is the plate that you take first. A call cannot return before the calls that it made return. Thus the program always releases the frames in the reverse order. This rule has a result, and a large group of bugs comes from it: when the call returns, that memory is not yours any more. Nothing erases or marks the memory. The mark only moves back, and the next call gets the same bytes. The program What just happened Three calls were live at the same time, and no two of them shared an address. main called outer, and outer called inner. Each call had a local variable at a different place. Nothing controlled this. Each call only moved the mark forward by the size of the space that the call needed. The direction that the program prints is not a rule. On this target, the frames go upward. On most machines that you will use, the frames go downward. F

title: Functions and Frames
description: A call needs a place for its own variables, and a way to return to the caller.
text: The interpreter so far has one set of variables. Functions break that design immediately. Two calls to the same function must not share one set of variables. A recursive call must have several sets alive at the same time, one set for each call. Thus a call needs its own storage, and that storage is a frame . A frame is the run-time equivalent of the machine-level idea in The Stack. The difference is that here you build the frame yourself, and the hardware does not supply it. A call pushes a frame, a return pops the frame, and the array of frames is the call stack. The second problem is less obvious. return can be anywhere: inside an if, inside a while, or inside a block inside both. return must leave all of those statements and arrive at the call site. The exec function is recursive. Thus return must unwind an unknown number of Zig frames. The program What just happened fact(5) gave 120 and fib(10) gave 55. Thus several values of n were alive at the same time, and no value of n changed a different one. fib(10) alone makes 177 calls. Each call got a frame, used the frame, and released the frame. bump(1) printed 2, and the global x stayed 100. The interpreter defines the parameter in the new frame. Thus the parameter shadows the global, and does not overwrite it. Look at lookup: it searches the current frame first, the globals second, and nothing else. Those two lines are the complete rule for scope in this language. return is an error in the implementation. error.Return is not a failure, and it does not mean that an operation failed. It is the only mechanism in Zig that unwi

title: sort
description: To sort lines is easy. To own the lines is the part that has a cost.
text: The first three tools never held more than one full buffer. sort cannot do that. You cannot know which line comes first until you see the last line. Thus in this chapter, the streaming loop stops. The chapter has a question that the earlier tools did not have. Where are the lines in memory? To read the lines, the program must hold all of them. To sort the lines, the program must move them. After the sort, something must still point at the correct bytes. This is the ownership question from Who Owns This Memory. sort is the first program where you cannot avoid the question. There are two answers that work: Copy each line into memory that you allocated. Keep the full input in one buffer, and sort a list of pointers into the buffer . For all input that fits, the real sort uses the second answer. To move an 8-byte pointer costs less than to move a 200-byte line, and the preparation costs nothing. The program What just happened The program copied nothing. The last line shows this: 40 bytes of pointers and zero bytes of copied text. Each entry in the sorted list is a slice that points back into the original input. Thus the sort of five lines moved five pointers, and the text stayed exactly where it was. The contract of the function states the cost of that decision: the result is valid only while the input buffer is valid. Assume that a function owns the buffer and returns those slices. Then you have the dangling pointer from The Stack, but now you have a full array of dangling pointers. Zebra sorted before apple. This is not a bug. It is byte order. Z is 90 and a is 97, so each ca

title: Routes and Query Strings
description: All text after the question mark, and the dispatch table that ignores that text.
text: A request target is two parts with a ? between them. Before the ? is a path. The path decides what runs . After the ? is a query string. The query string is input to the code that runs. The two parts have different parsing rules and different uses. If a program uses the two parts as one string, many bugs occur. Routing is the first part, and routing is simpler than many people expect: a comparison with a table. A framework adds shorter ways to write the table. The decision that the framework makes is the same. The program What the program did hello+world became hello world, and %26 became a literal &. Both results are important. In a query string, a plus sign means a space. This rule applies only in the query string, not in the path. Thus the decoder is a separate function, not a flag. The program decoded %26 after the split on &. Thus a value that contains an ampersand stayed one value, and did not become two parameters. Decode after you split on the structural characters. That order is the opposite of the order in the last chapter. The reason is the same: decode at the point where the result is data and not structure. empty= and flag both gave an empty value. empty= is a parameter with an empty value. flag has no =. This parser stores both values as "". This choice has a cost: you cannot know the difference between a field that the user cleared and a key that had no value. An optional value keeps the difference. A browser always sends the first form. Thus keys without a value come from hand-written URLs and from APIs. q occurred two times, and the last value won. Servers

title: A Scripting Engine
description: The language knows nothing about documents. The host makes the connection between them.
text: Many people think that the DOM is a part of JavaScript. It is not. The JavaScript specification does not mention document, window, fetch or an element. The specification defines a language: values, functions, objects and control flow. A browser embeds that language, and then adds a set of names to its global scope. These names are host objects . They are the only connection between a script and a page. Node has a different set of names. A game engine that embeds a scripting language has a third set. The language is the same in all of them. The program What just happened The host walked the document and defined three ordinary variables. paragraphs is 3, because a walk through the tree counted three elements. For the evaluator, paragraphs is a name with an integer value. It looks the same as a variable that the script declared. The script has no syntax for documents, and it needs none. print paragraphs + images is arithmetic. No part of the grammar knows what an image is. To give the page a new capability, the host defines one more name. The language does not change. A name that the host did not define is an ordinary undefined variable. The request for stylesheets gave UndefinedVariable. A typo in a local name gives the same error. There is no separate type of "DOM error". For the same reason, in a real browser, document.foo is not a function and myTypo is not defined come from the same code. The evaluator here is intentionally very small. It supports names, integers, + and print. That is sufficient to show where the language and the host meet. The Tiny Language section build

title: A Query Engine
description: The parser asks what. The planner asks how, and the planner does the real work of a database.
headings: The question that this planner does not ask
text: Until now, each part of this section got exact instructions. Append this record. Find this key. Replay this log. A query is different. SELECT name FROM people WHERE id = 3 says what you want, and says nothing about how to get it. Some part of the engine must decide if it examines one row or all rows. The query does not contain that decision. Thus a query engine has two halves: A parser, which changes text into a structure. A planner , which changes that structure into a strategy. The program What the program did The same query ran in two ways and gave the same answer. With an index, WHERE id = 3 examined 1 row. Without an index, it examined 8 rows. The result and the SQL were the same, and the second run did eight times the work. The query did not change, because the query never said how. Declarative languages have this design. The same design also causes a problem: you cannot see the cost when you read the code. For this reason, all databases have an EXPLAIN command. This program prints two lines: the plan and the rows examined. When a query is slow, you spend most of your time on those two lines. WHERE role = engineer used a scan, because role has no index. The planner is one comparison: is the filtered column the column of the index? A real planner asks the same question, and then asks a second question. The section below describes the second question. The parser is a sequence of expectations, not a precedence climb. The grammar is fixed. Thus the parse is: expect SELECT, take a word, expect FROM, take a word. Compare that with the recursive descent parser in the languag

title: Who Owns This Memory
description: Memory that must stay valid after a call returns needs a request, and a person or a function must give it back.
text: A frame ends when the call returns. What do you do when the answer must stay valid after the call that calculated it? You ask for memory that does not belong to a frame. A second pool of memory exists for this purpose. Its usual name is the heap , and its rules are different: Frame memory costs nothing, is automatic, and has a short life. Heap memory needs a request. It stays valid until the program gives it back. If the program never gives it back, the program holds the memory until the program exits. The name for this problem is a leak . Thus some part of the program must give the memory back. Memory management is the answer to one question: who owns this memory, and when does the owner release it? Each method that you know is an answer to this question: A garbage collector answers "nobody, the runtime decides later". Rust answers "the compiler tracks it". C answers "you do, and nothing helps you". Zig answers "you do, and the type signature shows it". The last part makes Zig different. In Zig, a function that allocates takes an allocator as an argument . Zig has no global malloc that a function can use. Thus a function that needs memory cannot hide the request. The allocator is in the signature, and you can see it at each call site. A function without that parameter cannot allocate without your knowledge. The program What just happened The first function allocated nothing. writeGreeting takes a buffer from the caller and writes into the buffer. The function owns nothing. Thus it has nothing to release, and it cannot leak. Use this method more frequently than a beginner i

title: A Bytecode Compiler
description: The compiler walks the same tree one time at compile time, not one time for each run.
headings: What this compiler does not do
text: The interpreter walks the tree each time the program runs. Inside a loop, the interpreter walks the same subtree on each iteration. It follows the same indices, it switches on the same node kinds, and it compares the same variable names with the same strings. None of that work depends on the values. Thus that work never needs to occur more than one time. A compiler removes that repeated work. The compiler walks the tree one time . It does not calculate an answer. It writes down the steps, and the steps are bytecode . Then, to run the program, a loop goes over a flat array, not over a tree. The program What just happened 1 + 2 3 became push, push, push, mul, add. The operands come first, and then the operator. That order is a post-order traversal, and it is all that you need to translate a tree for a stack machine. When an operator runs, its two inputs are the top two values on the stack, because the code for the children put them there. No instruction ever names its operands. Variables became numbers. The listing shows load 0 with a comment that says total, and the comment is only for you. The interpreter chapter showed that the interpreter does a linear search over names each time it reads a variable. That chapter promised this fix. The search still occurs here, one time for each mention, at compile time. At run time, a variable is an array index. This change is a large part of the reason that compiled languages are faster. The compiler patched the forward jump. When the compiler emits jmp if false, it does not know the target address, because the body that the jump skips

title: cut
description: How to split a line at a delimiter, and the edge cases that decide if the split is correct.
text: cut -d: -f2 takes the second field from each line. It is the smallest tool here. Its correctness depends fully on its edge cases. Thus the chapter must state exactly what a split is. Split a:b:c at :, and you get three fields. One rule covers all the other cases: n delimiters make n+1 fields, always. The split does not merge a run of delimiters, and it does not skip empty fields. With that rule, the difficult inputs have clear answers. With a different rule, you must add more and more special cases to fix them. The program What just happened carol::berlin has three fields, and the middle field is empty. There are two delimiters and three fields, as the rule says. Many splitters that look correct get this case wrong. A programmer can want to treat a run of delimiters as one delimiter, because a split at whitespace usually works that way. For a delimited data format, that is wrong, and no error shows the mistake. Each field after the run moves by one. Field 3 of a CSV row becomes field 2, and the data is corrupt, but no error tells you. An empty field and an absent field print differently. In carol::berlin, field 2 is "". In dave, field 2 is (no such field). For this reason, the function returns ?[]const u8, not []const u8: An empty string is a field that exists and is empty. Null means that there is no field. If you merge the two, a caller cannot see the difference between "this record has no email" and "the email of this record is blank". A program that acts on the record must know which of the two it has. Each field is a slice of its line, as in the last chapter. The progr

title: Form Bodies
description: The same encoding as a query string, but in the body, where it can be much larger.
text: A submitted HTML form comes as name=Ada+Lovelace&role=engineer. That text is exactly a query string without the ?. This is intentional. HTML specifies one encoding. The method decides if the encoding goes in the URL or in the body. Thus the parser is the parser from the last chapter. The new parts are around the parser, because a body is not a URL. A body can be megabytes, and it comes after the headers. Also, the client tells you the size of the body . This chapter is about what the server does with that number, because the client can lie. The program What the program did The program uses the same parser without a change. parseForm puts a ? at the front and calls parseQuery. There is one encoding, thus there is one parser. No second implementation exists that can become different from the first. 100%25+done became 100% done. The rules are the same as for a query string: + is a space, and %25 is a literal percent. A form that contains a percent sign is a good test. If the code is incorrect, the value looks almost correct. The program compared Content-Length with a ceiling. The program refused 99999999 before it read one byte of the body. Without that check, this sequence occurs: 1. The client says that the body is 4 GB. 2. The server allocates or reads toward 4 GB. 3. The server stops with a failure. The check costs nothing. Without the check, the client controls how much memory the server uses. A GET has no body and sends no length. Suppose the length is absent, and the server uses "no limit" for it. Then the server waits forever on a connection that has no more data to se

title: The Whole Pipeline
description: Bytes, tree, styles, boxes, pixels. Five stages, in one direction.
headings: What a real browser adds, largest first
text: Each stage has a chapter. This chapter runs the stages one after the other. The pipeline answers the question "how does a browser work?", and here you can see the answer in about 50 lines of code. bytes ─► tree ─► boxes with widths ─► boxes with positions ─► pixels (HTML) (CSS + layout) (layout) (paint) There are five stages. Each stage uses only what the previous stage made. This separation is the reason that a person can build a browser at all. The HTML parser knows nothing about pixels. The painter knows nothing about tags. The program What just happened One declaration changed, and the page changed its arrangement. h1 { height: 30 } became height: 60, and each box below the h1 moved down. Nothing else in the stylesheet or the document changed. This is the reason that stylesheets exist. The height of the box is an input to layout. The program calculates each position below the box. It does not store the positions. When you change the input and run the two passes again, you get a new set of positions. The program writes no value two times, thus no two copies can disagree. The program prints the counts for each render. The counts are 11 nodes, 4 rules and 11 boxes. Here, the box tree and the node tree have the same size. Usually they do not. Some elements make no box. One element can make several boxes, for example one box for each line of text or one for each table cell. You can replace each stage. The renderer writes characters. A renderer that writes RGBA changes nothing in the earlier stages. The layout engine does block flow. To add flexbox, you add a different functi

title: Off the End
description: A length is a value. Languages are different in who must check the length.
text: An array of four numbers uses a length of memory, and that length has an end. What is at the address immediately after the end? Something is always there: a different variable, part of a frame, or the internal parts of the program. Memory continues after the end of your array. Only your right to use the memory stops there. Thus what must row[4] do? Only three answers are possible, and each language selects one: Read the value that is there, and continue. Stop the program. Refuse the request, and make the caller check first. The third answer needs nothing from the language except an if. Thus the program starts with the third answer. The program What just happened The slice knew where it ended. A slice is a pointer and a length that go together as one value. Thus a function that receives a slice always knows the size. For this reason, []const u32 is the usual way to pass a sequence, and a bare pointer is not. The pointer alone tells the function where the data starts, but not where to stop. The slice printed as 8 bytes. The pointer uses four bytes and the length uses four bytes, on this 32-bit WebAssembly build. If you compile the program for your own machine, it prints 16. The reason is the same reason that a pointer on your machine is 8 bytes and not 4. The checked read returned an error instead of a number. at compares the index with .len. When the index is too large, at returns error.OutOfBounds. The function read nothing. The return type told the caller that the answer can be absent. Thus the caller had to handle both cases before it could use the result. All of this cos

title: A Virtual Machine
description: Fetch, decode, execute. A loop over an array, with no tree.
text: The compiler made an array of instructions. This chapter runs that array. The program that runs the array is the smallest program in the section. The machine has an instruction pointer, which is an index into the array. The machine does these steps in a loop: 1. Read the instruction at the instruction pointer. 2. Move the instruction pointer forward. 3. Do what the instruction says. 4. Do the steps again. This loop is called fetch, decode, execute . A physical processor runs the same loop. Thus this program is called a virtual machine, not an interpreter. The machine needs only a stack and a table of slots. Instructions never name their operands. The instructions take the operands from the top of the stack, and put the result back on the stack. The program What just happened The answers are exactly the same as the answers of the tree-walking interpreter. The sum of squares gives 55 and 1, and the arithmetic results are the same. Compilation and interpretation do the same calculation. The compiler only makes its decisions earlier. If the answers were different, one of the two would have a bug. A jump is an assignment. ip = instr.arg is the full implementation of while, if and else. All the structure that the parser found is gone. The tree became a flat array, and control flow is arithmetic on an index. This change is the meaning of "lowering". It is the reason that a disassembly is hard to read and fast to run. Operand order is an easy bug to make in this loop. The code pushed the right operand last, thus the loop must pop it first. If you reverse the order, + and still look

title: printf
description: How to change a number into text, one digit at a time, from the last digit to the first.
text: Each tool before this one moved bytes that already existed. printf makes new bytes. For the number 42, some code must make the two characters 4 and 2. Nothing in the computer does this for you. 42 is a bit pattern, "42" is two bytes, and you write the arithmetic for the conversion. The algorithm is division: 1. Divide the number by ten. 2. The remainder is the last digit. 3. The quotient is the rest of the number. 4. Do the steps again until the quotient is zero. These steps give you all the digits correctly, but in reverse order, because you get the last digit first. Thus write the digits into the end of a buffer, and move to the front. When you stop, the number is the tail of the buffer. Return a slice from the position where you stopped. You never have to reverse the digits in a second pass. The program What just happened Zero needed its own line of code. The loop runs while the value is more than zero. Thus for zero, the loop never runs, and you get an empty string. An integer formatter that you write by hand needs this special case at the top. Without the special case, a count of 0 prints as nothing. The most negative number printed correctly. This is the main trap in this program. The obvious way to handle a negative number is to keep the sign and negate: n = -value. For i64, that works for all values except one. The range is -9223372036854775808 to 9223372036854775807. Thus the smallest value has no positive equivalent, and -value overflows. In C, that is undefined behaviour. In practice, C gives you the same negative number back. After that, the loop makes garbage o

title: Cookies and Sessions
description: A cookie is a string that the client stores and sends back. All the rest is policy.
text: HTTP has no memory. Each request comes with no information about the requests before it. Because of this property, you can restart, replicate and load-balance a server, and no user sees a difference. A cookie is the smallest possible solution to this problem. The server sends Set-Cookie: session=abc, and the client sends Cookie: session=abc on each later request. That is the full mechanism. The server trusts a string that the client stores and can edit. Thus a session cookie holds an identifier , not information. If you put user=admin in a cookie, any person can log in as admin if they edit the cookie. The program What the program did The parse is a split on ;, then on =. There is no percent-decoding, because cookies have no encoding. Thus a value cannot contain a semicolon or a space. For this reason, session ids are hex. Hex never contains those characters, thus the problem does not occur. The parser ignored novalue. An item with no = is not a cookie. The parser removes the item, and it does not make an empty value. The second line kept its inner spaces. spaced = value gave the name spaced and the value value, with the spaces. The parser removes whitespace around each pair , not inside the pair. The grammar does not allow those spaces, and browsers never send them. Thus a strict rule here costs nothing. A parser that removes spaces inside the pair accepts input that a stricter parser later in the chain rejects. When two parsers do not agree about the same bytes, an attacker can use the difference. The program uses a fixed seed. Thus the output is the same on each build. A

title: When the Checks Are Off
description: What undefined behaviour is, and what each build mode promises.
headings: The one that depends on the build
text: The last chapter ended on a difficult fact: the program that you ran said that its safety checks were absent. The reason for this absence is the difference between systems programming and all the levels above it. A high-level language answers each question. If you read past the end of a list, Python raises IndexError. Python does this always, on each machine, in each configuration. This guarantee has a cost, and you pay the cost when you need the guarantee and when you do not. A systems language does not answer some questions, on purpose. This does not mean "answered in a way that you cannot predict". It means not answered . The specification says: if your program does this thing, the language makes no promise about what occurs next. The name for this is undefined behaviour . Undefined behaviour is not a special word for "crash" or for "garbage value". It is neither of these. Think of undefined behaviour as a promise that you made. When the language leaves integer overflow undefined, the language tells the compiler to assume that overflow never occurs. The compiler uses that assumption, because the assumption makes the generated code fast. The compiler can delete a check that you wrote, because your check can be true only in a situation that you promised would not occur. Thus undefined behaviour is worse than a wrong answer. A wrong answer stays in one place. A broken promise can change code in a different place. Zig uses this method: the checks exist, and for each build you decide if you pay for them. The program What just happened The program read its own build mode. Each

title: A Calling Convention
description: Where the arguments go, which side removes them, and how the machine returns to the caller.
text: The compiler and the VM stopped before functions. Calls are not difficult to implement. But to implement them, you must answer four questions that have no obvious answers. The set of answers is called a calling convention . 1. Where do the arguments go? 2. How does the callee find its own variables? 3. Where does the machine go when the function returns? 4. Which side removes the arguments after the call? Each question has more than one answer, and real machines make different choices. Code that uses one convention cannot call code that uses a different convention. Thus you cannot link a library that uses a different convention. The answers in this convention The caller pushes the arguments on the stack, in order. This answer is the oldest and the simplest. Real machines put the first few arguments in registers, because registers are faster. For example, the System V AMD64 ABI passes the first six integer arguments in rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9. A local is a slot that the code counts from the frame base. When a call starts, the base points at the first argument that the caller pushed. Thus parameter 0 is at base + 0. No code has to tell the callee where its arguments are, because the arguments are already on the stack at its base. No code copies the arguments. The call saves the return address. The instruction pointer already points past the call when the VM pushes the frame. Thus the save costs no extra work. The callee removes the arguments. On ret, the callee resets the top of the stack to the frame base, which discards the arguments. Then the callee pushes the result. T

title: make
description: A dependency graph, a topological order, and a comparison of timestamps.
text: People know make as a language with strange rules about tabs. Remove the syntax, and two small ideas remain. This chapter builds both ideas, so that the tool is easier to understand. The first idea: the targets make a graph. app needs main.o and util.o, and each object needs its .c file. To build in the correct order, visit a node only after all of the nodes that it depends on. That is a topological sort. The second idea: a timestamp decides if work occurs. A target is stale if one of its dependencies is newer than the target. Because of this one comparison, make is faster than a shell script that builds everything again. The program The stamps are in place of file modification times, and a higher stamp is newer. main.c is 30 and main.o is 20. Thus someone edited the source after the last build of the object. util.c is 10 and util.o is 20, so util.o is current. What just happened The build order put the objects before the binary. No line declared that order. The order is the result of two rules: visit the dependencies first, and append each target only on the return. This is depth-first post-order, and it is how you write a topological sort in code. Only main.o needed a new build. Its source is newer than main.o. util.o is newer than its source, so the program skipped util.o. Here, make saves time. On a large project, almost all targets are current, and the check costs one integer comparison for each target. The state array is the cycle check. The program marks each target 1 while it visits the dependencies of that target. It marks the target 2 when the visit is complete. I

title: A Template Engine
description: Substitution is the easy half. Escaping by default is the more difficult half.
text: Until now, each response was a string literal in Zig source. That method does not work for long. People must edit HTML without a new compile. Also, when a program makes a page from joined strings, the markup and the data are the same type of thing. A template engine keeps the markup and the data separate. The engine reads a file with holes in it, fills the holes, and sends the result. To fill the holes is a substring search, and you can write that code in an afternoon. The important part is what occurs when the value contains What the program did The script tag became harmless. The binding for name was alert('xss') , and the page got <script>.... A browser shows that text as text. Without escaping, a guest book runs the JavaScript of any person in the session of each visitor. That script can then use the session cookie from the last chapter. Escaping is the default. To stop escaping, you must type more. The engine escapes {{name}}, and it does not escape {{{banner}}}. You need an extra brace to turn off escaping. Thus the safe form is shorter to type. The dangerous form uses three braces, and three braces are easy to see in a code review. Template engines that made escaping opt- in all have lists of security vulnerabilities (CVEs). The engine escapes five characters, not three. &, are the obvious ones. The two quote characters are important because a value is not always in a text node. An attribute is a different context. In an attribute, a quote ends the attribute, and all text after the quote is markup. An escaper that handles only the first three characters is safe

title: Strings Are Bytes
description: Zig has no string type. A literal is bytes, with a zero at the end.
text: Chapter one said that everything is bytes. With text, that fact starts to have a cost. In the language that you know, a string is a thing. A string knows its length, and you can compare two strings with ==. When you ask for the length, you get the number of letters that you count with your eyes. A different person made all of that for you. In Zig, nobody made it. Zig has only a sequence of bytes. Thus Zig has the same question that C had to answer first. If you get the address of some text, how do you know where the text ends? C put a zero byte after the last character. This method costs little: one byte for each string, and a pointer is all that you must pass. But to find the length, the code must read all the text and look for the zero. If the zero is not there, the read does not stop at the end of the text. Zig keeps the zero for code that calls C, but Zig does not depend on it. The program What just happened The type printed as const [5:0]u8. Read it as: a pointer to an array of 5 bytes, with a sentinel 0 after them. The type does not say "a string". The type describes a specific number of specific bytes at a specific place. .len was 5, and the array was 6 bytes. The terminator is really there, and it uses memory, but the length does not count it, on purpose. Thus Zig knows the length without a search. Zig can also give the pointer to a C function that expects the zero. You get both answers to the question above, and you do not have to select one. The index gave 104, not 'h'. The two are the same byte. The memory stores 104, and 'h' is a way to print it. This fact is th

description: A format where the client selects the delimiter, and a filename that you cannot trust until you check it.
text:
Each other format in this section has a delimiter that the specification fixes. & separates query parameters, ; separates cookies, and

Thus the client selects a string, checks that the data does not contain the string, and announces the string: Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----zig42 The parser reads the delimiter from a header, and then searches for the delimiter. For this reason, the multipart parser is separate from the urlencoded parser. It is not a variation of the urlencoded parser. The program What the program did The body has two parts, and only one part is a file. Both parts come in the same way. The difference is a filename attribute in the Content-Disposition header. If the attribute is present, the part is a file. If the attribute is absent, the part is an ordinary field. A form can contain the two types together. Thus an upload handler is also a form handler. The photo is 9 bytes, not 11. The data is PNG
data, and the body has
