title: Structs Are Layout
description: Fields are next to each other in memory, and the size is not the sum of the parts.
text: When you put some values together under one name, you get a struct. In a managed language, that is all. At the level of the machine, there is a second part: the values must go to a place in memory, in some order. The machine has a preference about the place. The name of that preference is alignment . A processor reads memory in blocks. If a four-byte number starts at an address that is divisible by four, the processor can read the number in one operation. If the number goes across the boundary, the processor needs two reads and some extra instructions. On some processors, that read is not permitted. Thus the rule for a number is: the number starts at an address that is divisible by its own size. Apply that rule to a struct with fields of different sizes, and the result can be a surprise: the struct is larger than its fields . The name of the gaps that keep each field aligned is padding . You pay for the padding when you know about it and when you do not. The program What just happened Six bytes of data used twelve bytes. The fields are u8, u32 and u8. The offsets show the reason: flag at 0, count at 4 , tag at 8. count could not start at byte 1, because 1 is not divisible by 4. Thus three bytes are not used. Then the compiler adds padding at the end, and the struct becomes 12 bytes. Thus in an array of these structs, each count is also aligned. The same fields, with the largest first, used eight bytes. The struct lost no fields. count is at 0, flag at 4, tag at 5, and two bytes of padding are at the end. The order of the fields decides the size. In C, you alone must get the

title: What You Will Build
description: A chat room over WebSocket with only the standard library, and the four decisions that the next chapters make.
text: This project builds a chat room. A client connects over WebSocket and picks a nickname. Then each message that a member sends goes to each member of the room. When a member joins or leaves, the others see a notice. The server uses only the Zig standard library. It uses the parts from the four WebSocket chapters of Networking: The WebSocket Handshake: the server answers the upgrade with std.http.Server. WebSocket Frames: the header, the length forms and the mask. A WebSocket Client: the client in the last chapter of this project is that client, imported from its file. A WebSocket Server on a Socket: the gaps in std that this project must fill. Read those four first if WebSocket is new to you. The parts The server has four parts. Each part is one file, and each file is a snippet that CI compiles and runs: File What it does Runs where chat-protocol.zig Parses commands from clients and formats events for clients browser chat-hub.zig Keeps the members and copies each line into their outboxes browser chat-frames.zig Reads frames from a client, with fragments and close codes browser chat-server.zig Puts the parts on real sockets, with three clients native The first three files take bytes and return bytes. They never see a socket, thus their chapters run in your browser. The last file imports the other three and adds the sockets and the tasks. Four decisions A chat server looks simple: read a message, and send it to everybody. Four questions make it difficult, and each chapter answers one of them. 1. What does a message mean? WebSocket frames the bytes. It does not say what the byt

title: Binary Search
description: The half-open window, the invariant that keeps the window correct, and the two bounds that std already has.
text: Binary search is a small loop, but some details must be correct. One common mistake gives the wrong index. A different mistake makes the loop run forever. Both versions compile. Thus you must know exactly what each variable means. The program below prints each step of the search. Each line shows lo, hi, mid, the value at mid, and the part of the array that the search did not remove. The search window lo and hi give the part of the array that the search did not remove. This part is the search window. The range is half-open, items[lo..hi]. The window includes lo, but it does not include hi. At each step, the loop keeps one rule: each index that can be the answer stays inside the search window. The loop has two branches: If items[mid] The program calculates the midpoint as lo + (hi - lo) / 2. You can also see (lo + hi) / 2 in other code. The second form is shorter, but lo + hi can overflow if the two values are sufficiently large. The first form does not have this problem. The overflow is more probable with small integer types and very large arrays. lo + (hi - lo) / 2 is the safer form, and the cost is only one subtraction. The off-by-one bug A common mistake is to write lo = mid instead of lo = mid + 1. At first, lo = mid can look correct. If mid is too small, the answer is not before mid. But mid also cannot be the answer. Thus the loop must remove mid from the search window. If the loop keeps mid, the loop can stop progress. When hi - lo becomes 1, integer division gives mid == lo. Then lo = mid does not change a value. The next iteration gets the same values again. step 3

title: Async, Future and Group
description: async, Future, and Group, all through the Io interface.
headings: async can run a task inline, and concurrent cannot
Shared state still needs a lock
text: Concurrency in Zig now goes through std.Io. The Io Interface explains that interface, and this section expects you to know it. Each chapter here takes an Io and gives it to the functions that it calls. Press Run. The program runs in your browser, on a target with no threads . io.async returns a Future var first = io.async(slowDouble, .{ &a, 10 }); var second = io.async(slowDouble, .{ &b, 20 }); first.await(io); second.await(io); The Io implementation decides the meaning of "async". A threaded implementation runs these calls in parallel. The single-threaded WASI implementation runs them inline. Your code does not change. For this reason, you can run this page, and you cannot run the Threads page. async can run a task inline, and concurrent cannot io.async promises only one thing: the result is ready after you await it. io.async can call the function immediately, complete it, and return a Future that is already resolved. On this page, that occurs. io.concurrent makes a stronger promise: the caller continues while the task runs. Not all Io implementations can keep that promise. Thus io.concurrent returns an error union: if (io.concurrent(slowDouble, .{ &c, 30 })) handle { var pending = handle; pending.await(io); } else err { // error.ConcurrencyUnavailable } The snippet above prints concurrent: ConcurrencyUnavailable. The single-threaded wasm that runs the snippet has no second unit of concurrency to give. If you give the same binary an Io.Threaded, it prints concurrent: 60. The difference has an effect on correctness, not on performance. If a task must make progress before yo

description: Three ways to read a file, and what each one does when the file is larger than you expect.

A file that does not exist
If you used an older version of Zig
text: Zig has three common ways to read a file: readFileAlloc reads the full file into new memory. readFile reads the file into a buffer that you supply. openFile gives you a handle. Then you decide how to read from the handle. Each of the three functions needs a size limit. The functions are different in two ways: where the limit comes from, and what occurs when the file is larger than the limit. The program below uses the three functions on the same 18-byte file. A newline follows each line. The three lines are 6 + 1, 5 + 1 and 4 + 1 bytes, thus the file is 18 bytes. Read the full file readFileAlloc opens the file, reads all of the file, closes the file and returns the bytes. The memory comes from the allocator that you give to the function. Free the memory with the same allocator. The last argument is a limit, and the limit is necessary. No version of this function reads a quantity of data that has no limit. A file can be of any size. title: A Game You Can Test
description: A three lane endless runner that you can play here, and the one rule that lets you test the rest.
headings: One rule makes the tests possible
text: Press Play. To change lane, use the arrow keys or A and D. Space starts a run. M stops the sound. The game has three lanes. Blocks move toward you. Coins add to the score. The game becomes faster until you lose. A run lasts approximately half a minute. Games are difficult to test The behaviour of a game is inside a loop. The loop reads the keyboard, sends commands to a GPU and runs sixty times each second. A test must not contain any of these three things. Thus most small games have no tests. The developer plays the game and adjusts it. The difficulty becomes the level that the developer could play that week. This game has fifty-five tests. No test needs a window. One rule makes the tests possible The rules of the game are in one module. That module does not import raylib, a library for windows, or a clock. The module never allocates. It changes a seed and a list of inputs into a list of states. All other code reads from that state. The renderer draws the world. The audio code plays a note when an event occurs. The renderer and the audio code cannot change the result of a run. The networking chapters use the same design. Their protocol code parses from a Reader and not from a socket. If code runs only inside the full program, nobody tests that code. What the tests do A bot plays the course for four minutes of game time at each seed. The bot must never crash. If the generator can make a row that nobody can pass, this test finds the row. The test also found a bug in the bot. The bot steered into blocks whose centres were behind the player but whose bodies were not. The same b

title: Assignment
description: const by default, and var only when you must change the value.
headings: Use const unless you must change the value
const is about the binding, not the contents
The compiler infers types, but literals have no size
undefined is a promise, not a value
text: Zig has two ways to declare a value. The default is the immutable one. Use const unless you must change the value const is not a hint. The compiler enforces it. A new assignment to a const is a compile error. A var that you never change is also a compile error. If you know C, the second rule can surprise you. Because of this rule, a var in Zig always means this value changes . This rule helps when you read code that you do not know. For each const, you can find its single assignment and stop. For each var, you must follow all of its changes. Some languages use var as the default and allow a var that never changes. In those languages, the difference gives no information, because most variables are var only from habit. The same rule applies to unused declarations. They are errors, not warnings. Zig has no lint level to change here. If the code does not use a variable now, the code does not build until you remove the variable. const is about the binding, not the contents A const slice or pointer prevents a new assignment to the variable. It does not prevent a write through the slice or pointer: const items = try allocator.alloc(u8, 4); items[0] = 1; // fine: items still points at the same memory items = other; // error: cannot assign to constant The element type controls the write. You cannot write through a []const u8. You can write through a []u8, and the const or var of the variable does not change this. These are two separate questions. The answer to one question tells you nothing about the other question. Pointers has the same split for T. The compiler infers types, but l

title: Know What the Compiler Knows
description: The rule that decides which values the compiler can use, and four ways to use them.
headings: A runtime value where a type must go
The caller decides where a function runs
A comptime parameter in the return type
text: Each value in a Zig program is one of two kinds: A comptime-known value is a value that the compiler knows during compilation. A runtime-known value is a value that only the program knows when it runs. Some places in the language accept only comptime-known values. An array length, a type and a comptime parameter are three of these places. Thus you must know which kind each value is. Comptime in Language Basics gives the idea in one page. This section starts at that point. const and var The first part of the program declares two values: const width = 8; var height: u32 = 3; The output shows their types: 1. width: comptime int, height: u32 width is a const with a literal value. The compiler knows the value, and the type is comptime int. A comptime int has no fixed size. It becomes a sized integer when you use it in a place that needs one. height is a var. The program never changes it, but the compiler does not use that fact. A var is runtime-known, always. A const is not always comptime-known. const n = readNumber(); is a const, but the value comes from a function that runs when the program runs. The rule is about the source of the value, not about the keyword. A runtime value where a type must go width is comptime-known, thus [width]u8 is a valid type. The program uses it for a row of 8 characters. The next program tries the same thing with a var: The length of an array is part of its type, and the compiler must know each type. A var cannot supply a value to a type. To repair the program, use one of these two changes: Change var to const, if the value is a literal. Use a sli

title: What a Socket Is
description: An address, a mode, and a handle that you read and write like a file.
headings: Port 0 tells the kernel to select a port
After the connection, the code does not use sockets
text: A socket is a file descriptor with an address. That is almost the full definition. When two sockets have a connection, all the work uses the reader and writer interface from Readers and Writers. A file uses the same interface. An address is data IpAddress.parse does not use the network. It opens nothing and sends nothing. It fails only if the text is not an address. No network action occurs until you call listen, bind or connect. const wanted = try std.Io.net.IpAddress.parse("127.0.0.1", 0); Port 0 tells the kernel to select a port If you ask for port 0, the kernel gives the socket a free port when it binds the socket. The socket records the port in server.socket.address. A test that uses a fixed port such as 8080 can fail in three conditions: Two copies of the test run at the same time. The server from the last run is still active. A different program on the computer already uses port 8080. Each snippet in this section binds port 0 and reads the port that it gets. Thus all of the snippets can run on the same CI computer at the same time. Stream or datagram var client = try bound.connect(io, .{ .mode = .stream }); .stream is TCP. TCP keeps the bytes in order, is reliable, and uses a connection. .dgram is UDP, and UDP has none of these three properties. UDP Datagrams, at the end of this section, gives more information about UDP. You select the mode one time, on the socket. Each difference between the two protocols comes from that mode. After the connection, the code does not use sockets var writer = client.writer(io, &write buf); try writer.interface.writeAll("ping\n"); try

title: What Is an Ecto-Style ORM?
description: The Elixir design that these chapters copy, explained for readers who never wrote Elixir.
headings: Why this maps so well to Zig
Where each idea lives in this group
text: This group builds a small ORM in the style of Ecto , the database library of Elixir. Most readers here never wrote Elixir. Thus this page explains that style, and the reasons to copy it, before the next chapters build it in Zig. The idea in one sentence Ecto divides database work into parts that are plain data and pure functions. Each real database operation goes through one explicit gateway, the Repo . What that looks like In Ecto, an application defines a schema, builds queries as values, and gives the queries to the Repo: Elixir (Ecto), for flavor only defmodule User do schema "users" do field :name, :string field :age, :integer end end query = from u in User, where: u.age 18 adults = Repo.all(query) These lines contain three separate ideas: 1. The schema is a declaration , not a class with behavior. It gives the shape of a row and nothing more. 2. A query is a value. When you build a query, no SQL runs. You can compose the query, give it to other functions, and examine it. The query touches the database only when you give it to the Repo. 3. The Repo is the only gateway. There is no user.save(). Records do not know how to save themselves. One object owns the connection, and all operations go through that object. Why this maps so well to Zig Each of these ideas matches a Zig feature closely: Ecto idea Zig mechanism --- --- schema as declaration a plain struct, read by @typeInfo at compile time query as a value a builder struct; a chain is functions that return the struct Repo as the gateway Repo(Adapter), a type function with one stateful field validations on the schema a

title: A File Descriptor Is a Number
description: Each thing that the operating system gives you to read or write is an integer.
text: Open a file, accept a connection, or create a pipe. Each of these operations gives you a small non-negative integer, and you hold only that integer. Your side has no object. The kernel keeps one table for each process, and the number is an index into that table. Each later call identifies the thing that you opened, because you give the number back to the call. Press Run. What a File is handle: Handle, flags: Flags, pub const Handle = std.posix.fd t; This is the full declaration of std.Io.File in the standard library, without its methods. A File is a descriptor and one bit. The bit tells if the file was opened non-blocking. On all POSIX targets and on WASI, fd t is i32. On Windows, fd t is a HANDLE. For this reason, the declaration uses the name of the type and does not write out the type. The struct holds nothing more. Thus you can build a File from a raw number, and the operation needs no cast: const by hand: std.Io.File = .{ .handle = 1, .flags = .{ .nonblocking = false } }; That value and std.Io.File.stdout() are the same eight bytes. When you write through either value, the bytes go to the same place. The three that you get A process starts with descriptors 0, 1 and 2 already open. No code in your program opened them. The shell, or the parent process, prepared them before your first instruction ran: Number Name Convention --- --- --- 0 standard input where the program reads from 1 standard output where its results go 2 standard error where its diagnostics go The numbers are a convention. But the kernel and all programs agree on the convention, so in practice the convent

title: A Paint Program You Can Test
description: A paint program that you can use on this page, and the one rule that lets tests check each brush.
headings: The same pixels in all builds
Explain before you read the answer
text: Press Start painting and draw. You can use a mouse or a finger. If your pen has pressure, the line is thicker when you push harder. Try the Calligraphy brush. Lines in one direction are thin, and lines across them are wide. Draw on the bottom layer. Then select the top layer, draw again, and erase there. Where you erase, you see the bottom layer. One rule The program has two parts: The engine calculates the value of each pixel. The engine is about 2,100 lines of Zig, and about 1,050 more lines of tests. The front end changes mouse and pen events into calls to the engine. Then it copies the pixels from the engine to the canvas. The rule is that the engine never sees a mouse, a window or a clock. Points go in, and pixels come out. The main type of the engine is a document. A document holds the layers, the current stroke, the history, and the data for the screen: A front end calls a small number of methods on the document. A stroke is one beginStroke call, some moveStroke calls, and one endStroke call. Each call takes a point: an x, a y and a pressure. After these calls, render updates display and returns the rectangle that changed. The front end copies that rectangle to the screen. The front end does nothing more. What the rule gives you The engine needs no window. Thus a test can draw. A test can start a stroke, move it, end it, and then examine the pixels. This test makes sure that a stroke looks the same while you draw it and after you release the pointer: There are 80 tests of this type, and no test opens a window. title: Errors Are Values
description: Zig has no exception mechanism below your program. Thus a failure must be part of the value that a function returns.
text: In a higher-level language, a failure has a place to go. You raise or throw an exception. Then code that you did not write unwinds the calls between your code and the code that can handle the failure. This method works because a runtime monitors the program. In Zig, nothing monitors the program. No runtime is under your program to catch anything, and the machine does not know what an exception is. Thus a failure must move in the same way as each other result: as a value, in the return. Then one question decides if the language is easy to use: what stops the caller when it ignores the failure? The answer decides if the errors of a language work in practice. If code that ignores a failure is shorter than code that handles it, programmers ignore it. Then the program continues with a number that means "this did not occur". Zig puts the failure in the type . A function that can fail does not return a u16. It returns "a u16 or an error", and these are different types. You cannot use the u16 before you say what occurs in the error case. Until you do, you do not have a u16. The program What just happened The return type is !u16. The ! means "a u16 or an error". The caller receives one value in one of two states. The language does not let you use the value as a number until you handle the other state. if separated the two states. if (parsePort(text)) port ... else err gives a port to the success branch and an err to the failure branch. Neither branch can see the value of the other branch. At no time does a variable hold a result that the function did not make. try is the short way t

title: What You Will Build
description: A URL shortener with real storage, and the two decisions that control all the chapters after this one.
headings: One request, from start to end
What this project does not include
text: A URL shortener works like this: you give it a long address, and it gives you a short address. When a person follows the short address, the person gets to the long address. A URL shortener is a common first service. It is small enough to complete. But it needs all the parts that a larger service needs: a database, a schema, validation, and an HTTP surface with all four verbs. The completed service has five routes: Route Action Operation --- --- --- POST /links shorten a URL, answer with the slug Create GET /{slug} redirect, and count the hit Read GET /links/{slug} report target and hit count Read PUT /links/{slug} point the slug to a different target Update DELETE /links/{slug} retire the slug Delete The storage is PostgreSQL, with one table: CREATE TABLE links ( id bigserial PRIMARY KEY, slug text UNIQUE NOT NULL, target text NOT NULL, hits bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 ); The design Each chapter in this project builds one box in this diagram, from the bottom to the top: Browser / curl │ ▼ HTTP Server │ ▼ Routes ──────────► Slug logic │ ▼ Store │ ▼ Postgres Client │ TCP socket │ ▼ PostgreSQL The diagram has two halves: All the boxes above Store are about HTTP: what a request means, and what to answer. All the boxes below Store are about Postgres: how to send the query, and how to read the answer. Store is the line between the two halves. Because of Store, most of this code runs without a network. One request, from start to end This service uses no JSON. The body of a POST is the URL, and the answer is the slug. Thus the parsing stays in the chapters that are about parsing. cur

title: Arrays
description: Fixed-length sequences whose length is part of the type.
text: You write an array as [N]T. The length N is part of the type . Thus [3]u8 and [4]u8 are as different as u8 and u16. Arrays are values When you assign an array, Zig copies the array. C does the opposite: in almost all expressions, a C array changes into a pointer. If you want a reference, take one explicitly with &. The result is a slice. .len is a compile-time constant. The program does not read it from a field at runtime. An array is a value. Thus, when you give a [4096]u8 to a function, the compiler can pass all 4096 bytes. When you give &buffer, the call passes a slice, which is a pointer and a length. For data that is larger than a few words, pass the slice. Write an array literal With [ ]T, the compiler counts the elements for you. Use this form, because then the length always agrees with the contents: const a = [ ]u8{ 1, 2, 3 }; // [3]u8 const grid = [2][3]u8{ // rows of columns .{ 1, 2, 3 }, .{ 4, 5, 6 }, }; Multidimensional arrays are arrays of arrays. Thus grid[1][2] is 6, and grid.len is 2, the number of rows. Zig has no separate matrix type, and no index syntax with commas. Compare and join arrays == does not work on arrays: error: operator == not allowed for type '[3]u8' Zig does not make a silent selection between a comparison of the contents and a comparison of the addresses. To compare the contents, use std.mem.eql(u8, &a, &b). This function takes slices. Thus it also compares an array with a slice of a larger buffer. ++ joins arrays at compile time. The result is an array, and its length is the sum of the two lengths: const joined = a ++ [ ]u8{ 4 }; // [4]u8

title: Talk to the Operating System
description: Your program gets streams that it did not open, and it must return a status.
text: Each chapter before this one was about the inside of your program: its bytes, its memory and its failures. This chapter is about the edge, because a program cannot do anything from the inside alone. A program cannot read a file, write to your terminal or open a connection. It can only calculate. For each operation that goes outside the program, the program asks the operating system. The name of that request is a system call . Your program stops. The kernel does the operation, with privileges that your program does not have. Then control returns to your program with a result. That is the boundary, and all I/O goes across it. The arrangement has three parts. It is older than almost all the other tools that you use, and it did not change: The operating system gives your program some things when the program starts. The program does not ask for them. Your program asks for all other things by number. It uses a small integer, not a name, to refer to each thing that it opened. When the program ends, it gives back one number. The operating system guarantees only that number to the parent process. The program What just happened Three streams were already open. The program did not open them, and it cannot select their numbers. Descriptor 0 is standard input, 1 is standard output, and 2 is standard error. This is true for each process on each system that comes from Unix. A shell uses this fact to connect two programs, and the two programs do not have to agree on anything first. A descriptor is an integer and nothing else. A descriptor is not a handle object with methods inside it. It i

title: If Expressions
description: No truthiness: if takes a bool.
text: In Zig, if is a control-flow statement. It is also an expression that can give a value. C, JavaScript and most other languages have truthy and falsy values. Zig does not. The condition must be a bool, and no other type converts to bool. Zig also has no ternary ?:. An if that you use as an expression does that job: const x = if (a) 1 else 2;. Zig has no truthiness. if (1) does not compile, and if (pointer) does not compile. The condition must be a bool: error: expected type 'bool', found 'u8' This rule removes a full family of bugs, where code uses a value as a flag by accident. Some examples from C: if (strcmp(a, b)) is true when the strings are different . if (n = 0) is an assignment, and it is always false. if (ptr) and if ( ptr) have one character of difference, but their meanings are completely different. None of these examples parse in Zig. if gives a value Zig has no ternary operator, because it does not need one: const x: u16 = if (a) 1 else 2; The two branches must have the same type. When you use if as an expression, the else is necessary. Without the else, the absent branch gives void, and the error gives the name of that type: error: expected type 'u16', found 'void' An if with no else has no value when the condition is false. Thus its type is void. Read the message as "this expression does not always give a value". One case gets past this rule: a condition that the compiler knows. If the compiler knows the condition at comptime, it compiles only the branch that runs. Thus const x: u16 = if (true) 1; builds. If you make the condition a runtime value, the build fa

title: While Loops
description: Conditions, continue expressions, and loops that produce values.
headings: Loop until there are no more values
text: The counting loop in Zig is while (i while takes a condition, and runs the body until the condition becomes false. Zig has no C-style for (init; cond; step). A while with a continue expression is that loop. Zig uses for only for a value that has elements. The continue expression while (i 20) break i; } else 0; This code is a search with a fallback, as one expression. It needs no sentinel variable, and you cannot forget the "not found" case. Loops as expressions gives the rules, and the error that the compiler gives when there is no else. Infinite loops while (true) is the usual infinite loop, and the compiler knows that it cannot end normally. When you use it as an expression, it needs no else, because break is the only exit. Use while (true) when the code decides the exit condition in the middle of the body, not at the top. This is usual for code that reads input until it sees a terminator. Give the loop a name A while can have a label. Thus break :outer and continue :outer work on it exactly as they do on for. See labelled loops. That chapter also explains one rule that can surprise you: a labelled continue still runs the continue expression of that loop.

title: For Loops
description: Iterate over sequences and ranges, never over a bare counter.
headings: You get an index only when you ask
for can also break and give a value
text: In Zig, for loops over a slice, an array or a range. To get the index, add a second sequence to the loop: for (items, 0..) item, index . Zig has no for with three clauses, such as for (i = 0; i 0) { i -= 1; use(items[i]); } The decrement comes first for a reason. items.len is a usize. A loop with while (i = 0) : (i -= 1) never stops, because an unsigned counter cannot go below zero. In a safety build, the loop panics on the wraparound instead, thus you see the problem. Zig accepts this cost on purpose. The forward loop cannot make this mistake. When you iterate backwards, you must control the index yourself again. for can also break and give a value break, continue, labels and else work here exactly as they work on while. A for that you use as an expression gives a value with break x. It needs an else for the case where no elements remain. Thus a linear search is a single expression. See loops as expressions and labelled loops. inline for unrolls the loop at compile time, and the compiler knows the capture at comptime. Thus a loop can visit the fields of a struct or the tags of an enum. inline for is a different tool with a different purpose. Inline loops explains it.

title: Functions
description: Immutable parameters and explicit discards.
headings: The compiler decides how to pass arguments
text: Zig function parameters are constant. If a function returns a value that is not void, and you do not use the value, the result is a compile error. Thus you write a discard explicitly: = addFive(1);. Parameters are constant For example, this code does not compile: fn addFive(x: u32) u32 { x += 5; // error: cannot assign to constant return x; } If you want a mutable local, make one. The benefit is that a parameter always has the value from the call site, through all of the function body. In a long function, x on line 60 is the x that the caller gave. You do not have to read the 59 lines above to be sure. To let the function change a value of the caller, take a pointer, and write the pointer in the type: fn addFiveInPlace(x: u32) void { x. += 5; } Now the change is visible at the call site as addFiveInPlace(&n). Zig has no reference parameters that write to the caller without a visible sign. The compiler decides how to pass arguments A parameter is a value. But the compiler decides if it copies the value or passes a pointer to it. The compiler uses the type and the calling convention of the target to decide. When you pass a large struct, the compiler does not always copy it. Parameters are immutable. Thus the code inside the function cannot see which method the compiler used, and the compiler can use either method. Unused values are errors Zig has no "unused variable" warning , because an unused variable is an error: error: value of type 'u32' ignored note: all non-void values must be used A discard is explicit: = addFive(1); This rule finds the case where you called a functio

title: The Io Interface
description: Each operation that can block takes an Io. The caller selects how the Io works.
headings: If you used an older version of Zig
text: Modern Zig has one idea in all of its standard library. Each operation that can block takes an std.Io parameter. Examples are a file read, a socket open, a sleep, and a clock read. Nothing blocks secretly, as nothing allocates secretly. If the signature of a function has no Io, the function cannot do I/O. What Io is std.Io is an interface: a pointer and a vtable. This is exactly the shape of std.mem.Allocator. The vtable holds function pointers for the primitive operations: read, write, wait and schedule. A concrete implementation supplies these pointers. The standard implementation is std.Io.Threaded, and a real thread pool is behind it. Choose an Io tells you about the other implementations, and when to change to one of them. The allocator uses the same dependency-injection pattern for memory, and Io uses it for blocking. For this reason, this chapter is next to Allocators. When you know the two interfaces, you know the pattern of most of the standard library. The source of an Io You almost never make an Io yourself. The Io arrives at the top of your program, and you pass it down to the functions that need it: Context The Io that you use --- --- main init.io, a field on the std.process.Init that main receives A test std.testing.io A library function the Io that the caller gives you: take io: std.Io A function that must block does not use a global value. It accepts an Io, and it gives the Io to the calls that block. For this reason, std.Io.Dir.readFile, std.Io.Clock.Timestamp.now and Io.Mutex.lock all take an Io as their first argument. The reason for one interface Each I/

title: Defer
description: Cleanup code that runs on each path out of a scope.
headings: The order of defer and the return value
errdefer for the failure path only
If you know C++ or Rust
text: In Zig, you write cleanup code with defer. Put the release on the line below the acquisition. When the scope exits, the deferred statements run in reverse order. errdefer does the same, but only when the function returns an error. The scope is the block around the defer, not the full function. Each path out of the block counts: The end of the block. An early return. An error that try returns to the caller. The reverse order is necessary Deferred statements run in reverse order. The last statement that you register runs first. If you acquire A and then B, the cleanup releases B and then A. This is almost always the correct order. Write the release directly below the acquisition. Then you can see the two lines together: const buf = try allocator.alloc(u8, n); defer allocator.free(buf); The release is on the next line. Thus, to check an allocation for a leak, you read one line. You do not have to search for the free that matches it lower in the function. The scope is the block A defer inside a loop body runs at the end of each iteration . It does not wait until the function returns: var n: u32 = 0; for (0..3) { defer n += 1; } // n == 3 Go is different here. In Go, defer has function scope. Thus the deferred calls in a loop collect until the function ends, and Go gives no warning. In Zig, if you open a file inside a loop and defer its close, the file closes on each pass. Thus the loop cannot use all of the descriptors. Because of this rule, a bare block is also a way to put a tight limit on a cleanup: { const lock = mutex.acquire(); defer lock.release(); // held only inside th

title: Errors
description: Errors are values in a union, not exceptions.
headings: Four ways to handle an error
Find where an error comes from
Why error unions are better than exceptions
text: Zig has no exceptions. A function that can fail returns an error union . You write it as E!T. The value is an error from the set E, or a T. Error sets are types const FileOpenError = error{ AccessDenied, OutOfMemory, FileNotFound }; A narrow set coerces into a wider set. Thus a function that returns FileOpenError can call a function that returns error{OutOfMemory}, and it needs no extra code. anyerror is the set of all errors. It is convenient, but it removes the list of possible errors. That list is the reason that error sets are useful. You combine sets with . A function that calls two subsystems uses to declare that it can fail in the two ways: const Error = ParseError std.Io.Reader.Error; If you write !T with no set, the compiler infers the set from each error that the body can make. Inside a program, this is the correct default. At the public boundary of a library, it is the wrong default. The inferred set is part of your interface, and the set changes without a warning when the body changes. An error is only a value with a name. It does not contain a payload, a message or a stack trace. Thus you can compare errors, use them in a switch, and return them at no cost. When a failure needs detail, put the detail in a place where the caller can ask for it. Do not put it into the error. Four ways to handle an error Form Meaning --- --- try x unwrap, or return the error to my caller x catch fallback unwrap, or use this value instead x catch \ err\ { ... } unwrap, or handle the error here if (x) \ v\ ... else \ err\ ... branch on both outcomes try is the most common form, and

title: Switch
description: Exhaustive by construction.
headings: A switch can have a label
text: In Zig, switch can match single values, lists such as 10, 100, and inclusive ranges such as -1...1. You can also use switch as an expression, and put its value directly into a const. The Zig switch has no fallthrough, and it must be exhaustive . Each possible value needs a branch, or the program does not compile. Because there is no fallthrough, an arm does not need a break at its end. Thus there is no bug from a break that you forgot. An arm for many values lists the values. In C, that was the usual reason to use fallthrough. Ranges and lists of values switch (x) { 1...1 = ..., // inclusive range 10, 100 = ..., // several values, one branch else = ..., } A ... range includes the two ends. The .. range in a for does not include the upper bound. The difference is intentional, and it is easy to make a mistake with it: 0..3 in a for gives three values, and 0...3 in a switch matches four. Cases must not overlap. If two arms can match the same value, the code does not compile. There is no rule that the first match wins. Thus the order of the arms never changes the behaviour. A statement or an expression The snippet has the two forms: In a statement, each arm does an action. In an expression, each arm produces a value, and the full switch has that value. const y: i8 = switch (x) { 1...1 = -x, 10, 100 = @divExact(x, 10), else = 0, }; Use the expression form where possible, for the same reason as loops as expressions. The result goes directly into a const, and each arm must produce a value. The benefit of exhaustiveness When you switch over an enum and cover each tag, do not write

title: Runtime Safety
description: Checked illegal behaviour, and where the checks go.
headings: Safety depends on the build mode
text: Zig inserts runtime checks for a group of mistakes that C leaves undefined. Examples are an out-of-bounds index, integer overflow, an invalid cast, and the unwrap of a null optional. When a check fails, the program panics with a clear message. It does not silently read the next data in memory. Press Run . The program reads index 5 of an array that has three elements: panic: index out of bounds: index 5, len 3 The message gives the index that the program used and the length that was the limit. The std.debug.print on the next line never runs, and the program reads no memory outside the array. In C, the same three lines produce a number. The number depends on the data that is in memory after the array. Integer overflow Arithmetic gets the same treatment. This program adds 1 to a u8 that holds 255: panic: integer overflow C gives you 0 here, without a message, and the bug then causes a problem in a different part of the program. Zig stops at the line that is wrong. Plain + does not guess if you want the value to wrap. A wrap is correct in a hash function or a checksum. Thus Zig gives the wrap a different operator, and the choice is visible where you write the operation: +% wraps. + saturates at the limit of the type. @addWithOverflow returns the wrapped value and a flag that tells if an overflow occurred. All three have a defined result in each build mode, because you asked for that behaviour. Plain + means "this operation must not overflow, and tell me if it does". A null optional .? on an optional is an assertion, not a conversion. It says that the value is not null. When the

title: The Protocol
description: Commands in, events out. A text protocol inside WebSocket messages, a tagged union for each direction, and a line size that the compiler checks.
headings: Commands: parse into a tagged union
Events: format into a fixed line
text: WebSocket delivers messages with clear edges. One message is one frame, or one set of fragments, and the receiver gets the whole message. Thus this protocol needs no delimiter and no length prefix, unlike the protocols in Three Ways to Frame. The protocol only says what the bytes in one message mean. The protocol has two directions: A client sends commands : nick tejas to pick a name, and say hello to talk. The server sends events : welcome, joined, left, msg and error. Text is easy to read in a trace and easy to type into a test client. A binary protocol would be smaller, and a chat line is small already. Commands: parse into a tagged union The result is a Command, a tagged union with one field for each verb. The code after the parser uses a switch, and the compiler requires a case for each verb. If you add a verb, each switch that forgets it fails to compile. commands from a client: nick tejas - nick "tejas" say hello, room - say "hello, room" say two spaces - say " two spaces" nick Tejas - error.BadNick nick aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa - error.BadNick say - error.MissingArgument (long input) - error.TextTooLong shout hello - error.UnknownCommand error.UnknownCommand Three rules in the parser are deliberate: The text of say is exact. The parser splits at the first space only. say two spaces keeps the second space as the first byte of the text. A nickname is lowercase letters, digits and , 16 bytes or fewer. Each event prints the nickname, thus a nickname with a space or a colon could make a msg event look like a different event. Text has a limit of 120 bytes. The next section shows

title: Two Pointers
description: Two indices that start at opposite ends, and the argument that tells which index must move.
headings: Use the same method for a palindrome
text: The input is a sorted array and a target sum. The task is to find two values with a sum that is equal to the target. One method is to try each possible pair. That method takes O(n²) time. For an array with 100,000 values, the number of comparisons is much too large. The values are in ascending order. Thus a better method is possible: 1. Put one index at the start and a second index at the end. 2. Add the two values. 3. Use the result to move one of the indices toward the center. Each step removes one value from the search. The trace below shows each step. Marks show the two active indices. A dot shows a position that the search removed. Decide which pointer moves lo and hi mark the part of the array that the search did not remove. The current range is items[lo..hi + 1]. The search removed each value outside this range. At each step, the loop calculates items[lo] + items[hi]. There are three possible cases: If the sum is equal to the target, the loop has the answer. If the sum is smaller than the target, lo must move. If the sum is larger than the target, hi must move. When the sum is too small, look at items[hi]. It is the largest value in the range that can be a pair with items[lo]. If that pair is too small, no other value in the range can make a sufficiently large sum with items[lo]. Thus items[lo] cannot be part of the answer. The loop removes it with lo += 1. When the sum is too large, look at items[lo]. It is the smallest value in the range that can be a pair with items[hi]. If that pair is already too large, each other possible partner for items[hi] gives an equal or

title: Cancellation
description: How to stop a task that runs, and the cancellation points that make it possible.
headings: cancel is await plus a request
A cancellation point is a call on Io
A Group cancels as a whole
Use concurrent for a task that you intend to cancel
Cancellation is why lock can fail
text: Sometimes you must stop a task that you started. For example, the client closed the connection, the timeout occurred, or the user pressed Ctrl-C. In Zig, cancellation is a request. It does not kill the task. You send the request, and the task gets the request at its next cancellation point . cancel is await plus a request var sleeping = try io.concurrent(nap, .{io}); if (sleeping.cancel(io)) { ... } else err { ... } Future.cancel blocks until the task is done, exactly like await. Then it returns the value that the task returned. The difference is that cancel first asks the task to stop. Thus a cancelled task still runs its defer statements and releases its resources. The task always stops before the runtime removes its stack. If you cancel a task that is already complete, the result is not an error. The task has no cancellation point left to reach. Thus cancel only returns the result. cancel and await are both idempotent, and neither is threadsafe. A cancellation point is a call on Io The task gets the request at the next call on its Io that can return error.Canceled. Examples are a sleep, a read, a lock and an accept. That is the rule, and the rule has a result: fn count(io: std.Io, counter: u64) std.Io.Cancelable!void { while (true) { try io.checkCancel(); counter. += 1; } } Pure computation calls nothing on Io. Thus it has no cancellation point, and you cannot cancel it. If you delete the checkCancel above, the loop runs forever, and the task never gets the request. io.checkCancel adds a cancellation point to code that has no other one. A long computation loop needs one.

title: Pointers
description: Single-item pointers that are never null.
headings: Alignment is part of the type
Get the address as a number
text: A T refers to exactly one T. Use & to get an address. Use . to dereference the pointer. . is a postfix operator, so a chain of operations reads from left to right, as field access does. Exactly one A T is not a cursor into a sequence, and it has no pointer arithmetic: p + 1 does not compile. Code that moves through memory needs a type that tells how much memory there is. Thus there are three types. In Zig, the main purpose of pointer types is to help you select the correct one: Type Means --- --- T one T, and only one [ ]T many T, count unknown, arithmetic allowed []T many T, count carried alongside Usually, use []T. It is a pointer and a length together. Thus an index into it can have a bounds check. You cannot forget the length, because the length is part of the value. [ ]T is for the C boundary, where the count is in a different place or in a sentinel. See slices and many-item pointers. Never null A T cannot be null. If a pointer can be absent, its type says so: ? T. The compiler enforces this rule. It does not let you dereference the optional before you unwrap it. The representation has no cost. Zig uses the null address as the null tag. Thus ? T has the same size as T. The result is that "did I check this pointer for null" is a question about the type, not about the code: A function that takes T cannot receive nothing. A function that takes ? T cannot use the pointer before it says what occurs for null. There is no third case, where the two types have the same syntax and one of them is a bug. Constness stays with the pointer &some const gives you a const T, and you can

title: Build Lookup Tables
description: The compiler calculates a CRC-32 table, and the program checks it against the standard library.
text: A lookup table replaces a calculation with an array read. You calculate each answer one time and keep the answers in an array. Then the program reads the answer for an input from the array. In many languages, you calculate the table with a separate script and paste the numbers into the source. In Zig, the compiler calculates the table from usual Zig code. The source keeps the calculation, and the binary keeps only the numbers. This chapter builds the table for CRC-32. CRC-32 is the checksum in Zip files, PNG files and Ethernet frames. The program then compares its results with std.hash.Crc32. The calculation without a table CRC-32 processes the input one bit at a time. For each bit, it does one shift and one conditional xor with a constant, the polynomial 0xEDB88320. A byte has 8 bits, thus each byte of input costs 8 steps. The result of the 8 steps depends only on one byte. A byte has 256 possible values. Thus there are only 256 possible results, and a table can hold all of them. Build the table const table: [256]u32 = blk: { @setEvalBranchQuota(256 8 + 256); var t: [256]u32 = undefined; for (&t, 0..) entry, byte { var c: u32 = @intCast(byte); for (0..8) { c = if (c & 1 != 0) poly ^ (c 1) else c 1; } entry. = c; } break :blk t; }; table is a const at the top level of the file. The compiler always calculates a top-level const during compilation. Thus this block does not need the comptime keyword. The output shows the first entries: table: 256 entries, 1024 bytes table[0] = 0x00000000 table[1] = 0x77073096 table[2] = 0xee0e612c table[3] = 0x990951ba The table in the zlib sou

title: A TCP Round Trip
description: Listen, connect, and echo through std.Io.net, all in one process.
headings: One interface for sockets and files
text: In current Zig, a TCP server uses three calls: std.Io.net.IpAddress.parse, then address.listen(io, .{}), then server.accept(io). A TCP client uses addr.connect(io, .{ .mode = .stream }). The reader of a connected stream is the same std.Io.Reader that you use for files. The problem You want a TCP server and a client that talks to the server, in Zig, with the current API. Old tutorials cause many problems on this topic. The network code moved from std.net to std.Io.net, and each operation now takes the Io instance. If you copy code from a guide of last year, the compiler rejects the code. The recipe runs the two halves in one process. You can use the same method for an integration test of any protocol code. The plan 1. Parse 127.0.0.1 with port 0 , and call listen. Port 0 tells the OS to select a free ephemeral port. server.socket.address holds the port that the OS selected. Thus no code uses a fixed port that another program can already use. 2. Start a thread for the server half. The thread calls accept, reads a line and sends a reply. 3. In the main thread, connect to the recorded address. Send a line and read the reply. 4. Join the thread. CI runs exactly this program and compares the output. What changed from std.net If you learned to write network code in Zig before the change to std.Io, use this table: Then Now --- --- std.net.Address.parseIp(...) std.Io.net.IpAddress.parse(...) address.listen(.{}) address.listen(io, .{}) listener.accept() server.accept(io) std.net.tcpConnectToAddress(addr) addr.connect(io, .{ .mode = .stream }) stream.reader() / .writer() stream.reader

title: A Type Function as the Front Door
description: The central pattern of a Zig library: take the type of the caller, and return a richer type.
headings: The SQL exists before the program runs
The type of the caller does not change
text: These pages build a small ORM in the style of Ecto from Elixir. Each page takes one pattern and makes it into a snippet that is small enough to verify. A full ORM adds drivers, pools and migrations around these same basic parts. The problem A Zig library has a difficult interface question: how does the caller give you the data shape of the caller ? Dynamic languages take a dict or use reflection at runtime. C takes void pointers and trusts you. The Zig answer is a function that runs at compile time. The function takes a type and returns a new type that wraps the first type. In the ORM, the caller defines a plain struct. Then Table(User, "users") becomes the typed gateway of the caller to all the operations that the library can do with that struct. The pattern 1. Accept comptime T: type, and the configuration that goes with it (the table name). 2. Read @typeInfo(T) one time, at compile time. 3. Return a struct whose declarations hold all the derived data: metadata, generated SQL, and later the query and insert functions. The SQL exists before the program runs A comptime block makes create sql with ++ concatenation. At runtime, create sql is one string constant in the binary. No formatting, allocation or reflection remains to do. The test compares create sql with the exact expected SQL text. This site uses the same type of gate on each snippet: a comparison character by character. Look at the location of the errors. If a schema field has a type that the library cannot map, the mapping function gives a compile error. The user of your library sees the error at build time. The m

title: The Three Standard Streams
description: The buffer belongs to your writer, not to the descriptor under the writer.
headings: Which stream a line belongs on
isTty, and why programs ask it
text: The output of the snippet below is not in the order in which the program wrote it. Two writers, one descriptor var buffered = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &buf); var unbuffered = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &.{}); try buffered.interface.writeAll("written first, into a buffer\n"); try unbuffered.interface.writeAll("written second, straight to the fd\n"); try buffered.interface.flush(); Both writers write to descriptor 1: The first writer has a 1 KB buffer. It holds bytes until the program flushes the buffer. The second writer has an empty slice, so it has no place to keep bytes. Thus each write goes out immediately. The second line gets to the terminal first. When you read the source from top to bottom, you cannot see that. The descriptor has no buffer. Your writer holds the buffer, on your side of the call. Thus the fix is flush, not a flag on the file. Hello, World explains the mechanics. Here, see this fact: two writers on one descriptor have two independent buffers, and neither writer knows about the other. Interleaved output often goes wrong in this way. A program prints progress to standard error without a buffer, and it prints results to standard output with a buffer. Then the log shows the work in an order that did not occur. Which stream a line belongs on Descriptor 1 is for the output that the program must make. Descriptor 2 is for all the messages that the program has about that work. A pipe tests the split. zig build 2 /dev/null wc -l must count results, not warnings. It does this only if each line went to the correct stream. Put on descr

title: Strokes
description: Pointer samples come at irregular distances. Move along the path, put a dab at a fixed distance, and keep the distance that remains for the next segment.
headings: Explain before you read the answer
text: A brush stroke is a row of marks. Each mark is a dab , and a dab is one stamp of the brush tip. If many dabs are near each other at equal distances, they look like one continuous line. The obvious answer is wrong While you hold the button, the pointer sends its position again and again. Each position report is a sample . The obvious answer is one dab for each sample. That answer fails, because the samples do not come at equal distances. The browser sends a sample when it can, about one time for each screen frame: A slow movement gives samples that are one or two pixels apart. A fast movement gives samples that are 40 pixels apart, with nothing between them. Thus one dab for each sample draws a solid line when you move slowly. When you move fast, it draws a row of separate dots. Distance and lerp The stroke code needs two small tools first. The distance between two points is the length of the straight line between them: From (10, 20) to (40, 60), the change in x is 30, and the change in y is 40. The distance is √(900 + 1600) = 50 pixels. A movement in the opposite direction gives negative changes, but the distance is the same. lerp gives the value at a fraction t of the distance from a to b: From 20 to 100, t = 0.25 gives 40. t = 0 gives 20, and t = 1 gives 100. t = 1.5 gives 140, which is after the end. lerp does not clamp, and the stroke code never needs a clamp. Move along the path The solution is to ignore the positions of the samples. Between two samples, the pointer moved along a line. The stroke code moves along that line and puts a dab after each gap pixels. The gap

title: Allocators
description: Explicit memory management, with the allocator given as a value.
headings: defer makes this easy to manage
text: Zig has no global allocator and no garbage collector. All code that needs heap memory takes an std.mem.Allocator parameter. Thus the signature of a function always shows if the function allocates. Select an allocator The Allocator interface is one type, but you select the strategy behind the interface: Allocator Frees memory Use for --- --- --- ArenaAllocator at deinit(), all at the same time Request handlers, compilers, all work that occurs in phases FixedBufferAllocator never (bump pointer) Embedded code, hot loops, code that has no heap SafeAllocator at each free, with leak detection Development builds std.testing.allocator at each free, and the test fails on a leak Tests The arena is correct for more programs than most people expect. Some programs do one unit of work and then discard all of the memory. For such a program, an arena changes hundreds of free calls into one deinit. An arena also removes a full category of leak. defer makes this easy to manage const numbers = try allocator.alloc(u32, 10); defer allocator.free(numbers); defer runs when the scope ends. It runs on all paths, and an early return and an error return are two of these paths. In Zig code, the free is on the line directly after the alloc. Thus you see the two calls together. The test above uses std.testing.allocator. If a test leaks memory, the test fails. Tests check for leaks by default. You do not have to remember to run a separate tool. The usual operations Call Gives you Use with --- --- --- alloc(T, n) a []T of n items free create(T) a T, one value destroy dupe(T, slice) an owned copy of slice

title: A Postgres Client
description: Startup, password auth, a row iterator and error recovery, with tests against scripted bytes.
headings: The server selects the auth method
The client lends rows, and does not give them
An error is a message, not a disconnection
text: A PostgreSQL client in Zig uses the wire protocol directly. PgClient does these tasks: It sends the startup message. It answers the password request from the server. It returns rows through an iterator. It changes an ErrorResponse into a Zig error, and keeps the connection. The client reads from a Reader. Thus its tests use scripted bytes, not a database. The problem The cookbook recipe showed that the wire protocol is only messages with a tag and a length prefix. But a recipe is not a client. The service in this project needs a client that it can call without attention to bytes. The client must keep the connection after an error. A shortener gets constraint violations in normal operation. If a client stopped the connection on each error, the client would connect again all the time. The plan 1. PgClient holds a reader, a writer, and the last known state of the server. The client never opens a socket. The owner of the connection gives the streams to the client. 2. connect sends the startup message and does the handshake. If the server asks for a password, connect sends the password. 3. query returns Rows, an iterator. The column names come in the RowDescription message. The values come in DataRow messages, one message for each row. 4. An ErrorResponse becomes a Zig error. The client keeps the SQL state code and the message. First, the iterator reads all messages until ReadyForQuery. Thus the connection is immediately usable again. The demo talks to a scripted backend. The backend is the server half of two conversations, written into a buffer before the demo starts. The clien

title: Pointer Sized Integers
description: usize, isize, and why they are not the same as u64.
headings: The width depends on the target, and this is intentional
text: In Zig, use usize for lengths, indices and byte offsets into memory. Use a fixed width such as u64 for values that get their range from the problem, for example a file offset or a timestamp. usize and isize are exactly as wide as a pointer on the target. .len is a usize, and a value that you use as a slice index is a usize. The width depends on the target, and this is intentional The snippets on this site compile to wasm32-wasi. Thus @sizeOf(usize) is 4 . If you build the same source for x86 64, the size is 8. For this reason, the last test above asserts 4. The value 4 is a fact about the target, not about Zig. This page is the one place on the site where an assertion shows the wasm target. When you run the snippet, you get the 32-bit answer. For this program, the browser is a 32-bit machine. Be careful when you select between the two types: If you write u64 where you mean usize, the code works on your machine. It fails on a 32-bit machine. If you write usize where you mean "a 64-bit counter", the value becomes narrower on wasm, and you get no error. Which type to use Select the type from what the number is , not from how large you expect the number to become. usize : use it for a count of memory that exists, or an index into that memory. Examples are .len, an index, a byte offset into a buffer, and a capacity. The quantity of memory that the machine can address limits these values, and that limit is the definition of pointer width. A fixed width (u32, u64): use it for a value that gets its range from the problem, not from the machine. Examples are a file offset, a timestam

title: ArrayList
description: The array that can grow, now unmanaged.
headings: Allocate the capacity first when possible
Give the ownership to the caller
When to use a different container
text: std.ArrayList is the array in Zig that can grow. On master, an ArrayList holds no allocator. Create the list with .empty. Then give the allocator to each method that can allocate, as in list.append(gpa, x). The list is unmanaged now Of all the changes, this change most often breaks code that you find online. In the past, std.ArrayList stored its allocator: var list = std.ArrayList(u8).init(allocator); // old defer list.deinit(); try list.append('a'); On master, ArrayList is the unmanaged variant. It holds no allocator. Thus you give an allocator to each method that can allocate: var list: std.ArrayList(u8) = .empty; // current defer list.deinit(gpa); try list.append(gpa, 'a'); You type more, but the allocator is visible at each call site that can fail. Also, the struct is two words smaller. The second reason for the change is visible at scale. A program with ten thousand small lists stored ten thousand copies of the same allocator pointer and vtable. Now the program stores no copies. A struct with several list fields does not keep one allocator for each field. .empty is a declaration on the type. Thus var list: std.ArrayList(u8) = .empty; works by inference. If you know approximately how many items will come, use try .initCapacity(gpa, n). It allocates one time at the start. The parts of a list A list has an items slice, a capacity, and a safety field. A later section tells you about the safety field. Outside a safety build, the safety field costs nothing. Thus a list is three words: a pointer, a length, and the number of elements that the buffer can hold before it must gro

title: Many-item Pointers
description: [*]T: a pointer to an unknown number of items.
text: In Zig, [ ]T is a many-item pointer. It points at an unknown number of T. You can use an index on it, but it has no .len and no bounds checks. When you know the length, slice the pointer with many[0..count]. The result is a []T with bounds checks. C has one pointer type, T , and C uses it for three different things: one item, many items, and "maybe nothing". Zig has a different type for each: Zig Meaning --- --- T exactly one T [ ]T many T, count unknown []T many T, count known (a slice) ? T one T, or nothing The different types have a purpose. In C, a function signature with a char parameter gives you no information. A comment or a convention must tell you three things: if the function can use an index, how far, and if null is acceptable. In Zig, the type gives the three answers, and the compiler enforces them. What [ ]T does not have A many-item pointer supports an index and pointer arithmetic. But it has no .len, thus it has no bounds checks . The type is mainly for C interop, and for the code that makes the safe abstractions above it. When you know the length, convert the pointer to a slice: const slice: []u8 = many[0..count]; This one step gives you bounds checks, for iteration and .len again. Use slices in all places, except at the boundary where no length is available. When you slice a [ ]T, you tell the compiler something that it cannot check. many[0..count] makes a slice of exactly count elements, also if that number of elements does not exist. If you are wrong, no check fails. After that line, all accesses have checks again. Thus the unchecked statement is in one

title: Hash Maps
description: Key-value storage, and the getOrPut pattern.
headings: Use getOrPut, not a get and then a put
The map does not copy the keys
text: In Zig, a hash map is std.AutoHashMapUnmanaged(K, V). When the keys are strings, use std.StringHashMapUnmanaged(V). map.getOrPut(gpa, key) inserts or updates an entry with one lookup. Select a map Type For --- --- AutoHashMapUnmanaged(K, V) keys that Zig can hash automatically (integers, enums, simple structs) StringHashMapUnmanaged(V) []const u8 keys std.array hash map.Auto(K, V) when you need a stable insertion order These maps are unmanaged, like ArrayList. Create a map with .empty, and give the allocator to each method that allocates. AutoHashMap refuses keys that it cannot hash safely, for example slices. The hash of the pointer is almost never what you want. For this reason, string keys have their own type. The refusal is a compile error, not a surprise at runtime. It is a good example of what comptime reflection can do. The map examines your key type at compile time. If the key type contains a pointer and the map must follow that pointer, the map stops and tells you. It does not hash the address without a report. Be careful with the third row. The iteration order of a plain hash map comes from the layout of the table, and the order changes when the map grows. An array hash map keeps the entries in a list next to the table. Thus an iteration gives you the insertion order, and the cost is one extra indirection. Use an array hash map when a person will read the output, or when a test compares the output with a fixture. A test that iterates over a plain hash map will fail one day for no visible reason. Use getOrPut, not a get and then a put This idiom counts words: const

title: Slices
description: A pointer and a length, together.
headings: Two words, and the two are both important
A slice is not a copy
text: A slice is a pointer plus a length. When you give a sequence to a function, use a slice by default. Two words, and the two are both important []T is exactly a [ ]T and a usize, side by side. All other properties come from that structure: An index can have a bounds check, because the length is in the slice. for knows when to stop. A function that takes []const u8 cannot receive a buffer without the length of the real data in it. Compare this with C. In C, the same job needs two parameters and a convention. Each function that does not give the length correctly causes a buffer overrun. A slice puts the two parts in one value. Thus an edit cannot separate the two parts. A slice is not a copy array[1..4] gives a view into the same memory. A write through the slice changes the array. The upper bound is exclusive, as in for ranges. array[2..] makes a slice to the end. A slice borrows memory. Thus the lifetime of a slice depends on the memory that it points at. A slice of a local array must not live longer than that array. Zig does not catch this error for you. The type does not check the lifetime, and this is the one hazard of a slice. The slice does not stop you when you use an index on it. For the type, the slice still has a valid pointer and a valid length. But the memory that it points at now belongs to a different part of the program. A usual example is a function that owns a stack buffer and returns a slice of that buffer. Who owns this memory shows the shape of this problem. The program does check the bounds. If you write array[1..10] on an array with three elements, and th

title: Stacks
description: ArrayList from one end, or no allocator at all.
headings: When the depth has a limit
text: In Zig, push and pop are append(gpa, x) and pop() on a std.ArrayList. pop() returns null when the list is empty. When you know the maximum depth, a fixed array and a length index make a stack with no allocator. Zig has no special Stack type, because it does not need one. An ArrayList that you use from the end is a stack: Operation Call --- --- push append(gpa, x) pop pop() (returns ?T) peek last() (returns ?T) size items.len pop() and last() both return an optional. Thus the type handles the empty case. You do not have to remember a precondition. In older tutorials, peek was getLast(), and it returned a T. It asserted that the list was not empty. Thus a call on an empty list was a safety-checked panic in a debug build, and undefined behaviour in a release build. That function still exists. It is deprecated, and it still asserts. last() is the replacement. It returns ?T, and thus the empty case is in the type. getLastOrNull() is a deprecated alias for last(). There is also lastPtr(), which returns ? T. Use lastPtr() when you want to change the top element in place and not copy it. The stack is cheap because it uses the end of the list, not the front. A removal from the end decrements the length one time. A removal from the front moves each of the other elements. For this reason, an array is a good fit for a stack, but not for a queue. When the depth has a limit If you know the maximum, do not use an allocator. A fixed array and a length index are a complete stack that cannot fail. This is important for embedded targets and hot paths, and in Zig it is ordinary code. var buf:

title: Enums
description: Named values, fixed tags, and methods.
text: A Zig enum is a type. Its value is exactly one tag from a fixed set of named tags. An enum can do three more things: It can set its integer tag type with enum(u8). It can declare methods. It can accept values that are not named tags. A at the end of the tag list makes the enum non-exhaustive. Inferred literals When the compiler knows the expected type, the dot at the start is sufficient: const d: Direction = .north; takeDirection(.south); Thus switch prongs and struct literals stay easy to read, and you do not write the type name again in each place. .north alone has its own type, the enum literal type. This type coerces to each enum that has a tag with the same name. Thus the same .north works for two unrelated enums in two different calls. Set the representation const Value = enum(u8) { zero = 0, one = 1, hundred = 100 }; When you specify the tag type, you fix the size and the numeric values. This is important for wire formats and for C interop. To convert, use @intFromEnum and @enumFromInt. In safety builds, Zig checks @enumFromInt, because not all integers are valid tags. Without a tag type, the compiler selects the smallest integer that fits. It gives the tags numbers from zero. Thus @intFromEnum still works on a plain enum, and the values still have the order of the declaration. But do not write these numbers into a file format. When the numbers go out of your program, set the tag type. Non-exhaustive enums A at the end of the list says that values outside the named tags are legal: const Opcode = enum(u8) { get = 1, set = 2, }; Use this type for a byte that comes from

title: PriorityQueue
description: A binary heap where the comparator is part of the type.
headings: The comparator is part of the type
It is unmanaged, as the other containers are
text: std.PriorityQueue(T, Context, compareFn) is the binary heap in Zig. push and pop are O(log n). pop returns the element that the comparator puts first, or null when the queue is empty. The comparator is part of the type std.PriorityQueue(T, Context, compareFn) puts the order into the type. std.sort uses the same shape. The function returns a std.math.Order. Return .lt when the first argument must pop before the second argument. Thus the comparator answers the question "which comes first". If you swap its two arguments, a min-heap becomes a max-heap. The Context parameter is void when the comparison needs no external data. To compare against runtime data, give the parameter a real type. An example is distances to a target that you know only at runtime. Give the value to the queue through initContext. The comparator is in the type and not in a field. Thus each comparison is a direct call that the optimiser can inline. Also, two queues with different orders are different types. You cannot use one of them where the code expects the other. It is unmanaged, as the other containers are var q: std.PriorityQueue(u32, void, ascU32) = .empty; defer q.deinit(gpa); try q.push(gpa, 30); const smallest = q.pop(); // ?u32 The rules are the same as for the other containers: Use .empty to create the queue. Give the allocator to each method that can allocate. pop returns an optional, thus the empty case is in the type. Older code calls init(allocator, {}) and uses add and removeOrNull. That is the older managed shape. Now the methods are push and pop, and you give the allocator to each call. p

title: Structs
description: Layout, defaults, and methods.
text: A Zig struct can give default values to its fields. It can also hold methods, and the first parameter of a method is the receiver. The layout of a struct is unspecified, unless the declaration is extern or packed. Defaults A field can declare a default. Thus a literal must name only the fields that are different: const v = Vec3{ .x = 5 }; // y and z default to 0 You must supply each field that has no default. Zig does not set it to zero for you. When each field has a default, .{} makes the full struct. For this reason, code in the standard library usually gives .{} and one changed field to an options struct. The compiler evaluates defaults at compile time, one time for each declaration. Think of a field with a default of an empty list. The field gets the same empty value each time. It does not get one shared mutable value, because the default is a value and not a constructor call. Methods and the receiver A method with self: Vec3 gets a copy. A method with self: Vec3 can change the original. To call a Vec3 method, you need a mutable value: v must be a var, and Zig takes the address for you. Select the receiver carefully: Vec3 for small value types that you want to copy. const Vec3 for large values that you only read. Vec3 to change the value. A method has no special properties. v.length() is Vec3.length(v). The only rule is that the first parameter is the receiver. There is no hidden this, and a method call never uses a vtable. The type at the call site always decides at compile time which function runs. A struct can also hold declarations that are not methods. Thus a type

title: MultiArrayList
description: A struct of arrays, with a memory layout that helps the cache.
headings: The same API with a different storage
text: std.MultiArrayList(T) is the struct-of-arrays container in Zig. Like an ArrayList(T), it takes full structs through append. The call items(.field) returns one field of all the elements as a separate slice. The same API with a different storage Ten monsters with hp, x and y become three arrays of ten values. They do not become ten structs next to each other. get still gives you full structs. You see the separate arrays only when you ask for one field. The two layouts have names, and books and papers use these names: ArrayList is an array of structs, "AoS". MultiArrayList is a struct of arrays, "SoA". The data is the same in the two layouts. Only the order of the bytes in memory is different. Why use it items(.hp) gives you a real []u32, with all the hp values next to each other. A loop that adds the hp values reads only that array. Thus the CPU loads no x or y bytes that it does not use. When a program uses one field frequently and the struct is wide, this loop reads only the bytes that it needs. It does not move the full struct through the cache. This layout also lets the compiler vectorize changes to one field of all the elements. The cache line gives the numbers. Memory comes from RAM in 64-byte blocks. The block size is the same when you need 64 bytes and when you need only 4. Take a 64-byte struct in AoS layout, and a loop that adds one u32 field. The loop gets 64 bytes to use 4 bytes, thus fifteen sixteenths of the memory bandwidth is lost. In SoA layout, the same loop uses all the bytes that it gets.
