On a large array, the layout causes all of the difference. Optimisat

title: Unions
description: One of several types, in one allocation.
headings: A bare union does not know the active field
A tagged union knows the active field
The cost of a tagged union
Where to use a tagged union
text: In Zig, you write a tagged union as union(enum). A tagged union is a sum type. The value carries a tag that names its active field, and a switch on the value must handle each field. A bare union has no tag. A read of a field that is not the active field is illegal behaviour. A union holds one of its fields at a time. The question is always: which field ? A bare union does not know the active field const Payload = union { int: i64, float: f64 }; A read of a field that is not the active field is illegal behaviour. Bare unions are for C interop, and for cases where a different part of the code already records the tag. "Illegal behaviour" means more than "you get incorrect data": In a safety build, the program catches the access to the wrong field and panics. In ReleaseFast, the access is undefined, and the optimiser can assume that it never occurs. Thus a bare union is a promise from you. Make that promise only when something outside the union already records the answer. A tagged union knows the active field const Tagged = union(Tag) { int: i64, float: f64, none: void }; Now the value carries its tag. switch can safely select the correct field, and the switch must be exhaustive. A tagged union is the sum type of Zig, and almost always it is the correct choice. Error unions and optionals also use the same construct. A pointer capture in a prong lets you change the value in place: switch (value) { .int = n n. += 1, ... } A void field says "this case carries nothing". Thus a tagged union can have states without a payload, and you do not have to make a dummy payload. union(enum) W

title: Bit Sets and Enum Collections
description: A set of small integers in a word, and containers with an enum as the key.
headings: A set that fits in registers
Containers with an enum as the key
text: std.bit set.Static(N) stores a set of the integers 0..N as bits, with no allocator. EnumSet, EnumArray and EnumMap change an enum into one of three containers: a set a table with a value for each tag a map with values for some tags A set that fits in registers Older code calls this type std.StaticBitSet. The type stores the bits inline. When N is small, the type is one integer. When N is larger, the type is an array of words. The API is the same for the two layouts: set, unset, isSet, count. If you know the size only at run time, use std.bit set.DynamicManaged. This type takes an allocator. Union and intersection are single instructions on the backing words. Thus unionWith and intersectWith are cheap. With findFirstSet and the ascending iterator, you can find the members without a scan of each index. Containers with an enum as the key Three types change an enum into a container. The difference between them is the result for a key that you did not set: Type Holds A key that you did not set --- --- --- EnumSet(E) membership only not present EnumArray(E, V) a V for each tag not possible: init sets all keys EnumMap(E, V) a V for some tags get returns null An EnumArray always has a value for each tag. Thus its get returns V, not ?V. The compiler makes you supply each field at initialization. Use EnumArray for lookup tables that must cover the full enum, for example a duration for each state of a traffic light. EnumMap is the partial version. Use it when the absence of a key has a meaning. The three types use the same bit-set machinery. Thus they are compact, and they do not allo

title: Integer Rules
description: Arbitrary widths, explicit narrowing, chosen overflow behaviour.
headings: A wider type has no cost, a narrower type has a cost
Division and shifts also have rules
text: Zig integer types have an explicit width, such as u8, i32 or u3. A conversion from a wider type to a narrower type needs @intCast. For plain +, overflow is illegal behaviour, and safety builds panic on it. When you want a different result, use one of the two other operators: +% wraps. + saturates. Any width that you want u3, i7, u64 and u1000 are all real types. u8 is not special. It is only the width of a byte. Packed structs use these widths to describe bitfields exactly. The width is part of the type, and the width never depends on the platform. Zig has no int whose size changes with the compiler, and no integer promotion rules to remember. Your computer and the CI computer calculate the same results. The only integer type that depends on the target is usize. It depends on the target on purpose, because it is the width of a pointer. See pointer-sized integers. @sizeOf(u3) is 1, because memory addresses are in bytes. Inside a packed struct, the same u3 uses exactly three bits. Unusual widths are for the description of a layout and for a limit on a value. Alone, they do not save memory. A wider type has no cost, a narrower type has a cost A conversion from u8 to u16 is always safe. Thus Zig does it implicitly. The reverse conversion can lose data. Thus you must write it: const c: u8 = @intCast(b); In a build with safety checks, @intCast panics if the value does not fit. In ReleaseFast, a value that does not fit is illegal behaviour. In the two cases, the cast is visible in the source. Thus you cannot lose the top bits by accident. The sign is also information. For Zig, a c

title: Floats
description: IEEE-754 types and explicit conversions.
headings: No implicit mix of ints and floats
text: Zig never converts between integers and floats implicitly. @floatFromInt and @intFromFloat do the conversion. @intFromFloat truncates toward zero. Zig has f16, f32, f64, f80 and f128. All of them are IEEE-754, except f80, the x87 extended format. No implicit mix of ints and floats Zig does not do a conversion in either direction automatically: const f: f32 = @floatFromInt(n); const n: i32 = @intFromFloat(f); // truncates toward zero Zig does this on purpose. An implicit conversion from int to float loses precision for large integers, and you get no warning. An implicit conversion from float to int truncates, and you get no warning. The two conversions cause many bugs. Thus the two extra words are a good cost. @intFromFloat truncates. It does not round. The target type must be able to hold the result. A value outside the range of the target, or a NaN, is illegal behaviour, and a safety build finds it. If you do not know that the input is in range, clamp the input or check it first. If you want the saturating version, use std.math.lossyCast. Between float types, @floatCast makes a value narrower. A change to a wider type is implicit, because it cannot lose data. comptime float is f128 An earlier version of this page had this fact wrong. comptime int really has arbitrary precision, but comptime float does not: it uses f128. Arithmetic at compile time gives you more bits, but it does not give you exact decimal values: const x = 0.1 + 0.2; // x != 0.3, even at comptime Comptime floats still have rounding error. Compare them with a tolerance: std.math.approxEqAbs(f64, a, b, 1e-12

title: Labelled Blocks
description: Blocks that produce a value.
headings: The label makes the block an expression
Where real code uses labelled blocks
text: In Zig, a labelled block computes a const with more than one statement. The block ends with break :blk value. The scope of the intermediate variables in the block ends at the closing brace. Give a label to a block, and use break with a value to leave the block: const count = blk: { var sum: u32 = 0; for (0..10) i sum += i; break :blk sum; }; You can use any name instead of blk. The important point is that a computation with many statements still produces one const. Thus the intermediate var cannot be visible in the outer scope, and you cannot use it again by accident later. Use a labelled block when you need a few lines to compute a value, and you want the result to be immutable. Without a labelled block, programmers often use a mutable variable with a scope that is wider than necessary. Or they write a function that they use only one time. The label makes the block an expression A block without a label is a statement. It groups code and starts a scope, but it has no value. The label gives break a name to use. The statement break :blk x gives the block a type. If you remove the label, you cannot get x out of the block. The compiler also checks the opposite case. A label that no break uses is an error: error: unused block label Labelled loops get the same error, for the same reason. Usually, an unused label is a part of control flow that a programmer deleted, and the label stayed. break :blk is not return In a block inside a function, it is easy to confuse the two statements. They do different things: break :blk x ends the block and gives x to the variable that receives the

title: The Hub
description: One writer for each socket. The hub keeps the members, copies each line into a bounded outbox, and never touches a socket.
headings: Say: the sender gets the line too
A slot number is not a name
text: Each connection in the server has its own task, which reads from its socket. When tejas says something, the task of tejas must send a line to vishaka and to shivam. The simple design is to write to their sockets directly. That design has a race. A WebSocket frame is a header and a payload, and a large frame can need more than one write. Two tasks can write to the socket of shivam at the same time, for example the tasks of tejas and vishaka. Then the bytes of the two frames can mix. Then shivam gets a frame that is not valid, and closes the connection. A lock for each socket would prevent the mix. But a task that holds that lock waits for the network of shivam, and a slow network then stops each member who talks. One writer for each socket The hub uses a different design: 1. Each connection has an outbox , a bounded queue of lines. 2. Each connection has one writer task . Only the writer task writes to the socket. It takes a line from the outbox and sends it. 3. The hub puts lines into outboxes. It never touches a socket. Thus no two tasks write to one socket. A task that talks only puts lines into queues, and a queue operation is short. The outbox is std.Io.Queue, the bounded channel from Queues. Its capacity comes from the buffer that you give to init. A Peer belongs to the connection, and the hub keeps a pointer to it. The program below plays three members in memory. After each action, it takes the lines out of each outbox, as a writer task would, and prints them. Join join holds the std.Io.Mutex of the hub from the check to the last delivery. Two clients can ask for the

title: Sliding Window
description: One addition and one subtraction instead of a new sum, the window that grows and shrinks, and the count that shows the total stays linear.
headings: Use one addition and one subtraction
Use a window that changes size
Why the inner loop is still O(n)
text: The example uses ten numbers and two questions about them: 1. What is the largest sum of four consecutive values? 2. What is the shortest consecutive range with a sum of 19 or more? The two problems use a contiguous part of the array. A sliding window solves them with two indices that move from left to right. The trace below shows the window at each step. Each line also shows the value that entered, the value that left, and the current sum. Calculate each window again A simple solution calculates the sum of each possible window from the start. This solution gives the correct answer. For a window size of four, there are seven possible windows in an array of ten values. Each window needs four additions. The problem is the quantity of repeated work. There are n - k + 1 windows, and each window needs k additions. Thus the time complexity is O(n k). For 200,000 values with a window size of 1,000, the result is approximately 200 million additions. Most of these additions are not necessary. Two adjacent windows share k - 1 values. Do not add these values again. Keep the previous sum, and change the sum only for the two values that are different. Use one addition and one subtraction First, calculate the sum of the first window in the usual way. After that, each new window is different from the previous window by only two values: One value enters from the right. One value leaves from the left. Thus you do not calculate the full sum again. Change the current sum in two steps: 1. Add the new value. 2. Subtract the old value. The first four windows are: move enter leave sum window firs

title: Select
description: Wait for the task that completes first, and cancel the other tasks.
text: Future.await waits for one task. Group.await waits for all of the tasks. std.Io.Select is the third shape. It waits for the task that completes first. Then you decide what to do with the other tasks. The most frequent case that you will write is a request against a timeout. The union is the result const Outcome = union(enum) { reply: u32, timeout: void, }; var slots: [2]Outcome = undefined; var select: std.Io.Select(Outcome) = .init(io, &slots); Each arm is a field. Select(U) is a Group and a Queue(U) together. Thus the buffer that you pass is the buffer of the queue. The buffer must have space for each task that you spawn. If you cancel with less space than that, the result is a deadlock. The cancelled tasks still need a place to put their results. try select.concurrent(.reply, request, .{ io, reply after }); try select.concurrent(.timeout, deadline, .{ io, timeout after }); switch (try select.await()) { .reply = value ..., .timeout = ..., } The field name is comptime, and the return type of the function must agree with that field. Thus, if an arm returns the wrong type, the result is a compile error, not a union with the wrong tag at run time. await returns when one arm completes. Call await again for the next arm, or stop. The other arms still run select.cancelDiscard(); A select owns its tasks, the same as a Group. When await returns, the arm that lost still runs. cancelDiscard sends a cancellation request to all of the tasks. It waits until they are done, and it discards their results. Use cancel instead when an arm can return a value that you must free. cancel returns

title: Write Text Files
description: Truncate or keep, create only if new, append, the flush that the program forgot, and how to replace a file in one step.
headings: Replace a file in one step
text:
To write a file looks simple. You create the file, write some bytes and close the file. But some options change the bytes on disk, and the default values do not always do what you expect. The program below writes six small files. Then it shows the contents of each file. The helper Each write in this chapter uses the same three steps: 1. createFile opens the file for write operations. If the file does not exist, createFile creates the file. 2. file.writer(io, &buf) gives you a File.Writer with a 64-byte buffer. 3. The program writes through writer.interface. Then it calls flush(), which sends the bytes that remain in the buffer to the file. The options argument controls what occurs when the file exists already. Truncate By default, createFile truncates the file. The function removes the old contents before the program writes. truncate = true: "v2
" truncate = false: "v2
st version
" With .truncate = false, the file keeps its old bytes. The writer starts at offset 0. Thus "v2
" replaces the first three bytes of "first version
". The other bytes, "st version
", stay in the file. For a text file, you almost never want this result. But it is useful for a file of records of fixed size, where you change one record and keep the other records. The Random Access chapter shows this. Create only if new .exclusive = true creates the file. If the file exists already, the call fails. attempt 1: created attempt 2: PathAlreadyExists The check and the create occur in one step. This is important when two programs run at the same time. If you check first with statFile and create the file

title: The World
description: A field with its own units, a player that slides between lanes, and the order of the work in a tick.
headings: The other objects in the field
The game has its own random numbers
text: The simulation never uses pixels. It uses a fixed field of 360 by 640 units. The renderer maps the field onto the window, whatever the size of the window. This design has two results: A change to the size of the window cannot change the difficulty, because a wider window does not show more road. A test can assert that a block is at y = 520, and the test opens nothing. The three lanes divide the width. Thus a lane is 120 units wide. Thus laneCenter(0) is 60, laneCenter(1) is 180 and laneCenter(2) is 300. These three numbers are the only x positions where an object stops. The player is at a fixed height near the bottom. The world moves toward the player. The player has two positions One position is the lane that the player steers toward. The other position is where the body of the player really is. lane changes immediately when the player presses a key. x slides toward the centre of that lane during lane change time. After each press, the two values are different for approximately a tenth of a second. That difference gives the game its feel. The slide has a constant speed. It does not start slowly or stop slowly. A slide that starts and stops slowly looks smoother. But with that slide, a move of two lanes costs less than two times a move of one lane. The spacing rule needs a move of two lanes to cost exactly two times a move of one lane. A constant speed looks less smooth, but it keeps the spacing rule correct. Because x is continuous, the player really occupies the space between lanes. If the player touches a block during a slide, the game counts a crash. The other objects i

title: Labelled Loops
description: Break or continue an outer loop by name.
headings: continue :outer runs the outer continue expression
An unused label is a compile error
Labels are not only for loops
text: In Zig, break :outer leaves a labelled outer loop from inside a nested loop. continue :outer starts the next iteration of the outer loop. Thus you do not need a flag variable. By default, break and continue affect the innermost loop. To select a different loop, give that loop a label: outer: for (0..5) i { for (0..5) j { if (found) break :outer; // leaves both loops if (skip) continue :outer; // next i, abandon remaining j } } A label is an identifier and a colon, before the loop keyword. You can use any name. outer and blk are usual names, but the compiler does not require them. Usually, a label that tells what the loop examines (rows:, candidates:) is easier to read at the break. The break is where a reader looks. The cost of the alternative Without labels, you need a flag to leave two loops at the same time: var found = false; for (rows) row { for (row) cell { if (matches(cell)) { found = true; break; } } if (found) break; } The flag adds three lines of bookkeeping. You must also repeat if (found) break at each level of nesting. The flag also continues to exist after the loop, so later code can read it. And the break in the inner loop does not tell you what it does until you read the next two lines. In C, you use goto to jump past the loops. That method works, but then the label names a place in the code, not a loop. A loop with a name also keeps the code correct when a person edits it later. If you put one more level of nesting around either loop, a break without a label changes its meaning and gives no error. break :outer keeps its meaning. continue :outer runs the out

title: Read a Type
description: Use @typeInfo to list the fields of a struct, an enum and a union, then write a generic diff.
headings: Questions with a yes or no answer
Use the walk: a diff for any struct
If you used an older version of Zig
text: @typeInfo(T) returns a description of the type T. The description is a usual Zig value of type std.lang.Type. It contains the names of the fields, the type of each field and the default values. The description is comptime-known, thus a function can walk it with inline for. The function then has one copy of its body for each field. This is how one function can work with every struct type. The shape of the description std.lang.Type is a tagged union with one variant for each kind of type. To get the description of a struct, take the @"struct" variant: const info = @typeInfo(T).@"struct"; The name has quotes because struct is a keyword. The enum, union and fn variants use the same syntax. For a struct, info has three arrays of fields: field names holds the name of each field. field types holds the type of each field. field attrs holds the default value, the alignment and the comptime flag of each field. The three arrays have the same length. Item i in each array describes the same field. The fields are in the order of the source file. Walk the fields inline for (info.field names, info.field types, info.field attrs) name, F, attrs { try out.print(" {s}: {s}", .{ name, @typeName(F) }); if (attrs.defaultValue(F)) default { ... } } A for with three arrays walks them together. The loop must be inline, because F is a type, and a type must be comptime-known in each copy of the body. attrs.defaultValue(F) returns the default value as a ?F. The result is null when the field has no default: Config: 4 fields, 2 declarations name: []const u8 = "server" port: u16 = 8080 verbose: bool = fal

title: Bytes Have No Edges
description: A read that returns 7 bytes does not tell you where a message ends.
text: If a server ignores the subject of this chapter, the server can work in tests and fail under load. TCP is a byte stream. TCP keeps the bytes in order and delivers all of the bytes. TCP does not make a promise about how it groups the bytes. The sender made three writes, and these writes can arrive as one read or as seventeen reads. The socket API does not tell you which of these occurred. TCP does not record where one write ended and where the next write started. Press Run. The program delivers the same bytes one byte at a time, and then all together. The parser cannot see a difference. The bug // Wrong, and it works on your machine every time. var buf: [256]u8 = undefined; const n = try socket.read(&buf); const message = parse(buf[0..n]); This code is correct only when the full message arrives in one read. On loopback, with a small message and a computer that has no other load, the full message always arrives in one read. In these conditions, the full message possibly does not arrive in one read: The message is larger than one packet (the MTU). The network has a high load. The sender uses two writes. The connection uses a proxy. The failure occurs in production. It looks like data corruption, not like a message that is too short. Two indices and no copies const Incoming = struct { buf: [256]u8 = undefined, len: usize = 0, // bytes received at: usize = 0, // bytes handed out }; len increases when the network delivers bytes. at increases when the parser removes a complete message from the front. The parser does not move bytes, thus the slices that next returns stay valid. You

title: A Typed Query Builder
description: Compile-time field checks and output that stops injection, with no allocator.
text: A typed query builder in Zig takes columns as std.meta.FieldEnum(T). Thus a misspelled column is a compile error. The builder writes values as numbered placeholders ($1, $2), and the values never touch the SQL text. The builder is a plain value, and you can chain its calls without an allocator. The problem Each database library has the same two failure modes: A query names a column that does not exist. You find the error at runtime, in production, as a database error. A value goes into the SQL string directly. You find the error as an injection. A Zig library can prevent both at the type level, and the code for this is small. The pattern 1. std.meta.FieldEnum(T) changes the field names of the schema struct into an enum. A filter takes that enum. Thus .where(.emial, .eq) is a compile error, and the error shows the misspelled name. 2. The builder is a plain value. where copies the builder, appends to a bounded array, and returns the copy. Thus the caller can make many queries from one base query. 3. render writes numbered placeholders, and the values go to the driver separately. What the enum gives you The Field enum exists only at compile time. At runtime, a filter is an integer tag. {t} formats the tag name back into SQL. Thus the enum checks the column and also supplies its name. That gives three properties: A typo does not compile. The check costs nothing at runtime. No string table must stay the same as the schema. The same method works in code that is not an ORM. A library can accept "one of the fields of this struct" as an argument, for example a sorter, a serializer o

title: The Environment
description: A map from string to string. The parent process selects the map, and your process gets the map at startup.
headings: The map is ready at startup
Case, and the platform that is different
text: The environment is a list of KEY=value strings. The parent process selected the list, and the kernel copied the list into your address space at startup. The environment belongs only to your process. After startup, a change that you make to the environment does not get to any other process that runs. The map is ready at startup pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void { const env = init.environ map; const path = env.get("PATH"); } init.environ map is a std.process.Environ.Map. The startup code filled the map from the raw block before the call to main. The startup code allocated the map with the same gpa that is on init. You do not free the map, and you do not build the map. In the playground above, the count is 0. The count is the real result, not a stub. A wasm module in a browser tab has no parent process, so the module inherits no environment. Thus the environment is really empty. In the playground, env.get("PATH") returns null. A program must be ready for this result on all platforms. If you did not set a variable yourself, the variable can be absent. Your copy belongs to you try env.put("ZIG GUIDE", "live"); This line changes the map of this program and nothing else. It does not change the shell that started your program. Alone, it does not change the environment of a child process either. A child process inherits a copy of a block. The block is the one that existed when you spawned the child. When you spawn the child, you select the block. If you give null, the child gets the environment of the parent. Many people expect the other direction to work, but it does not wo

title: Smoothing, Pressure and Scatter
description: Make a shaky hand steady with a moving average. Get the size of each dab from pen pressure. Scatter dabs with a random generator that repeats.
headings: Explain before you read the answer
text: The last chapter changed samples into dabs at equal distances. This chapter changes the dabs. There are three changes, and each change is a small number of lines: Smoothing moves the path, to make a shaky hand steady. Pressure changes the size of each dab. Jitter and scatter change the size and position of each dab at random. A brush such as a spray can uses them. The third change has a condition. The random values must repeat exactly. If they do not repeat, no test can compare two pictures. Smoothing A hand is not steady, and a mouse is less steady than a hand. Smoothing keeps a second position, the filtered position. For each new sample, smoothing moves the filtered position only part of the distance to the sample: The first line of move does all of the smoothing. follow is the fraction of the distance to move. An example The filtered x is 100. A sample comes at x = 120. follow is 0.25. The filtered x moves a quarter of the distance: 100 + (120 − 100) × 0.25 = 105. The next sample is at 120 again. The filtered x moves a quarter of the distance that remains: 105 + 15 × 0.25 = 108.75. A small movement of a few pixels gets the same calculation. Thus the movement becomes a quarter of its size. At follow = 1, the filtered point moves directly to the sample, and there is no smoothing. The cost is a delay. The stroke is behind the pointer. When you release the pointer, the stroke ends before the last position of the pointer. A lower follow gives a steadier line and a longer delay. That is why the Ink brush in the studio uses 0.35, and the Spray brush uses 1. Pressure A pen sends

title: Strings
description: Search, trim, split, join. All of these functions are in std.mem.
headings: What allocates and what does not
text: In Zig, a string is a []const u8. The functions that search, trim, split and join strings are free functions in std.mem, for example std.mem.find, std.mem.trim and std.mem.splitScalar. There is no string type A string is []const u8, a slice of bytes. Thus you cannot compare two strings with ==, because the compiler rejects == on slices. To compare the contents, use std.mem.eql(u8, a, b). To put two strings in order, use std.mem.order(u8, a, b), which returns .lt, .eq or .gt. All the other functions that you expect from a string class are free functions in std.mem. They work on all slice types. For this reason, each call gives the element type first. indexOf is now find Zig renamed the search functions in the 0.17 development series: // older tutorials std.mem.indexOf(u8, haystack, needle); std.mem.lastIndexOfScalar(u8, path, '.'); // current master std.mem.find(u8, haystack, needle); std.mem.findScalarLast(u8, path, '.'); All the functions in the family changed in the same way: indexOfScalar became findScalar. indexOfAny became findAny. indexOfPos became findPos. lastIndexOf became findLast. indexOfNone became findNone. The old names still exist, as one-line aliases with the Deprecated mark in std/mem.zig. Code that uses the old names compiles and behaves in the same way. Nothing fails. Thus a guide can teach the old names for another year, and the authors do not see the problem. split or tokenize The two functions look interchangeable until the input has two delimiters next to each other: Input "a,,b" with , Yields --- --- splitScalar "a", "", "b" tokenizeScalar "a", "b" s

title: Slugs Are Arithmetic
description: Base62 over the row id, and the validation that a redirect service needs.
headings: Why the scheme check is necessary
text: The slug of a URL shortener can be the database row id in base62. Then each slug is unique, and the service needs no collision check. The service must check the target URL before it stores the URL, because a shortener is an open redirect by design. The problem The service needs a short name for each stored URL. One attractive design is a random string. The service checks the string against the database for collisions, and tries again if necessary. A simpler design uses a value that the database already has. The database gives each row a unique integer, the bigserial id. A slug that is only that integer in a compact form is unique, because the ids are unique. A compact form needs a larger base. Base 10 writes a billion as ten characters. Base 62 uses the digits and both alphabets, and it writes a billion as six characters. The plan 1. encode: divide the id by 62 again and again. Write one character for each remainder. The one-billionth link is still six characters. 2. decode: the opposite operation, for the redirect path. With the id, the lookup can use the primary key. Reject all characters outside the alphabet before they get to a query. 3. checkTarget: the targets that the service accepts for a redirect. This is security logic. Why the scheme check is necessary A shortener sends visitors to the targets of its stored URLs. Only the check on the stored URLs stops attackers from the misuse of the shortener. A stored javascript: URL changes the redirect into script execution in the browser of the visitor. Control characters can let a stored URL smuggle extra bytes into the HT

title: Labelled Switch
description: A switch that you can jump back into with a new value.
headings: When the next state is only known at run time
text: A switch can have a label, as a block or a loop can. When a switch has a label, two statements become available: continue :label value runs the switch again, with value as the new operand. break :label value leaves the switch, and the full switch has the value value. With these two statements, you can write a state machine without a loop and without a state variable. This form came in Zig 0.14. The shape const tag: Tag = state: switch (State.start) { .start = switch (src[i]) { 'a'...'z' = { i += 1; continue :state .identifier; }, '=' = { i += 1; break :state .equal; }, // ... }, .identifier = switch (src[i]) { 'a'...'z', '0'...'9' = { i += 1; continue :state .identifier; }, else = break :state .identifier, }, }; State.start is the first operand. Each prong is a state. continue :state .identifier means "go to the .identifier prong now". break :state .equal means "stop, and the answer is .equal". The label is before switch. You can select any name for the label. See the jumps The program above tokenizes n2 = 40;. Before each prong decides where to go, it prints its state and the byte that it examines. A line that starts with a state name is one entry into the switch. A line without an indent is a token that a break gives. source: "n2 = 40;" start src[0] = 'n' identifier src[1] = '2' identifier src[2] = ' ' identifier "n2" start src[2] = ' ' start src[3] = '=' equal "=" start src[4] = ' ' start src[5] = '4' number src[6] = '0' number src[7] = ';' number "40" start src[7] = ';' semicolon ";" start src[8] is the terminator eof "" Read the first three lines: 1. .start sees n. A n

title: Loops as Expressions
description: The else branch gives the value when no break runs.
headings: What else means on a loop
The error when there is no else
The two arms must have one type
When to use a loop as an expression
text: In Zig, for and while loops are expressions. Thus a search can return its result directly. You do not need a mutable result variable before the loop. A loop can produce a value. break x gives x. If the loop ends and no break runs, the else branch gives the value. return for (haystack, 0..) c, i { if (c == needle) break i; } else null; These lines are a complete linear search. The structure makes it impossible to forget the "not found" case: if you remove the else, the code does not compile. Compare the usual alternative: var result: ?usize = null; for (haystack, 0..) c, i { if (c == needle) { result = i; break; } } return result; The behaviour is the same. But now result is mutable, and it lives longer than necessary. Also, nothing makes you initialise it correctly. What else means on a loop The else of a loop is not the else of an if. It runs when the loop ends normally : the for has no more elements, or the while condition becomes false. A break skips the else. This rule makes the construct safe for searches. There are exactly two exits from the loop, and each exit produces a value. The third test in the snippet shows this rule. It has a break that can never run: const result = while (i < 3) : (i += 1) { if (i == 99) break @as(u32, 1); } else @as(u32, 2); i never gets to 99, the condition becomes false, and result is 2. The error when there is no else The error can confuse you, because it does not mention else. A loop without an else has no value when it ends normally. Thus its type is void: error: expected type '?usize', found 'void' The error points at the full for expr

title: Unicode
description: A string is bytes until you select UTF-8 support.
headings: A slice can cut a character in half
text: In Zig, a string is a slice of bytes. UTF-8 support is something that you select, through std.unicode. There, Utf8View validates the bytes and iterates over code points. Grapheme clusters, case folding and normalisation are not in the standard library. len is bytes "héllo".len is 6, not 5, because é encodes to two bytes. Nothing in the language layer knows about UTF-8. Source files must be valid UTF-8, but a []const u8 at runtime is only bytes. When you need a count of characters, std.unicode.utf8CountCodepoints walks the encoding. This is a design decision, not something that the designers forgot. Most code that handles text never needs the character boundaries. Copy, hash, equality comparison, a write to a socket, and a substring search all work on bytes. Thus they are faster and simpler. Only a small number of cases really need characters, and these cases ask for the UTF-8 code explicitly. Three different lengths The word "length" has three answers. Bugs frequently occur when code uses the wrong answer. Bytes. .len gives you this length. You need it for buffers, offsets, and all data that you write to a file. Code points. utf8CountCodepoints gives you this length. A code point is one Unicode value, encoded in one to four bytes. Grapheme clusters. A grapheme cluster is what a person calls a character. A letter and its combining accent are two code points and one character. An emoji with a skin-tone modifier can be several code points. The standard library gives you the first two lengths. Grapheme clusters need Unicode tables, and std does not include them. Thus "how many

title: Payload Captures
description: The |value| syntax that unwraps all wrapper types.
headings: Why the test and the unwrap are one construct
Capture a pointer to change the value
text: In Zig, value after if, while, for, switch or catch names the unwrapped payload. The payload is the non-null value, the success value, the active variant or the current element. value captures a pointer instead. Thus writes change the original. The value syntax is one idea. Zig uses it in each place where a value is inside a wrapper: Construct Captures --- --- if (optional) \ v\ the non-null payload if (error union) \ v\ else \ e\ the value, or the error while (iter()) \ v\ each value until null switch (tagged union) { .a = \ v\ ... } the active variant's payload for (slice) \ item\ each element catch \ err\ the error When you know the syntax for one wrapper type, you know it for all wrapper types in the language. Why the test and the unwrap are one construct The capture makes these constructs safe. Zig has no isSome() with a separate unwrap(). An edit can move those two calls apart, and then the unwrap runs without the test. In Zig, the payload has a name only inside the branch where the payload exists. Outside that branch, there is no name that you can use incorrectly. The capture also explains why some operations do not exist: You cannot ask an optional "are you null" and get a bool that you can store in a variable. You cannot name the payload of a union variant that is not active. The language gives you the payload exactly where it is valid, and in no other place. Capture a pointer to change the value value captures a pointer, not a copy. Thus you can change the original value in place: if (maybe) value value. += 1; switch (shape) { .circle = r r. = 2, ... } Without the

title: Formatting
description: Format strings that the compiler checks.
headings: A width makes a signed integer show its sign
The compiler checks the format string
text: A format string is a string that is known at compile time. It has one {} placeholder for each argument. {d} prints a number, {s} prints a string, and {any} prints all other values. The compiler checks the placeholders against the arguments. Thus a mismatch is a compile error, not wrong output at runtime. The destination of the output Function Writes to --- --- std.mem.print a buffer that you supply (no allocation) allocator.print new memory (the caller frees it) writer.print any writer std.mem.print returns a slice of the part that it filled. If the buffer is too small, it fails with error.NoSpaceLeft. It does not truncate the text. Specifiers Spec Meaning --- --- {d} decimal {x} / {X} lower / upper hex {b} / {o} binary / octal {s} string {c} a byte as a character {any} structural dump Width, alignment, precision The form is {[fill][align][width]}. For alignment, use : "{d:5}" // " 42" (right by default for numbers) "{d: 5}" // "00042" "{d:.2}" // "3.14" Right alignment is the default for each type, also for strings. This often causes mistakes: {s:8} puts the padding before the text, not after the text. A column of strings has three more rules for alignment. String Recipes gives these rules. To write a literal brace, write it two times: {{ and }}. A width makes a signed integer show its sign The outputs above are the result of a literal, and a literal is comptime int. If you give the same width to a signed value, a + appears in front of the value: const signed: i32 = 42; "{d:5}" // " +42" "{d: 5}" // "00+42" "{d}" // "42" no width, no sign An unsigned value has no sign. Thu

title: Optionals
description: The Zig answer to null, checked by the compiler.
headings: Optional pointers use no extra space
text: A ?T holds a T or null. The compiler does not let you use the value before you handle the null case. Thus an accidental null dereference cannot occur. These are real tests. Run executes the real zig test runner, compiled to WebAssembly. Payload capture The if (maybe) value form is payload capture . Inside the block, value is a plain i32, not an optional. The unwrap and the null check are the same syntax. Thus they cannot become different. When you want only a fallback value, use the short form orelse: const port = maybe port orelse 8080; On the right, orelse takes an expression, not only a value. That expression can exit: const port = maybe port orelse return error.MissingPort; const item = list.pop() orelse break; Read the two lines as "or else stop in this way". In the two lines, the usual path has no indent. Use this form when the function cannot continue after a null. Force the value with .? maybe.? unwraps the value and asserts that the value exists. It is the same as orelse unreachable: In Debug and ReleaseSafe, the program checks the assertion, and a null causes a panic. In ReleaseFast, a null causes undefined behaviour. Use .? where the invariant is local and visible. For example, use it immediately after you insert a key, when the next line reads that key. Do not use .? to stop a compiler error on a value from outside the function. In that case your assertion is about the code of a different person. Operations that Zig omits intentionally Zig has no way to compare an optional to its payload without an unwrap. Zig has no implicit conversion from ?T to T. Zig has no

title: Advanced Formatting
description: Custom format methods, and the format specifiers that changed.
headings: The shape of a custom format method changed
text: In Zig, a custom format method takes only a std.Io.Writer. print calls the method only when the format string asks for it with {f}. Width, fill and alignment go after a colon, as in {d:0 4}. The formatter does that work, not the type. The shape of a custom format method changed Zig 0.15 rewrote the format method. The method now takes only a writer: pub fn format(self: Point, writer: std.Io.Writer) std.Io.Writer.Error!void { try writer.print("({d}, {d})", .{ self.x, self.y }); } The old signature also received the format string and an options struct. That signature no longer applies. A tutorial that shows format(self, comptime fmt: []const u8, options: FormatOptions, writer: anytype) is older than the change. The reason for the change explains the rest of this page. In the old design, the format method of each type had to parse the format string itself. Each method decided what {d: 8} meant for its type. Thus each implementation was slightly different, and most implementations ignored the options completely. Now a type tells one time how it prints. The formatter controls the specifiers for width and alignment. {f} calls the method {} and {any} do not use a custom format method. You must ask for the method with {f}: try writer.print("{f}", .{point}); // (1, 2) This rule is the other half of the same change. It often breaks code that you port from an older version. In the old design, {} found your method. Thus a type with a format method printed correctly in all places, and you did not have to ask. Now {} prints the struct as the compiler sees it, and {f} asks for your method.

title: Comptime
description: Usual Zig code that the compiler runs.
headings: Generic types are functions that return types
What can and cannot run at compile time
text: comptime is the Zig solution for templates, macros, generics, reflection and constant folding. It uses one mechanism for all of them: the compiler runs usual Zig code at compile time, and types are values there. Zig has no second language for this. The code that runs during compilation is the same Zig, with the same syntax and the same standard library functions. To debug it, you read it. You do not expand a macro. C++ templates, C macros and the declarative macros of Rust are each a separate language with separate rules. You cannot step through any of them. Types are values A type is a usual comptime value. Because of this one fact, Zig does not need a separate language for generics: fn max(comptime T: type, a: T, b: T) T { return if (a b) a else b; } comptime T: type says that the compiler must know this parameter at compile time. The compiler makes a separately compiled function for each different T. The name of this process is monomorphisation, and it needs no special syntax. Values that are not types can also be comptime. A function uses such a value to specialise on a configuration instead of a type: fn hash(comptime seed: u64, data: []const u8) u64 { ... } Each call with a different seed gets its own compiled copy, and the compiler folds the constant into that copy. These copies are also the cost. comptime parameters multiply the quantity of generated code. Use them for parameters that have a small number of different values, not for parameters that have a thousand values. Generic types are functions that return types fn List(comptime T: type) type { return struct {

title: Parsing and Encoding
description: Text to numbers, and bytes to hex or base64.
headings: A parse can fail, and the type shows it
base64: select the alphabet for the destination
text: In Zig, std.fmt.parseInt(T, text, base) changes a string into an integer. It returns an error when the text is not a number, or when the number is too large for T. std.fmt.bytesToHex changes bytes into hex, and the codecs in std.base64 change bytes into base64. A parse can fail, and the type shows it std.fmt.parseInt returns an error union. Thus a bad character or a value out of range is a value that you must handle. It is never a silent zero. The target type sets the limit. parseInt(u8, "300", 10) gives error.Overflow, because 300 is too large for a u8. With base 0, the function reads the prefix as a Zig literal does: 0x, 0o, 0b, or decimal. The function also accepts underscores. Give a user a different report for each of the two errors: error.InvalidCharacter means that the text was not a number. error.Overflow means that the text was a number, but the type is too small. A config parser that says "port must be a number" for 70000 does not help the user. The error already told you which problem occurred. The target type does the bounds check, thus you do not write a separate range check. The check cannot disagree with the field that gets the value, because the type of the field is the range. A parse into u16 for a port number rejects 70000, and you write no code for that check. parseFloat accepts the usual decimal and scientific forms. It also accepts inf and nan. The two functions parse the full string. Thus whitespace at the end or an unwanted newline causes an error. The function does not ignore the whitespace. When the input comes from a file or a terminal, remove the

title: Interfaces
description: No interface keyword. Four shapes instead, and what each shape costs.
headings: 1. anytype: a check at each call
Give the caller a better error
2. A tagged union: a closed list
3. A pointer and a vtable: an open list
text: Zig has no interface keyword. It has no trait, no impl and no implements. But the standard library has many interfaces. std.mem.Allocator is one, std.Io is one, and std.Io.Writer is one. The standard library makes them from parts that you already know: anytype, tagged unions, function pointers and @fieldParentPtr. There are four common ways to put those parts together. Each way loses a different thing. This chapter makes the same small interface in the four ways. Thus you can see the cost of each way. The task A sink takes lines of text. The program has two sinks: Counter counts lines and bytes. Last keeps a copy of the most recent line. The two types have a method with the same signature, write(self, line: []const u8) void. Neither type knows about the other type. The question is how to write code that works with the two types. 1. anytype: a check at each call sendAll never names a type. It calls target.write and expects that the method exists. The compiler checks this at each call. sendAll(&counter, ...) compiles one copy of sendAll for Counter. sendAll(&last, ...) compiles a second copy for Last. anytype counter: 3 lines, 24 bytes last: "network down!" Each call to write is a direct call. The program does no lookup at runtime. Thus the optimizer can inline write into the loop. This is how generic code works in Zig. Comptime shows the comptime T: type form. anytype is the same idea, but the type comes from the argument. You do not pass the type yourself. The standard library uses anytype in many places. std.mem.sort takes its context as anytype, and most functions that ac

title: Inline Loops
description: Unrolled loops where each iteration can have a different type.
headings: Iterate over values of different types
The compiler knows the loop variable
If you used an older version of Zig
text: In Zig, inline for compiles the loop body one time for each iteration. Thus each iteration can handle a value of a different type. Code uses inline for to visit the elements of a tuple or the fields of a struct. inline for unrolls the loop at compile time. Sometimes this helps performance, but the main reason for inline for is types . Iterate over values of different types The elements of a tuple have different types. The compiler compiles a normal loop body one time, thus a normal loop cannot handle the different types. The compiler compiles an inline for body separately for each iteration. Thus @TypeOf(value) can be different each time: inline for (tuple) value { if (@TypeOf(value) == bool) { ... } } std.debug.print uses inline for to visit its arguments. Serialisation code uses it to visit the fields of a struct. The if in that body is not a runtime branch. In each unrolled copy, the compiler knows @TypeOf(value) at comptime. Thus the condition becomes true or false during compilation, and the compiler generates only the branch that remains. A chain of twelve if conditions on types has no runtime cost, because eleven of the arms do not exist in the output. The compiler knows the loop variable Inside inline for (0..4) i , i is a comptime value. Thus you can use i where the compiler must have a comptime value, for example in array lengths, type construction or field names: const arr: [i]u8 = undefined; // only valid because i is comptime A comptime loop variable is the thing that makes reflection work. @typeInfo(T).@"struct".field names is a comptime array of strings. When

title: String Recipes
description: Padding, runtime concatenation, and the std.mem and std.ascii calls that the Strings chapter does not show.
headings: Padding is a spec, not a function
The width counts bytes, not characters
When you want a String type
text: To pad a string in Zig, give it a width in the format spec, as in {s: Padding is a spec, not a function Zig has no lpad, no rjust and no String.padStart. To pad a string, give {s} a width. The grammar is the one that Formatting shows: {[fill][align][width]}. For a string, two things are different: the default, and the unit of the width. Right alignment is the default for all types. Thus {s:8} puts the spaces before the text. This can surprise you if you know a language where strings align left and numbers align right. Write the alignment that you want: "{s:8}" // " zig" "{s: 8}" // ".....zig" The width is a minimum. If a value is wider than the field, the formatter prints the full value, and the column becomes wider. The formatter never truncates a value. The width counts bytes, not characters The formatter does not decode the value first. The standard library says this in its own docs: alignment "is not Unicode-aware; appropriate only when used with raw bytes or ASCII." A table of names stays aligned until one of the names has an accent. To count what a reader calls a character is a different problem. Unicode Recipes shows how to solve it. Join at runtime ++ is a compile-time operator. When the program knows the parts only at runtime, use std.mem.concat. It does the same work, and it takes an allocator. joinZ puts a separator between the parts and a null terminator at the end. Use it when you give the result to a C API. If you prefer to calculate the buffer size yourself, use std.fmt.count. It runs the formatter with a writer that discards its output, and it returns the ex

title: Opaque
description: Types with unknown size, used through pointers only.
headings: Why an opaque type is useful
text: In Zig, opaque {} is the equivalent of the incomplete type in C. Use it for handles that code can hold only through a pointer. translate-c produces handles of this type from a C header. An opaque {} type has an unknown size and layout. You can never have a value of the type. You can have only a pointer to a value. The compiler really does not know the size. If you ask for the size, the compiler refuses: error: no size available for uninstantiable type note: opaque declared here Thus each of these fails, because each one needs a size: @sizeOf on the type. A local variable of the type. An array of the type. A struct field of the type. Only a pointer works. The size of a pointer comes from the machine, not from the type that the pointer points at. Why an opaque type is useful An opaque type is the Zig form of an incomplete type in C: typedef struct Window Window; / definition not provided / Window create window(void); The library gives you a Window, and you can only give it back to the library. You cannot examine it, copy it, or put it on the stack. Its size is not part of the public interface. The compiler enforces this rule. Thus the rule does not depend on callers who read the documentation. When a library shows a struct definition, its layout cannot change. If the library adds a field, the size changes. Then each caller that put the struct on the stack has the wrong quantity of memory. An opaque type has no public layout. Thus the library can change its layout in a later version, and code that uses it does not have to compile again. Better than void The usual alternative i

title: Unicode Recipes
description: Truncate on a character boundary, decode one codepoint, and convert to UTF-16.
headings: Look ahead, and views that cannot fail
Bytes that you did not validate
text: To truncate a UTF-8 string in Zig without a cut through a character, walk nextCodepointSlice. Stop before the slice that goes past the limit. To convert to and from UTF-16, use std.unicode.utf8ToUtf16LeAlloc and utf16LeToUtf8Alloc. Length from the first byte UTF-8 puts the sequence length in the lead byte. Thus you can decode one character, and you do not have to scan forward to find the start of the next character. utf8ByteSequenceLength reads the length. utf8Decode2, utf8Decode3 or utf8Decode4 changes those bytes into a u21. The length is in the name because each of those functions takes an array of fixed size. An older version had one utf8Decode that took a slice, and that function is now deprecated. It asserted that the length matched the lead byte, and it could not tell you when the length did not match. The new way is to get the length first and then decode that number of bytes. It is the same work, and the design prevents the mistake. If you give utf8ByteSequenceLength a continuation byte, it returns error.Utf8InvalidStartByte. You want this check when an index comes from arithmetic and not from an iterator. utf8CodepointSequenceLength does the opposite work for the encoder. Use it to get the number of bytes that a codepoint needs, before you calculate the size of the buffer. Cut a string safely The Unicode chapter says to iterate over codepoint slices and stop at the last full character. This chapter shows that function: 1. Walk nextCodepointSlice. 2. Keep the end offset of the characters so far. 3. Stop before the first slice that would put the end past the limit.

title: Anonymous Structs
description: Struct literals with an inferred type, and tuples.
text: Zig has anonymous structs in two forms: A struct type that you write inline, at the place where you use it. A tuple. A tuple is a struct with numbered fields instead of named fields. The argument list that you give to print is a tuple. .{ ... } is a struct literal. The literal gets its type from the context. When the compiler knows the target type (a parameter, a field, a return type), you do not have to write the name: describe(.{ .x = 1, .y = 2 }); The same dot at the start occurs in each place where the compiler can infer a type: .north for an enum tag. .{ .ok = value } for a union variant. .{} for a struct with a default value for each field. These are one rule, not four. The dot means "you know the type, so I do not write the type again". If the compiler does not know the target type, it has no type to infer. Then you must write the name of the type in the literal: const p = Point{ .x = 1, .y = 2 }; // no context, so say the type Anonymous struct types You can also write a struct type inline. The describe function in the snippet does this: fn describe(point: struct { x: i32, y: i32 }) i32 { return point.x + point.y; } An inline type is useful for a shape that you use one time and that does not need a name. It is also useful when a function returns several values and you do not want to declare a type for them. Two anonymous struct types that you write separately are different types, also when their fields are the same. Thus, use them for local convenience. Do not use them for types that cross an interface. Tuples If you do not write the field names, you get a tuple. A t

title: Sentinel Termination
description: Sequences that end in a known marker.
headings: The sentinel can be a value other than zero
How this is different from C strings
text: In Zig, a string literal has the type const [N:0]u8. [:0]u8 is the slice form of a zero-terminated sequence, and [ :0]u8 is the pointer form. You can give these types to C without a copy. A sentinel-terminated type guarantees a specific value immediately after the end. In the syntax, the value comes after a colon: Type Meaning --- --- [3:0]u8 3 bytes, plus a guaranteed 0 at index 3 [:0]u8 slice with a 0 after the last element [ :0]u8 many-item pointer, terminated by 0 .len does not count the sentinel. But the sentinel is really in memory, and you can read it. A [:0]u8 has a length, as each slice has. Thus iteration over it has bounds checks, and .len is one instruction. The type also promises a zero after the last element. Thus you can give it to C without a copy. One value holds the length and the terminator. The sentinel can be a value other than zero 0 is the usual case, because C strings are the usual case. But the value is part of the type: [:255]u8 and [: '\n']u8 are legal. You can use this form for any data that has a known terminator. Sometimes a protocol buffer or a line reader can use the type to state its rule, and a comment is not necessary. String literals have a sentinel const literal = "hi"; // const [2:0]u8 literal.len; // 2 literal[2]; // 0 Thus, when you give a Zig string literal to a C function that wants const char , you need no conversion and no copy. Usual Zig code still has the length. Thus the C compatibility has no cost for Zig code. The type is a pointer to an array , not a slice. For this reason, a literal has a comptime-known length, and @TypeOf(

title: Vectors
description: SIMD with ordinary operators.
text: Zig gives you SIMD as a type, @Vector(N, T), not as a library of intrinsics. std.simd.suggestVectorLength selects N for the target. @Vector(N, T) is a SIMD vector of N lanes. Arithmetic operators work element by element across all lanes at the same time. Where the target has vector instructions, the operators compile to real vector instructions: const sum = a + b; // one operation, four lanes SIMD means "single instruction, multiple data". One machine instruction does the same arithmetic on many values at the same time. A 128-bit register holds four i32 values, and one add instruction adds all four. In Zig, you write that add with a usual operator on a vector type. You do not use an intrinsic with a name such as mm add epi32. The builtins for vectors Builtin Does --- --- @splat(x) fill every lane with x @reduce(.Add, v) collapse lanes to one value @select(T, mask, a, b) pick lane-wise between two vectors @shuffle rearrange lanes A comparison produces a @Vector(N, bool) mask, not one bool. Thus you use @reduce(.Or, mask) or @select to act on the result. The mask replaces branches. If you wrote only scalar code before, this needs practice: A scalar loop says "if this element matches, do the action". A vector version computes the condition for all lanes at the same time. Then it uses the mask to select between two answers that it already computed. There is no branch for each lane. For this reason, the vector version is fast. For the same reason, work that is different for each element does not vectorise. Select N std.simd.suggestVectorLength(T) asks the target how many lanes o

title: Slow Clients
description: A member that does not read fills its outbox. The hub puts with a minimum of 0, drops the member when nothing fits, and the room does not wait.
text: A client can stop. It reads nothing more. Its network can be slow, its laptop can sleep, or its process can stop in a debugger. The server still has lines for that client, and the lines wait in its outbox. The outbox has a fixed capacity, thus it fills. When the outbox is full, the hub has three choices: 1. Wait until the writer takes a line out. 2. Discard the line , and keep the member. 3. Drop the member. The first choice is the dangerous one. The hub holds its lock during a broadcast. If the broadcast waits for one member, each other member that talks waits for the lock. One laptop in sleep mode then stops the room. The second choice keeps the room alive, but a member who misses lines has a wrong view of the conversation, and nothing tells that member. This hub uses the third choice. Put, and never wait The last argument of put is min, the number of elements that put must add before it returns. With min set to 1, put waits for space. With min set to 0, put adds what fits now and returns at once. A return of 0 means that the outbox is full. deliver does not remove the member. It only marks the peer with close code 1008. deliver runs inside the loop of broadcast, and that loop reads members. A change to members inside the loop would skip a member or visit one twice. dropSlow runs after the broadcast. It removes each member that deliver marked, closes its outbox, and tells the others. The notice is a broadcast too, and it can fill another outbox. Thus dropSlow repeats until no member has the mark. Each pass removes one member, so the loop ends. A member that reads nothing

title: Prefix Sums and Difference Arrays
description: One subtraction instead of a loop, an extra cell for index 0, and the same method in reverse for range updates.
headings: Calculate a range sum with one subtraction
Change the differences back to values
A running sum undoes a difference array
text: A range-sum query asks for the total of one part of an array. This problem has many of these queries. For one query, a loop can add the values in the range. This method is satisfactory when there are only a small number of queries. But with 100,000 values and 100,000 queries, a loop over each range can need billions of additions. A prefix sum prepares the array one time. After that, one subtraction gives the sum of a range. Build the prefix array The prefix array keeps cumulative sums. pre[i] is the sum of the first i values. Because of this definition, the prefix array has one more cell than the original array. pre[0] is the sum of zero values. Thus pre[0] is 0. pre[1] contains the first value. pre[2] contains the sum of the first two values. The other cells continue in the same way. The prefix array for the example input is: idx 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 val 3 1 4 1 5 9 2 6 the prefix array holds 9 cells for 8 values idx 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 pre 0 3 4 8 9 14 23 25 31 The prefix indices are easier to understand as boundaries. pre[3] is 8, because pre[3] holds the three values before index 3: 3 + 1 + 4. pre[0] is the boundary before the first value. pre[8] is the boundary after the last value. Without the extra cell at index 0, a range that starts at index 0 needs a special case. For example, code that uses pre[lo - 1] fails when lo is 0. The extra zero at the start lets the same formula work for all ranges. Calculate a range sum with one subtraction Use the half-open range [lo, hi): pre[hi] contains the sum of all values before hi. pre[lo] contains the sum of all values before lo. Thus

title: Queues
description: Io.Queue as a bounded channel between tasks, with close and back pressure.
headings: Capacity is a buffer that you supply
put and get take a minimum
Close the queue to tell the receiver to stop
text: Tasks that only start and stop need a Future. Tasks that give work to other tasks while they run need a queue. std.Io.Queue is the bounded channel: It has a fixed capacity. The two ends can block. The sender can close the queue. Capacity is a buffer that you supply var storage: [4]u32 = undefined; var queue: std.Io.Queue(u32) = .init(&storage); The queue allocates nothing. It is a ring over the array that you give it. Thus you decide its capacity, its lifetime and its location, the same as with Io.Writer. Usually, the queue is on the stack of the function that spawns the two tasks. put and get take a minimum const accepted = try queue.put(io, &.{ 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 }, 0); The last argument is the number of elements that the call must move before it can return. putAll and putOne move all the elements or block. A minimum of zero never blocks. The call moves the elements that fit and returns the count. Above, the count is 4, because the capacity is 4. get works in exactly the same way. That parameter makes batches cheap. A consumer can ask for a minimum of one and give a buffer of 64. Then one call gets all the elements that are in the queue now. The call blocks only when the queue is empty. Close the queue to tell the receiver to stop queue.close(io); A closed queue rejects new elements immediately. But it delivers all the elements that are already in the buffer before it reports error.Closed. Thus the loop reads until the error, and it knows that it lost no elements: while (queue.getOne(io)) value { total += value; } else err { ... } The consumer does not need to know how many

title: Binary Files
description: A small binary format with a header, written one field at a time, and a reader that checks each byte that it did not write.
headings: Why not write the struct directly
text: A text file stores numbers as characters. The number 1200 is four bytes: '1', '2', '0', '0'. A binary file stores the number itself. As a u32, 1200 is also four bytes. But the bytes are the bits of the number, not digits. Binary files are smaller and faster to read, because the program does not have to parse them. But a person cannot read them. Thus you must write down the format exactly. The program below defines a small format for a list of players. It writes a file in that format and reads the file again. Then it gives the reader three bad files. Write the format first Before the code, the snippet writes down the format in a comment. // header, 10 bytes // 0 magic 4 bytes "SCOR" // 4 version u16 1 // 6 count u32 number of records // // record, 9 bytes + name // 0 id u32 // 4 score i32 // 8 name len u8 // 9 name name len bytes Each byte has a position, a size and a meaning. All integers are little-endian. This table is the format. The code only obeys the table. A program in a different language can read the file if it obeys the same table. Byte order A u32 is four bytes, and a computer can store the four bytes in two orders. little 04030201 big 01020304 Little-endian puts the smallest byte first. x86 and ARM computers use this order. Big-endian puts the largest byte first. Network protocols frequently use this order. The two orders are equally correct. The important thing is that the format says which order it uses, and that the code gives the order on each read and write. For this reason, writeInt and takeInt both take the byte order as an argument. There is no default.

title: The Loop Takes No dt
description: A fixed timestep, an accumulator, interpolation for the leftover time, and the split that the browser build needs.
text: The usual game loop reads the clock and gives the elapsed time to the world. while (running) { const dt = getFrameTime(); world.update(dt); // do not do this draw(world); } This loop causes three problems. The same inputs do not give the same run. The value of dt is the time that the machine gave. A 60 Hz laptop and a 165 Hz monitor move the world in different steps. If you add 1/60 sixty times, the result is not the same number as when you add 1/165 one hundred and sixty-five times. A slow frame becomes an advantage. The score in this game measures survival. A frame that takes 50 ms moves the world 50 ms forward in one jump. The game tests for collision at the two ends of that jump, and not between them. If the game stops for a moment, the player can move through a block. No run can replay. To report a crash, you must record a video of the crash. A seed and a list of key presses do not make the same crash on a different machine. Fixed steps step has no dt parameter. It moves the world forward by one tick, and a tick always has the same size. A caller cannot use step incorrectly. A caller cannot get half a tick. To get ten ticks, a caller calls step ten times. The tick rate is 120 Hz. This rate is more than each common refresh rate. Thus the simulation is never the cause when the motion of the game looks rough. The accumulator Real time arrives in parts of different sizes. The loop saves the time and uses it one tick at a time. The input goes to the first tick of the frame. The input for the other ticks is empty. A key press is an edge trigger. If one press went to three ti

title: Imports
description: Files are structs, and pub controls the boundary.
headings: A file can be the type
text: In Zig, each file is a struct. pub marks the declarations that other files can see. A declaration without pub is private to its file. @import takes a path and returns that file as a struct type : const shapes = @import(" shapes.zig"); shapes.Circle{ .radius = 2 }; Zig has no separate module system to learn. @import evaluates the file. Then you get its declarations with ., the same as for any other struct. The result is a value, thus you select the name for it. const s = @import("std") works exactly as well as const std = @import("std"). If you import the same file two times, you get the same type two times. Thus you get no problem with duplicate definitions, and you need no include guard. pub is the boundary Only pub declarations are visible to the files that import a file: pub const pi = 3.14159; // visible const secret = 42; // not Zig needs nothing more for visibility. Zig has no private keyword, no header files and no export lists. To give a type a private implementation, put the type in its own file. To let two files see the internals of each other, merge the two files. A file can be the type A file is a struct. Thus, if a file declares fields at the top level, the file is that struct. When you import the file, you get the type directly: // Point.zig x: f32, y: f32, pub fn magnitude(self: @This()) f32 { ... } const Point = @import("Point.zig"); const p: Point = .{ .x = 3, .y = 4 }; This convention is the reason for the capitalised filenames in the standard library. std.Io.Writer is in Writer.zig, and the file has no wrapper declaration around it. A lowercase filename m

title: Make a Type
description: Make integer, struct, enum and tuple types from comptime values, and write a Partial(T) patch type.
headings: An enum of the field names
A tuple from a list of types
If you used an older version of Zig
text: The last chapter read the description of a type. This chapter goes in the other direction: a function makes a description, and a builtin changes the description into a new type. Zig has one builtin for each kind of type that you can make: @Int makes an integer type. @Struct makes a struct type. @Enum makes an enum type. @Union makes a union type. @Tuple makes a tuple type. @Pointer and @Fn make pointer and function types. The program uses four of them. An integer of any width const U12 = @Int(.unsigned, 12); U12 is the same type as u12. @Int is useful when the width is a calculation, for example one bit for each item in a list: 1. u12: 12 bits, 2 bytes, max 4095 @bitSizeOf gives the 12 bits that the value uses. @sizeOf gives 2 bytes, because memory stores a value in whole bytes. A struct from another struct Partial(T) has the same fields as T, but each field is optional, with a default of null. A value of Partial(Config) is a patch: it sets only the fields that it wants to change. fn Partial(comptime T: type) type { const info = @typeInfo(T).@"struct"; var types: [info.field names.len]type = undefined; var attrs: [info.field names.len]std.lang.Type.Struct.FieldAttributes = undefined; for (info.field types, &types, &attrs) F, slot, attr { slot. = ?F; attr. = .{ .default value ptr = &@as(?F, null) }; } return @Struct(.auto, null, info.field names, &types, &attrs); } Partial is a usual function with a comptime parameter. It runs during compilation because its result is a type. The loop is a usual for, not an inline for, because the loop body builds arrays and does not need one

title: Three Ways to Frame
description: Length prefix, delimiter, self-describing, and the cost of each one.
text: The previous chapter showed that a stream has no message boundaries. Framing adds the boundaries again. There are three ways to frame a message. Each protocol that you know selects one of these three ways. The hex below shows each of the three. Length prefix 00 04 50 49 4e 47 ^^^^^ length ^^^^^^^^^^^ payload Before the receiver reads one byte of payload, the receiver knows exactly how many bytes to wait for. This property makes the parser in the last chapter possible. For this reason, a length prefix is the default selection for all binary data. The framing does not change the payload. Thus the payload can contain any byte, and also the newline that the next method cannot carry. The cost is that you must know the length before you start to write. Thus you must put the full message in a buffer, or know its size before you start. Delimiter 50 49 4e 47 0a ^^^^^^^^^^^ payload ^^ '\n' A delimiter is cheap to write and cheap to read. A person can also read it on the wire. For these reasons, HTTP, SMTP, IMAP and Redis use a delimiter for their text parts. You can debug the protocol with nc, because you can read the bytes. The cost is that the delimiter byte can never occur in a payload. The last line of the output shows what occurs when the payload contains the byte. The reader stops too early and does not report an error. For the reader, the message ended at the correct place for the end of a message. The reader uses the other bytes as the next message. Real protocols solve this problem in one of two ways: They escape the delimiter byte in the payload. They put a length prefix on

title: Validation from Declarations
description: Optional capabilities found with @hasDecl, the convention-over-configuration of Zig.
headings: Errors occur in the correct build
The standard library does the same thing
text: A Zig library finds optional behavior for each type with @hasDecl at compile time. A schema that declares pub const rules = .{ ... } gets validation. A schema without that declaration gets no validation code. The problem Your library needs optional behavior for each type: validation rules on one schema, custom serialization on another schema, and nothing on a third schema. The classical answers are interfaces and inheritance, and Zig has neither. Zig has a method that is better for libraries. The caller declares the behavior that it supports. The library asks for that declaration at compile time. The pattern 1. The convention: a schema can declare pub const rules = .{ ... }, with the names of its own fields. 2. The library checks @hasDecl(T, "rules") before it touches rules. If the declaration does not exist, there is no validation and no generated code. 3. inline for walks the rules. On each rule struct, @hasField decides which checks apply. Each lookup resolves at compile time. The work at runtime is only the comparisons. Errors occur in the correct build The compiler finds two mistakes when the caller builds. The library author does no work for this: A rule for a field that does not exist: @field(value, "nmae") cannot resolve. A min len rule on an integer field: v.len does not exist on u8. For this reason, use declarations and not registration functions. A call to registerValidator("name", ...) at runtime can fail only at runtime. The compiler analyzes a declaration against the schema while it has both open. The standard library does the same thing This pattern did not s

title: Spawn a Process
description: A child is a program, an argument list, and a status code that the parent receives.
text: To run another program, you make three decisions: What to run. What the program inherits. What to do with the number that the program leaves when it ends. The snippet runs itself const len = try std.process.executablePath(io, &path buf); const ok = try std.process.run(gpa, io, .{ .argv = &.{ path buf[0..len], "ok" } }); The snippet does not use /bin/echo, and this is intentional. A chapter that runs a system binary fails on each computer that keeps that binary in a different place. This site claims that CI ran each snippet today. executablePath gives the program that runs its own path. A first argument tells the copy which part of the program to run. Real programs also do this. A supervisor can start itself again with a flag to spawn workers. Thus the supervisor is sure that the workers have the same version as the supervisor. run against spawn std.process.run does four things in one call: 1. It spawns the child. 2. It reads standard output and standard error to end of file. 3. It waits for the child. 4. It gives you the two buffers. Use run when the output is small and you want all of the output.
