Do not use run when the output is large, or when you must react to the output when it arrives. .stdout limit sets the maximum quantity of output that run collects. If the output is more than that limit, run returns error.StreamTooLong. Thus run does not fill memory while a child continues to write. std.process.spawn returns immediately when the child exists. After that, you control everything: the streams that you asked for, when to read them, and when to wait. Pipes uses that cal

title: The Tip
description: A dab is a disc with a soft edge. Make it an ellipse, turn it, and the same twenty lines draw a soft brush, a calligraphy nib and a ribbon.
headings: Make the tip flat and turn it
Explain before you read the answer
text: A dab tells where the brush touched and how large the dab was. The tip decides which pixels the dab covers, and how much it covers them. For each pixel, the answer is a number from 0 to 1, the coverage . 1 is full coverage, 0 is no coverage, and 0.5 is half coverage. The engine calculates the coverage for three types of tip: A round tip with a soft edge. A flat tip, which is an ellipse. A flat tip at an angle. The angle is fixed, or it follows the stroke. Which pixels to examine A dab can touch only the pixels within its radius from its centre. Thus the code examines the square around the dab, cut at the edges of the image, and no other pixels: A 20-pixel dab examines a 40 by 40 square, which is 1,600 pixels. The full 640 by 400 image is 256,000 pixels. Thus, for each dab, the square is 160 times less work. The code calculates the square in f32 and clamps it before it changes it to an integer. A dab can start far outside the image. A direct conversion from a negative f32 to a u32 is illegal behaviour, and Zig examines it in safe builds. A soft round tip For a round tip, the coverage depends only on the distance d from the centre of the dab to the centre of the pixel. The hardness of the brush is the solid part of the radius. With radius 20 and hardness 0.6: Inside 12 pixels (0.6 × 20), the coverage is 1. From 12 to 20 pixels, the coverage decreases in a straight line from 1 to 0. After 20 pixels, the coverage is 0. At 16 pixels, which is the middle of the soft band, the coverage is 0.5. At hardness 1, the band has no width. Then the edge of each dab is a staircase of full p

title: Readers and Writers
description: The buffered Reader and Writer interfaces introduced in Zig 0.15.
headings: Flush, and where to put the flush
Read lines: select the correct variant
text: In Zig, code reads bytes through std.Io.Reader and writes bytes through std.Io.Writer. Thus one parser or formatter works with a file, a socket or a fixed buffer. Zig 0.15 replaced the old generic Reader and Writer with the non-generic std.Io.Reader and std.Io.Writer. Two of the changes are important in daily work: 1. The buffer belongs to the interface , not to the implementation. You supply the buffer. Thus there is no hidden allocation, and you control the size. 2. Writers have a buffer , thus you must call flush. A common mistake with the new API is to forget the flush. The important word in the first sentence is "non-generic". The old Writer was a type parameter. Thus each function that took a writer was generic, and the compiler compiled it again for each writer type. A struct that stored a writer also had to be generic. std.Io.Writer is a concrete type that holds a pointer and a vtable. Thus a function takes a std.Io.Writer and needs nothing more. Compile times become shorter, error messages become shorter, and you can put a writer in a field. Create them var reader: std.Io.Reader = .fixed("some bytes"); var writer: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&buf); var growable: std.Io.Writer.Allocating = .init(gpa); For files, file.writerStreaming(io, &buf) gives you a File.Writer. The .interface field of the File.Writer is the std.Io.Writer to use. Learn to recognise that .interface field, because it is a pattern. The concrete type holds the state that a file writer needs. It also contains the generic interface as a field. Thus you give &file writer.interface to each function that tak

title: Routes Over a Seam
description: All five CRUD routes as one pure function, with tests against an in-memory store.
headings: Read the trace as a contract
The order of the routes is important
text: All five CRUD routes of a URL shortener fit in one Zig function. handle takes request bytes and a store, and writes a complete HTTP response. An in-memory store is behind the seam. Thus the tests of each route need no server, no socket and no database. The problem In the HTTP surface, create, read, update and delete become routes. This layer also has the most cases that you must make correct: The slug that does not exist. The URL that fails validation. The method that no code handles. If you test those cases against a live server and database, you must start the server and the database for each case. The solution is the same seam that the ORM's Repo chapter built. Put the storage behind an interface. Then give the handler the implementation that it needs at that time. The in-memory store needs no server and no database. Thus this chapter runs in your browser. The plan 1. A Store that holds links in a fixed array. The store has only the methods that the routes can use: create and find. 2. handle: parse the request line, dispatch on the method and the path, and write a complete HTTP response. The request parsing is the minimum that works. The web server track shows the full parsing. 3. A demo that runs all five routes and the failure cases, and prints each exchange. Read the trace as a contract The demo is the specification of the service, with one exchange for each case: Create answers 201 with the slug. The bad scheme answers 400, before the storage gets the request. The redirect answers 302 and counts the hit. Update changes the target of the same slug. Delete answers 204.

title: Array Recipes
description: Grids, lookup tables made at compile time, and how to get an array from a slice.
headings: A grid is an array of arrays
The outer loop gives you a copy
Make a table at compile time
Change a slice back to an array
text: When arrays become larger than small examples, you need three things: A grid. A table that the compiler calculates at compile time. A fixed-size array that you take from a slice. The three are language mechanics. None of them needs an allocator. A grid is an array of arrays [3][3]u8 is nine bytes in one contiguous block. The two lengths are part of the type. grid.len is the number of rows, and grid[0].len is the number of columns. @sizeOf shows that the grid contains no hidden pointer. Use the row index first, then the column index. [3][3]u8 is not the same type as [][]u8, a slice of slices. A slice of slices is a list of pointers to rows, and the rows can be at any location in memory. The nested array is one block, and it needs no allocation. The slice of slices has as many blocks as the code that made it. The outer loop gives you a copy The Arrays chapter states that arrays are values. In a nested loop, this rule has a direct effect. for (grid) row copies each row. Thus a write through row changes nothing in grid. The compiler does not give an error, because the code is valid. for (&grid) row iterates over pointers, and then for (row) cell gets the elements. The two levels must be pointers before a write can change the grid. Use one flat array The other shape is [width height]T with the index y width + x. The type does not contain the geometry. Thus you must keep the stride correct yourself. In return, the dimensions do not have to be two separate compile-time constants. Use the nested array when the shape is fixed and small. Use the flat array in these three conditions:

title: JSON
description: Parse JSON into real types, and write the types back as JSON.
headings: How the types map to JSON
When you do not know the shape
text: std.json.parseFromSlice parses JSON into your own Zig struct. It matches the object keys to the field names. std.json.Stringify.value writes a value as JSON to any writer. Parse into a struct parseFromSlice(T, gpa, text, .{}) puts JSON into your type by the field names of the type. The result owns each allocation that it made: const parsed = try std.json.parseFromSlice(Config, gpa, text, .{}); defer parsed.deinit(); parsed.value.port; Look at parsed.value. The payload is behind the owner, thus one deinit frees the full tree. The strings in parsed.value point into that arena, thus they become invalid with the arena. If a value must live longer than the parse, duplicate the value. This design solves a problem that each JSON library has. A parsed document is a tree of small allocations with no single owner. To free the tree correctly, you must walk the tree. The Zig solution is to allocate the full tree from an arena in the Parsed(T) wrapper. Then deinit is one call that releases all of the memory at the same time, and it cannot miss a node. The cost is that the lifetime is all or nothing. If you keep one string from the document, the string does not keep the arena alive. After deinit, the arena is gone, and you have a dangling slice. Copy out the values that you need. Or keep the full Parsed alive while you use any part of it. How the types map to JSON The compiler decides the mapping from your struct at compile time. The validation comes from this mapping. Zig JSON --- --- bool, integers, floats the matching primitive []const u8 a string ?T the value, or null, or absent []T

title: Slice Recipes
description: Reverse, rotate, shift and search a slice, in place and without an allocator.
headings: In place means that the length does not change
An index belongs to its slice
text: A slice is a pointer and a length. Thus each recipe on this page writes to memory that already exists. No allocator is on this page. In place means that the length does not change std.mem.reverse and std.mem.rotate write to the same bytes and return nothing. The two functions work on each []T. When you reverse a []const u8, the function reverses the bytes, not the characters. Outside ASCII, this breaks each sequence of more than one byte, and the result is invalid UTF-8. Unicode Recipes is about this problem and others. Copies that overlap @memcpy requires that the source and the destination do not overlap. A shift of elements inside one slice always overlaps. A release build does not tell you about the error. The check is a safety check, so it is not in the build where the bug costs the most. @memmove handles the overlap. It works in the two directions. Before @memmove, there was the pair std.mem.copyForwards and std.mem.copyBackwards. With @memmove, you do not have to select a direction, and you cannot select the wrong direction. The two older functions are now deprecated, and the builtin replaces them. Use @memcpy when you know that the ranges do not overlap. Use @memmove when the ranges possibly overlap. Remove an element To remove an element, do these steps: 1. Move the tail one position lower, over the gap. 2. Make the slice one element shorter. The backing array always keeps its length. Only the slice becomes shorter. orderedRemove does these steps for you on an ArrayList. Here they are without the container. Stop at a value std.mem.sliceTo takes the part of a buffer

title: Filesystem
description: Each disk operation now takes an Io.
headings: A directory is a handle, not a string
text: Zig 0.16 moved the filesystem API onto std.Io. Of all the changes, this change most often makes older filesystem examples fail to compile. What moved Was Now --- --- std.fs.cwd() std.Io.Dir.cwd() std.fs.File std.Io.File dir.openFile(path, .{}) dir.openFile(io, path, .{}) file.close() file.close(io) The pattern is the same everywhere. Each function that can block takes the io instance as its first argument. You get the instance from main: pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void { const io = init.io; The reason for the change The signature of a function now tells you if the function does I/O. An Allocator parameter tells you in the same way that a function allocates. The caller decides how the I/O runs: threaded, evented or a different way. The standard library does not make the decision for you. title: Bristles and Paper
description: A row of thin hairs across the stroke gives separate tracks. A fixed grid of paper heights decides where a dry brush touches.
headings: Explain before you read the answer
text: A real brush is not a solid disc. It is a bundle of hairs. When the brush has much paint, the hairs push together and make one solid mark. When the brush is almost dry, each hair makes its own thin track. The tracks break at each dip in the surface of the paper. The Dry brush in the studio does both. It needs two new brush settings: bristles : the number of hairs, from 0 (a solid tip) to 16. contact : how much of the paper the brush touches, from 0 to 1. Hairs across the stroke A bristle brush stamps one small round dab for each hair, instead of one large dab. The hairs are in a row across the stroke, at right angles to its movement. If the stroke moves in direction θ, the direction straight across the stroke is: (−sin θ, cos θ) For a movement to the right, θ is 0, and the result is (0, 1): straight down the page. For a movement down the page, θ is a quarter turn, and the result is (−1, 0): to the left. In both cases, the direction is across the stroke. Each hair has an offset from −1 (one edge of the tip) to 1 (the other edge). The position of the hair is the centre of the dab, plus the product of the direction across, the offset and the radius. With radius 20 and offset −0.5, a stroke that moves to the right puts that hair 10 pixels above the centre. The direction comes from the stroke. Each dab now has its direction of movement, and also the angle of the tip. The two values are separate because you can turn a tip to any angle, but the hairs must always spread across the path. The positions of the hairs Hairs at exactly equal distances look like a comb. Thus the code move

title: Oil: Pickup and Paint Load
description: An oil brush carries paint. It collects some of the colour below it, and it becomes dry as it moves.
headings: Explain before you read the answer
text: Each brush in the previous chapters puts down one colour. The colour is the same at the end of a stroke and at the start. A brush with oil paint is different. Two things change while the brush moves: Pickup. The brush collects some of the paint below it. Thus its colour moves towards the colour below it. Load. The brush becomes dry. It has less paint after each centimetre, and the stroke becomes fainter. Select the Oil brush in the studio. Paint some colours, and then pull the Oil brush across them. The brush carries paint For these two effects, the stroke must keep two values from one dab to the next. The values are the colour on the brush and the quantity of paint that remains. Thus the stroke has two new fields: The first value of loaded is the brush colour. The first value of load is 1, which is a full brush. Each stroke starts with a full brush. Pickup Before each dab, the brush examines the paint below it. Then it moves its colour part of the distance to that paint: loaded = loaded + (under − loaded) × pickup This is lerp again, one time each for red, green and blue. For example, the loaded red is 200, the paint below it has red 100, and pickup is 0.2. The new loaded red is 200 + (100 − 200) × 0.2 = 180. Over the same paint again, the result is 180 + (100 − 180) × 0.2 = 164. The brush carries the colour to the next dab. Thus the paint from one area moves a short distance along the stroke, and that is the smear. The pickup occurs in emit: The code keeps loaded in f32, not in bytes. A small pickup moves each channel by less than 1. In bytes, the rounding removes that ch

The server does not get the close code, and the rest of the frame stays unread in the stream. The second gap has a cost that is easy to miss. If the server closes its socket with unread bytes, the kernel sends a reset in place of a normal close. Thus the server in A WebSocket Server on a Socket had to wait for the client to close first. RFC 6455 asks for the opposite order. The client in A WebSocket Client already reads frames itself. This reader is the server half of that code, with three differences: 1. Each frame from a client must have the mask, and the reader removes it. 2. The reserved bits must be 0, because the server agreed to no extension. 3. The reader reads a close frame to its end, and returns the code and the reason. The reader The structure is the same as the client: control frames first, then data frames, with the state of a message in fragments in two fields. The size check comes before the payload. The length field of a frame can say 2 63 bytes. The reader compares the length with the space left in buffer and refuses the frame before it reads one byte of payload. The reader allocates nothing, thus a large length cannot make the server use memory. Control frames use the buffer of the reader, not buffer. A ping can arrive between two fragments. title: The Monotonic Stack
description: A stack of the indices that still wait for an answer, and the two counters that show the inner loop keeps the total linear.
headings: The stack keeps the indices that wait for an answer
Why the nested loop is still O(n)
text: The problem: for each value in an array, find the first larger value to its right. Some values find a larger value immediately. Some values must look much farther. Some values do not have a larger value to their right. A simple solution starts at each index and scans to the right until it finds a larger value. That solution works, but in the worst case it checks almost each pair of values. A monotonic stack solves the same problem in one pass. The question changes. The question is not "What is the answer for this index?". The question is "Which earlier indices can the current value answer?". The stack keeps the indices that still wait for a larger value. Scan right from each index The direct solution is easy to understand. For each index, scan to the right until you find a larger value: If you find a larger value, store it. If you get to the end of the array, that index has no answer. This solution is correct. The problem is the number of comparisons, and the number changes with the input. For an array in ascending order such as 1 2 3 4 5, each value except the last value finds its answer immediately. Thus each of these indices needs only one comparison. For an array in descending order such as 9 8 7 6 5, no value finds a larger value to its right. The first index checks four values, the second index checks three, then two, then one. The total is n(n - 1) / 2 comparisons. Thus the worst-case time complexity is O(n²). The stack keeps the indices that wait for an answer The monotonic-stack solution examines the problem from the other direction. At index i, the solution does n

title: Locks and Semaphores
description: RwLock, Semaphore and Condition, for the cases where a Mutex is not sufficient.
headings: RwLock: many readers or one writer
text: Io.Mutex is sufficient for most shared state. When it is not sufficient, use RwLock, Semaphore or Condition. Each one takes the Io instance, for the same reason as the mutex. A blocking call goes through the interface. Thus you can cancel it, and it works on an implementation with no threads. RwLock: many readers or one writer try rw.lockShared(io); try rw.lockShared(io); Two readers hold the lock at the same time. A writer cannot get the lock with them, and a reader cannot get the lock with a writer. Use an RwLock only when these two conditions are true: Reads are much more frequent than writes. The reads hold the lock for a long time, and that time has an effect. An RwLock does more bookkeeping than a Mutex. Thus, for a short critical section, the plain mutex is usually faster. tryLock and tryLockShared never block. They tell you if they got the lock. The snippet uses them to show two results: while readers hold the lock, the writer cannot get it. When the readers release the lock, the writer gets it. Unlock with the call that agrees with the lock: unlockShared for a shared lock. unlock for an exclusive lock. Semaphore: a count, not exclusion var sem: std.Io.Semaphore = .{ .permits = 2 }; try sem.wait(io); sem.post(io); A semaphore counts permits. wait takes one permit, and it blocks while no permit is available. post adds one permit. A semaphore has no connection to the task that waited. This property makes a semaphore different from a mutex. Use a semaphore to set a limit on the number of tasks in one place at the same time. title: Handles, Not Pointers
description: A pool with a fixed capacity and generational handles, and the event stream that the particles and the sound use.
headings: The storage is a fixed array
text: The game creates blocks and coins above the screen. It destroys them after they leave the bottom. This occurs several times each second while the game runs. The storage is a fixed array A run of any length allocates one time at startup, and never again. The simulation has no allocator. That is one reason why the simulation imports nothing. Forty-eight slots are more than the field can hold. At the smallest spacing and the highest speed, approximately three rows are on the screen. Each row has a maximum of three entities, thus approximately nine entities exist at one time. A test asserts that the peak stays less than the capacity and more than six. Thus the test finds a change that stops the spawns without an error. An index is not sufficient The usual way to refer to an entity is by its index. This causes a bug that is very difficult to reproduce. An event says "the player collected coin 12". One frame later, the pool frees slot 12 and gives it to a new block. Any code that still has the number 12 now reads a block and thinks that the block is a coin. The program does not crash. The score is wrong approximately one time each hour, usually when nobody looks. A pointer instead of an index does not help, because the pool uses the slot again in both cases. Generational handles A handle contains the slot index and the generation of that slot at the time when the pool made the handle. When the pool frees a slot, it increments the generation of the slot. title: Dispatch with Comptime
description: Connect each tag of an enum to its handler at compile time, with a switch or with a table.
headings: Handlers with the same names as the tags
From a string to a tag
A new tag without a handler
text: A program that reads commands must connect each command to the code for that command. The name of this connection is dispatch. In Zig, the commands are often the tags of an enum. The compiler knows each tag, thus it can make the connection during compilation. If a tag has no handler, the build stops. The program below reads five commands from a script. It connects each command to its handler in two ways, and the two results must agree. Handlers with the same names as the tags const Op = enum { add, sub, mul, neg }; const Handlers = struct { pub fn add(a: i64, b: i64) i64 { ... } pub fn sub(a: i64, b: i64) i64 { ... } pub fn mul(a: i64, b: i64) i64 { ... } pub fn neg(a: i64, : i64) i64 { ... } }; Handlers is a struct with no fields. It is a namespace for four functions. Each function has the same name as one tag of Op. The program uses this rule to find the handler for a tag. Dispatch with inline else fn runSwitch(op: Op, a: i64, b: i64) i64 { return switch (op) { inline else = tag @field(Handlers, @tagName(tag))(a, b), }; } inline else makes one branch for each tag. In each branch, tag is comptime-known. Thus @tagName(tag) is a comptime-known string, and @field(Handlers, "add") finds the function Handlers.add. The compiler then has four usual branches, and each branch calls one function directly. The result is the same as a switch that you write by hand, with one line for each tag. The \r is not optional and not guaranteed
Escape the framing when you print it
text: A text protocol is delimiter framing with a grammar in it. This protocol uses the reply syntax of Redis, because that syntax is small and useful. The first byte of a reply tells the reader how to read the rest of the reply. The verb is an enum, not a string const Verb = enum { get, set, del, ping }; const verb = std.meta.stringToEnum(Verb, lowered) orelse return error.UnknownCommand; Convert the verb one time, at the edge. Then each switch after the conversion can be exhaustive. If you add a command to the enum and do not handle the command, the compiler rejects the program. If the verb stays a []const u8, the same mistake gives a request that does nothing and reports nothing. Then a user finds the problem later. parse is the one place where this conversion can occur. It is the only place that knows that the bytes came from outside the program. Normalise at the edge On the wire, commands are not case-sensitive, as in Redis, SMTP and HTTP methods. Change the command to lowercase one time, in parse. Then no later code must remember that GET, get and Get are the same command. If many functions must remember this rule, one of the functions will possibly get it wrong. Errors are replies } else err { try w.print("-ERR {s}\r\n", .{@errorName(err)}); } Do not close the connection because of a malformed command. headings: The statement and its values always agree
The Value union is the wire contract
text: A Zig ORM can derive its INSERT and UPDATE statements from the schema struct at compile time. The same walk over the fields also builds the values, as an array of tagged-union Values. Thus the statement and its values always have the same length and the same order. The problem The query builder reads rows. Writes are the other half. An INSERT must name each column and give a number to each placeholder. An UPDATE must separate the key columns from the data columns. If you write those statements by hand for each table, the work repeats, and the statements easily become out of date. The schema already has the data to make them. The pattern 1. Derive insert sql at compile time. Make the column list and the placeholder list from the same fields. 2. Derive update sql with a stated convention: the first field is the key. A convention that a library documents is part of its API, so select it carefully. 3. Pair each statement with bind. bind changes a row into an array of tagged-union Values, one for each placeholder, in the same field order. The statement and its values always agree The placeholders of insert sql and the output of bind come from one walk over one list of fields. If you add a column to the struct, both change together at the next compile. A common ORM bug is a statement with four placeholders that gets five values. Here you cannot write that bug, because both come from one list. comptimePrint formats the numbers during compilation. Thus even $3 is in the constant. At runtime, bind is a fixed sequence of stores. description: A pipe is a descriptor at each end and an end-of-file in the middle.
headings: Close the pipe to send the message
text: A pipe is a one-way buffer in the kernel, with a descriptor at each end. Write into one end, and read from the other end. A pipe carries only bytes. It has no message boundaries and no types. You cannot ask how much data will come. There is no std.posix.pipe The standard library does not have a std.posix.pipe function. pipe2 exists inside the Io implementations, std.Io.Threaded and std.Io.Uring. There, pipe2 is a detail of how the implementations schedule work. The standard library gives you the useful case. Ask for a pipe on a stream of a child, and you get the other end back as an Io.File. var child = try std.process.spawn(io, .{ .argv = &.{ self, "child" }, .stdin = .pipe, .stdout = .pipe, }); The of the shell does the same thing. .pipe on a stream has this meaning: do not give my stream to the child, make a new pipe, and give me the other end. Then child.stdin and child.stdout are ordinary files. All that you know about readers and writers applies to them without change. The descriptors are new numbers after the three that the process started with. Nothing makes the numbers certain. Thus the snippet checks that the numbers are more than 2. It does not check that they are 4 and 5. The numbers can be different with a different Io implementation. A test that asserts exact numbers fails on a computer that opened one more file at startup. Close the pipe to send the message try to child.interface.flush(); child.stdin.?.close(io); child.stdin = null; The child reads until end of file. title: Flow and Opacity
description: Dabs overlap. Put the coverage of a stroke in its own buffer and apply its opacity at the end. Then a stroke at 50% stays at 50% where it crosses itself.
headings: The rounding bug that a test found
Put the stroke on the layer
What you see while you draw
Explain before you read the answer
text: A brush has two settings, and both seem to mean "how much paint": Flow is the quantity that one dab adds. Opacity is the maximum coverage of the full stroke. The two settings are different. The difference is visible when dabs overlap. Each stroke is a set of dabs that overlap, thus the difference is visible in all strokes. The problem For example, the code draws each dab directly onto the layer at 50%. Two dabs overlap at a pixel. The first dab covers 50% of the pixel. The second dab covers half of the remainder, thus the pixel has 75% coverage. Along a slow stroke, ten dabs overlap, and the pixel is almost at 100%. Thus a stroke "at 50%" is solid in the middle. It is darker where it crosses itself, and darker again where you moved slowly. That result is correct for flow. An airbrush adds paint in the same way. The result is incorrect for opacity. Opacity must be a limit, and the full stroke must never go past that limit. The stroke buffer The solution is to keep the stroke off the layer until the stroke is complete. While you draw, the dabs go into a separate buffer. The buffer holds one number for each pixel: how much of that pixel the stroke covers. When you release the pointer, the stroke goes onto the layer one time. The code multiplies its coverage by the opacity. Dabs that overlap only increase the coverage towards 1. The opacity applies one time after that. Thus, where the coverage is 1, the stroke covers exactly 50%, and no more. Add coverage Each dab adds flow multiplied by the part that has no coverage. title: Sorting
description: In-place sorts with a comparator that you supply.
text: In Zig, std.mem.sort sorts a slice in place. The sort is stable, and it uses a less-than function that you supply. std.mem.sortUnstable is not stable, but it does less work. std.mem.sort(T, slice, context, lessThanFn); For simple orders, the standard library supplies the comparator: std.sort.asc(T) and std.sort.desc(T). The sort is in place and needs no allocator. Thus it takes a slice and not a list, because it changes the order of the elements that are already there. To sort the contents of an ArrayList, sort list.items. The context argument The sort gives the third parameter to each comparison. The parameter is {} (the void value) when the order depends only on the elements. The parameter is useful when the comparison needs external data. An example is a sort of indices by the values that they point at: std.mem.sort(usize, &indices, values, byReferencedValue); With the context parameter, you do not need a global variable. The pattern has more uses than you can see at first. Sort an array of indices, and not the data. Then you get several orders of one dataset, and you do not copy the data. You can also use it to sort data that is too large to move cheaply. The context is the data that the comparator needs for its work. title: Iterators
description: A convention, not an interface.
text: The iterators in the Zig standard library are plain structs with a next method. Examples are std.mem.splitScalar, std.mem.tokenizeAny and std.mem.window. They give slices of the original bytes, and they do not allocate. Zig has no Iterator trait, no IntoIterator, and no iterator protocol to implement. A type is iterable if it has a next() method that returns an optional. This loop needs exactly that method: while (it.next()) value { ... } To write your own iterator, make a struct with state and a next method. const Countdown = struct { n: u32, fn next(self: Countdown) ?u32 { if (self.n == 0) return null; self.n -= 1; return self.n + 1; } }; Nothing registers the struct, and the struct implements nothing. while (c.next()) v works because the shapes match. The convention is the interface, and the compiler checks the convention when you use it. An iterator is an ordinary struct, and this fact has two results: An iterator must be var, because next changes the state. If a function must advance the iterator, give the function a pointer. After one iteration, the iterator has no more values. To iterate a second time, make the iterator again. title: Random Numbers
description: Seeded generators that you give to your code as arguments.
text: Zig has two random number generators: std.Random.DefaultPrng is fast, and you can give it a seed. Use it for tests and simulations. std.Random.DefaultCsprng is the secure generator. Use it for tokens and keys. Zig has no global rand(). You create a generator, give it a seed, and give its Random interface to the code that needs it. Code gets allocators and I/O in the same way. var prng = std.Random.DefaultPrng.init(seed); const random = prng.random(); The two values in this code do different work. prng is the generator, and it owns the state. Thus prng must be a var, and it must exist longer than all the code that uses it. random is the interface. It is a pointer to that state and a function pointer, the same shape as Allocator. Functions take the interface, never the generator. Thus you can give a real generator to a function in production, and a generator with a fixed seed in a test. The function does not know the difference. Seeds A fixed seed gives a sequence that is the same each time. Tests need that. For values that nobody can predict, the entropy must come from the operating system. On master, the entropy comes through the Io interface, as all other operations that can block do: var source: std.Random.IoSource = .{ .io = io }; const random = source.interface(); std.Random.DefaultCsprng is the cryptographically secure generator. Use it for tokens, keys, and all other values that an attacker must not predict. DefaultPrng is fast, but it is not secure. Do not use it for secrets. Older code and tutorials use std.crypto.random. title: Crypto
description: Hashes, MACs, and constant-time comparison.
text: In Zig, a SHA-256 digest is one call to std.crypto.hash.sha2.Sha256.hash. To compare secrets such as MACs and tokens, use std.crypto.timing safe.eql, not std.mem.eql. For passwords, use std.crypto.pwhash, not a plain hash. Zig includes a large crypto library in std.crypto. The library has hashes, AEADs, key exchange and signatures, and it has no external dependency. In most languages, cryptography means that you link OpenSSL or a similar library. That adds a build dependency, a version to monitor, and a large quantity of C. In Zig, the crypto code is in the standard library, and the code is Zig code. It cross-compiles to each target that your program compiles to. Select the correct tool The names are difficult to learn. This table shows which problem each tool solves. Thus there is no sorted array to search. But for each capacity, you can ask a simple question: Can a boat with this capacity ship all of the packages in four days or fewer? For example, a capacity of 9 tonnes is not sufficient. A capacity of 61 tonnes is sufficient. Also, if a capacity works, each larger capacity also works. Thus the results have this shape: no no no no ... yes yes yes yes ... The answer changes from no to yes at one point. Binary search can find that point. title: Threads
description: Real OS threads, and why this page cannot run in your browser.
text: In Zig, std.Thread.spawn starts a real OS thread, and join waits until the thread stops. Use std.Io.Mutex to protect shared data. std.Thread.Mutex does not exist now. Spawn and join const thread = try std.Thread.spawn(.{}, function, .{ args... }); thread.join(); The arguments are a tuple, and the tuple must agree with the parameters of the function. join blocks until the thread stops. detach releases the handle and does not wait. You must join or detach each thread that you spawn. If you discard a handle and do not join or detach it, the resources of the thread leak. No destructor finds this error. Thus put defer thread.join() on the line after the spawn. The reason is the same as the reason for a defer free after an allocation. If two threads write to the same memory without synchronisation, the result is a data race. A data race is undefined behaviour, not only a wrong answer. The optimiser can assume that a data race does not occur. Synchronisation moved to std.Io This change breaks older code. On std.Io.Mutex, lock takes the io instance: var mutex: std.Io.Mutex = .init; try mutex.lock(io); defer mutex.unlock(io); lock can fail for one reason only: a task can cancel the call. Because of this, the mutex works together with the other parts of Io. See Cancellation for the meaning of cancellation. The move changes more than the name. A mutex that knows the Io instance can have a different implementation for each way that the program runs: Under a pool of OS threads, the mutex is a real futex. title: Read CSV

What this reader does not do
text: CSV looks like the easiest file format of all. Each line is a record, and commas separate the fields. Thus the first idea is to read a line and split the line at each ','. That method works until a field contains a comma. 2,"Widget, large",12.00 is three fields, not four. The quotes tell the reader that the comma in them is part of the text. There are two more cases: A field can contain a quote, as two quotes: "the ""best"" one". A quoted field can contain a newline. Thus one record can use two lines of the file. A split at commas and newlines gives incorrect results for all three cases. The Zig standard library does not include a CSV reader. Thus this chapter writes one. The reader is 150 lines, with comments and the code that prints the trace. At its centre is a state machine with four states. Four states The reader looks at one byte at a time. The meaning of a byte changes with the current state: A comma in field start or unquoted ends the field. A comma in quoted is only a comma. Thus the reader keeps one variable, state. A switch on state handles each byte. quote in quoted is the only state that is not easy to understand. In quotes, " can have two meanings: It can end the quoted field, as in "abc",. It can be the first half of an escaped quote, as in "say ""hi""". The reader cannot know which meaning is correct until it sees the next byte. Thus, after a quote, the reader goes to quote in quoted and waits for one more byte: Another " means an escaped quote. The reader adds one " to the text and returns to quoted. title: Reject Bad Input with @compileError
description: Check the type that a generic function receives, and stop the build with a message that names the problem.
headings: The message is a comptime string
text: A generic function accepts anytype. Thus a caller can give it a type that the function cannot use. The compiler always finds this mistake, but the error message can be bad. It often points at a line inside the function, not at the call. @compileError("text") stops the build with your text. Put it in a branch that the compiler reaches only for a bad type. Then the user of the function reads a message about their call. The same mistake, two messages sum adds the items of an array or a slice. The two programs below call sum with a list of strings. The first sum has no check: The message is correct, but it does not help. It points at total += v inside sum, and it talks about a comptime int. The caller did not write that line, and the caller did not use a comptime int. The 0 that sets the start value of total is the comptime int. The second sum checks the type first: The message names the argument type and the item type, and it says what is wrong. The note generic function instantiated here points at the call in main. That is the line that the caller must change. The check fn Item(comptime T: type) type { const I = switch (@typeInfo(T)) { .array = info info.child, .pointer = info switch (info.size) { ... }, else = @compileError("sum: expected an array or a slice, found " ++ @typeName(T)), }; switch (@typeInfo(I)) { .int, .float = {}, else = @compileError(std.fmt.comptimePrint( "sum: the items of {s} are {s}, not numbers", .{ @typeName(T), @typeName(I) }, )), } return I; } Item returns the item type of T, or it stops the build. sum uses Item in its return type: fn sum(values: any

title: Binary Protocols and Byte Order
description: A struct is not a wire format. Write the fields, and state which end is first.
headings: A struct is not a wire format
text: Each binary protocol starts with a fixed-size header. Thus the receiver can read a known number of bytes before it knows other information. To write a header, you must obey two rules. The rules are easy to state, and they are also easy to forget. A struct is not a wire format @sizeOf(Header) = 12, on the wire = 10 The struct is larger than the message. Zig can pad a struct, and Zig can change the order of its fields. You do not control the padding bytes. They contain the data that was in that memory before. If you send the struct, you send two bytes of other data. Also, the layout that you send is the layout that your compiler selected for your target today. // Do not do this. try socket.writeAll(std.mem.asBytes(&header)); extern struct makes the layout fixed. It is the correct tool for calls to C, as ABI shows. But extern struct does not make the byte order fixed, thus it is not sufficient here. Write the fields: try w.writeInt(u16, self.magic, .big); try w.writeInt(u8, self.version, .big); This method needs more code. It is also the only method that still works with a different compiler, a different target, or a peer in a different language. Say which end first length read as big-endian: 5 length read as little-endian: 83886080 No function returned an error. The length is only wrong, but it is wrong in a dangerous way. If a receiver trusts this length, the receiver tries to wait for 83 megabytes, or to allocate 83 megabytes. The cause is one message of five bytes. By convention, network byte order is big-endian. Obey the convention, also when the two ends are little-endia

SQLite uses positional question marks. MySQL puts identifiers in backticks. An ORM that supports more than one database needs a seam. The seam is the one place in the code that holds the dialect differences, and no other place holds them. The query builder above the seam must not know which database is below it. In a language with interfaces, you define IDialect. The Zig answer is structural. A dialect is any type with the correct declarations, and the code gives it as a comptime parameter. The pattern 1. Define each dialect as a small struct of pub declarations: a placeholder writer and a quote string. 2. The renderer takes comptime Dialect: type. It calls Dialect.placeholder(...) where the difference is important. 3. Each dialect makes its own copy of the renderer, with the calls inlined. title: Signals
description: A handler interrupts you between two instructions. Set a flag and return.
headings: Two things changed, and both cause compile errors
Set a flag. Do nothing else.
A block delays a signal and does not discard it
text: A signal is a call from the operating system to a function in your program, at a time that you did not select. A signal is not a queue that you poll, and it is not a message that you receive. The kernel stops your thread between two instructions. The handler runs on the stack of that thread. Then the next instruction runs, as if nothing occurred. Two things changed, and both cause compile errors var action: std.posix.Sigaction = .{ .handler = .{ .handler = onUsr1 }, .mask = std.posix.sigemptyset(), .flags = 0, }; std.posix.sigaction(.USR1, &action, null); sigaction returns void. In the past, it returned an error union. Thus a try in front of the call now causes an error about a value that is not an error. Also, a handler now takes a std.posix.SIG, not a c int: fn onUsr1(sig: std.posix.SIG) callconv(.c) void Each handler from before this change has the signature fn (c int) callconv(.C) void, and it does not compile. Here, a compile error is the better result. The enum parameter has two more advantages: The compiler checks a switch over the signal in a shared handler. You cannot confuse .USR1 with the integer 10 on one platform and 30 on a different platform. Set a flag. Do nothing else. var caught: std.atomic.Value(u32) = .init(0); fn onUsr1( : std.posix.SIG) callconv(.c) void { caught.store(1, .seq cst); } The handler interrupted code that can be anywhere. Assume that the code was inside malloc and held the lock of the allocator. If your handler allocates, the handler waits for a lock that its own thread holds. The result is a deadlock with one thread. description: Layers are transparent pixel arrays on white paper. Store them premultiplied, and the eraser becomes one multiplication.
headings: Blend in bytes, not in light
Explain before you read the answer
text: A layer is a sheet of clear plastic that you can paint on. Put two sheets on white paper. If you paint on the top sheet, the bottom sheet does not change. If you clean the top sheet, you can see the bottom sheet again. The engine has two of these layers, on white paper. A layer is an array A layer has one pixel for each position, row by row. Thus it has width height pixels. Each pixel has four bytes: red, green, blue, and alpha. Alpha is the coverage of the pixel. 0 is clear plastic, and 255 is solid paint. extern fixes the order of the fields in memory: R, G, B, A, one byte each. A browser canvas expects that order. Thus the code can copy the screen buffer to a canvas with no conversion. With a plain Zig struct, the compiler can change the order of the fields. Two layers at 640 by 400 hold 2 × 640 × 400 × 4 = 2,048,000 bytes. The program does not store the white paper. The white paper is the start value of the drawing. A solid pixel on the top layer hides the bottom layer. If you change the order of the layers, the result is the opposite. The engine does this only for the rectangle that changed. A dab touches some hundreds of pixels. Thus the engine composites only those pixels again. Premultiplied alpha There are two ways to store a red pixel with half coverage: Straight alpha stores the colour and the coverage separately: (255, 0, 0, 128). This is full red with half coverage. title: A Growable Array
description: A length, a capacity, and one rule for what occurs when the length reaches the capacity.
headings: Length and capacity are different numbers
Double the capacity to make append cheap
Reserve space to remove the growth
What the standard library gives you
text: A growable array is an array whose length can change. The standard library calls it ArrayList. Most programs use it first, and many programs never need a different container. The structure has three fields and one rule. The rule tells what occurs when the values fill all of the space. All of the cost of the structure comes from that rule. Length and capacity are different numbers const Array = struct { buffer: []i32 = &.{}, len: usize = 0, allocator: std.mem.Allocator, }; buffer.len is the number of values that the buffer can hold. len is the number of values that are in the buffer, and len is never larger than buffer.len. The live values are buffer[0..len]. An empty array allocates no memory. &.{} is a slice of length zero with no allocation behind it. Thus init cannot fail. If an array gets no append, the array never uses the allocator. Double the capacity to make append cheap When an append finds len == buffer.len, the buffer has no space for the value. The append allocates a larger buffer, copies the values into the new buffer, and frees the old buffer. The size of the new buffer decides the cost of all the operations that use the array: if (self.len == self.buffer.len) { try self.ensureCapacity(if (self.buffer.len == 0) 1 else self.buffer.len 2); } The program counts the copies. It does not only assert the result: append 1: capacity 1, copied 0 append 2: capacity 2, copied 1 append 3: capacity 4, copied 2 append 5: capacity 8, copied 4 append 9: capacity 16, copied 8 16 appends: 5 growths, 15 values copied in total Sixteen appends copied fifteen values. title: A Linked List by Hand
description: The smallest structure that needs an allocator, an optional pointer and a deinit with the correct order.
headings: The deinit has a rule about order
Two fields with a reason that is not clear
Where a singly linked list becomes difficult
When a linked list is the correct choice
text: A linked list is a poor container. Its elements are at many different places in memory. Thus a walk through the list is a chain of dependent loads, and the prefetcher cannot make these loads faster. For almost all the uses of a list, an ArrayList is better. But a linked list is the correct first structure to build. It is the smallest structure that makes you answer the three questions that each container in Zig must answer: Who allocates? How does the type system show "no next element"? Who frees? ? Node, not ?Node const Node = struct { value: i32, next: ? Node = null, }; ? Node is an optional pointer: it is null, or it is the address of a node. ?Node is a pointer to a slot that can contain a node. That slot must exist in a different location, and ?Node is a fully different structure. Read the order from the outside to the inside. Beginners with linked structures often write the order the wrong way around. The optional costs no space: @sizeOf(? Node) == @sizeOf( Node) - true @sizeOf(?i32) @sizeOf(i32) - true A valid pointer can never be zero. Thus Zig uses zero as the null value, and does not store a flag beside the pointer. An optional integer has no spare value for this purpose, so an optional integer is larger. For this reason, ? T is the idiomatic way to say "maybe a node". A sentinel value of your own gives no advantage. The deinit has a rule about order var current = self.head; while (current) node { const next = node.next; // read first self.allocator.destroy(node); // then free current = next; } If you read node.next after you destroy node, that read is a use-after-

title: Make It Generic
description: Zig has no generics syntax. A generic container is a function that takes a type and returns a type at compile time.
headings: @This() and the reason for the name Self
The result of the call is memoized
Each instantiation is a real struct
The standard library uses the same mechanism
text: The list in the previous chapter holds only i32. To make the list hold any type, you do not need a new language feature. Zig already has functions, and types are values at compile time. fn List(comptime T: type) type { return struct { head: ? Node = null, // ... const Self = @This(); pub const Node = struct { value: T, next: ? Node = null, }; }; } List is an ordinary function. Its argument is a type, and its return value is a type. The word comptime on the parameter tells that the argument must be known when the call occurs. You do not learn a separate generics system. This is the mechanism that comptime describes, applied to a struct definition. @This() and the reason for the name Self Inside a type function, the struct is anonymous. Thus the struct has no name that you can use. @This() returns the struct, and const Self = @This() gives it a local name. Almost all Zig containers have this line, because they must have it. The result of the call is memoized List(i32) == List(i32) - true List(i32) == List(u8) - false When you call a type function two times with the same argument, the two calls return the same type . They do not return two types with the same structure. Without this rule, you could not give a List(i32) from a different part of the program to fn takes(list: List(i32)), because the two would be different types. This rule lets you use type functions in signatures. Each instantiation is a real struct @typeName(List(u8).Node) = generic-list.List(u8).Node @typeName(List(Point).Node) = generic-list.List(generic-list.Point).Node List(u8).Node == List(i32).Node - false

title: The Lists in std Are Intrusive
description: std.SinglyLinkedList is not generic and does not hold your data. Put its node in your struct and get back to the struct with @fieldParentPtr.
headings: Put the node inside your struct
What to use for ordinary work
Change old code to the new lists
text: If you read a Zig tutorial about linked lists, the tutorial almost certainly showed this code: // Does not compile on current Zig. var list = std.SinglyLinkedList(i32){}; var node = std.SinglyLinkedList(i32).Node{ .data = 5 }; list.prepend(&node); std.SinglyLinkedList is no longer a type function, and its nodes no longer carry a payload. On current master, std.SinglyLinkedList is a plain type. Its node holds only a next pointer: var list: std.SinglyLinkedList = .{}; Put the node inside your struct const Task = struct { name: []const u8, priority: u8, node: std.SinglyLinkedList.Node = .{}, }; This is the meaning of intrusive. The container does not wrap your value. Your value contains the bookkeeping of the container. The list holds pointers to the nodes inside the tasks. To get from a node to the task that contains it, use this function: fn fromNode(node: std.SinglyLinkedList.Node) Task { return @fieldParentPtr("node", node); } @fieldParentPtr subtracts the offset of the field from the pointer. It looks dangerous, but the compiler checks it at compile time: The named field must exist on the result type. The type of the field must agree with the type of the pointer. Thus this function cannot silently make a pointer to the wrong thing. The compiler does not check one thing: that the node is really inside that struct. For this reason, write the conversion one time, next to the struct that owns it. Why std made this trade The advantages are practical. The list never allocates. In the snippet, the tasks are on the stack, and the program builds the list without an allocator. prep

title: Migrate from `std.Thread`
description: Seven names that Zig removed, where each one went, and why lock can now fail.
headings: The split, and the reason for it
The mutex, and why lock can fail
The pool is now the Io itself
text: Some code does not compile now, and the compiler gives this message: error: struct 'Thread' has no member named 'Mutex' Zig did not deprecate these names, and it did not rename them in place. std.Thread.Mutex does not exist now, and six related declarations also do not exist. They moved to std.Io. The table below comes from the compiler, not from a changelog. The program prints each line from @hasDecl. Thus, if the table becomes incorrect, the build finds the problem. If one of these names returns, the output changes and the nightly build fails. The split, and the reason for it Seven declarations moved. Five stayed. Look at where each one went, and you can see the rule. spawn, detach, getCpuCount, getCurrentId and yield are about an operating system thread. They are still on std.Thread, because that is their purpose. All the declarations that moved have one thing in common. Each one of them waits : A mutex waits until a holder is done. A semaphore waits for a permit. A wait group waits until a count is zero. A pool waits for work. Current Zig makes waits explicit. A function that can block must know how the program wants to block. The Io holds that knowledge. Thus each function that can block takes an Io. A thread is still only a thread, and it does not need such an argument. The mutex, and why lock can fail The old shape was a struct with a zero initialiser, and its methods could not fail: var mutex: std.Thread.Mutex = .{}; and then mutex.lock(). title: A Binary Search Tree
description: Two pointers instead of one give ordered iteration and O(log n) lookup, on a condition that the structure does not enforce.
headings: Insert through a pointer to a pointer
The order of insertion decides the shape
What the standard library gives you
text: Give the node a second pointer. Keep all smaller values on the left and all larger values on the right. Then each step of a lookup removes half of the search space. An in-order walk visits the values in sorted order, with no extra work. These two advantages are true only while the tree stays approximately balanced. Nothing in the insert code keeps the tree balanced. Insert through a pointer to a pointer Textbooks usually show a recursive version. This version is a loop: var link: ? Node = &self.root; while (link. ) node { if (value == node.value) return; link = if (value < node.value) &node.left else &node.right; } const node = try self.allocator.create(Node); node. = .{ .value = value }; link. = node; link points at the slot that will hold the new node. It does not point at the node above that slot. An insert into an empty tree writes through &self.root. An insert at a leaf writes through &node.left. The two cases use the same two lines. Thus the empty tree needs no special case, and the code needs no "was this the root" branch. Read ? Node slowly: a pointer, to an optional, to a node. Each layer has a function. The optional is the empty slot. The outer pointer lets you write into that slot. The deinit must be post-order fn freeSubtree(allocator: std.mem.Allocator, maybe: ? Node) void { const node = maybe orelse return; freeSubtree(allocator, node.left); freeSubtree(allocator, node.right); allocator.destroy(node); } Free the children first, then the node. title: Keep It Balanced
description: Store a height, check it after each insert, and repair the shape with a local rotation. Four cases, and each case has five lines or fewer.
headings: A rotation is four pointer writes
Four cases, and the reason for four
Check the invariant, do not only claim it
Deletion, and why this chapter does not include it
text: On sorted input, the tree from the previous chapter becomes a linked list. An AVL tree prevents this problem with three additions: A height, stored in each node. A check after each insert. A rotation that repairs the shape when the check fails. This is the result on the input that broke the plain tree: final height 4, ideal 4, rotations 11 balanced everywhere: true The program inserts fifteen values in ascending order. The tree has the minimum possible height, after eleven rotations. The invariant Each node stores its height, and the height of a leaf is 1. The balance factor is the left height minus the right height. The rule is that the balance factor stays in the range -1 to 1 at each node in the tree. fn balance(maybe: ? Node) i32 { const node = maybe orelse return 0; return heightOf(node.left) - heightOf(node.right); } A factor of 2 means that one side is a full level deeper than the other side. At that time, the tree must rotate. The bound keeps the height below approximately 1.44 log₂(n). A red-black tree allows a looser bound. Thus an AVL tree does more rotations on insert, and in exchange it gives slightly faster lookups. The height is a stored value, not a computed value. To compute the height, the code must do an O(n) walk, and the structure exists to prevent that walk. A rotation is four pointer writes y x / \ / \ x C - A y / \ / \ A B B C Read the two trees in order: A x B y C, before and after. The rotation keeps the order. Thus you can apply a rotation at any location and at any time, and you do not have to check the search property. Only B gets a different pa

title: A Hash Map from Scratch
description: Open addressing with linear probing, growth at 75%, and the tombstone. The tombstone looks like a hack, but it makes delete work.
headings: The capacity is a power of two
Linear probing, and its known flaw
Growth depends on the load factor
text: A hash map changes a key into an index and looks at that index. All of the difficult parts of a hash map come from one fact: sometimes two keys get the same index. This version uses open addressing. Each entry is in the array itself. When a collision occurs, the map tries the next slot. The alternative is separate chaining, where each bucket has a linked list. Most textbooks show separate chaining. std uses open addressing, and almost all modern implementations use it too. A probe that moves forward through one array touches far fewer cache lines than a probe that follows pointers. The capacity is a power of two var index: usize = @intCast(hash(key) & mask); With a capacity that is a power of two, the modulo is a bitwise and. A prime capacity spreads the results of a weak hash function better. But a prime capacity costs a real division on each probe step. The modern answer is a power of two, plus a hash function that is good enough without the prime. std.hash.Wyhash has this purpose. Linear probing, and its known flaw On a collision, try the next slot. Linear probing has the best cache behaviour of all probe sequences. The reason is that the next slot is usually in the cache line that the CPU already loaded. Linear probing also has the worst clustering. Two separate runs of occupied slots can grow until they touch. Then they become one longer run. Each key with a hash anywhere in that run must then probe through all of the run. title: Build Modes
description: Four modes, and the cost and the benefit of each one.
headings: When the checks go, the rules stay
Change the mode for one scope
Get the mode at compile time
text: Zig has four build modes: Debug, ReleaseSafe, ReleaseFast and ReleaseSmall. The modes are different in two ways: Some modes keep the runtime safety checks in the binary, and some modes remove them. The optimiser makes the code fast in some modes, and small in a different mode. Mode Safety checks Optimised Size --- --- --- --- Debug yes no large ReleaseSafe yes yes medium ReleaseFast no yes medium ReleaseSmall no yes small Select the mode with -O: zig build-exe main.zig -OReleaseSafe zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseSafe The purpose of each mode Debug is the default. Use it while you develop. The compiler does almost no optimisation, thus the compilation is fast. All safety checks are on. The compiler fills undefined memory with 0xaa, thus a read of memory without a value is easy to see. The binaries are large and the code is slow. That is not a problem while you edit the code. ReleaseSafe is the mode to ship, if you do not have a reason to use a different mode. It has full optimisation, and it keeps the checks. ReleaseFast removes the checks. Use it when a measurement shows that the checks make the program too slow. That occurs less frequently than people expect. ReleaseSmall makes the code small instead of fast, and it also removes the checks. Embedded targets use this mode. This site also uses it. A snippet here is about 60 KB. The same snippet in ReleaseSafe is more than one megabyte. The browser of the reader must download the file before the snippet can run. These numbers come from measurements of this project. title: Breadth-First Search on a Grid
description: The distance field as the frontier grows, and the one line with a position that decides if a cell can enter the queue two times.
headings: Why DFS does not guarantee the shortest path
Why BFS gives the shortest distance
Mark a cell when it enters the queue
Why the mark on push is important
Choose the size of the queue
BFS work is proportional to cells and edges
BFS depends on equal edge costs
text: Breadth-first search, or BFS, is useful to find the shortest path on a grid when each move has the same cost. The queue does not know about shortest paths. The shortest paths come from the order in which BFS visits cells: BFS processes the cells one move away before the cells two moves away. BFS processes the cells two moves away before the cells three moves away. Because of this order, the first route that BFS finds to a cell is the shortest route to that cell. The example uses a grid with 9 rows and 13 columns. The grid has walls, one cell that BFS cannot get to, a start position S, and a target T. The program finds the shortest route from S to T and prints the distance field. It also shows a common mistake with the mark on a cell. That is 20 moves. The walls make the route four moves longer. BFS still finds the smallest possible number of moves. title: Choose an Io
description: Threaded, the evented implementations, and how to build an Io yourself.
headings: Library code names none of them
text: Each other chapter in this section takes init.io and gives it to the functions that it calls. This chapter shows where that value comes from. The program makes the choice, and main is the only place in a codebase that must make it. Io.Threaded is the default var pool: std.Io.Threaded = .init(init.gpa, .{}); defer pool.deinit(); const io = pool.io(); Io.Threaded is a thread pool. It is portable to each target that Zig supports. init.io gives you this implementation, except when the target has no threads. The implementation uses the allocator only to spawn tasks. If you never call async or concurrent, you can pass Allocator.failing. The implementation still works for plain I/O. Two options are useful: async limit sets the maximum size of the pool for io.async. Past that limit, tasks run inline. They do not wait for a thread. concurrent limit sets the maximum for io.concurrent. Past that limit, the call returns error.ConcurrencyUnavailable. The snippet makes a second instance with .concurrent limit = .nothing. This instance shows what code sees on a target that cannot give real concurrency. You do not need a different host to see it. init single threaded spawns nothing var lone: std.Io.Threaded = .init single threaded; This instance is a compile-time constant. It needs no allocator, no threads and no deinit. async still works, because async can run the task inline. concurrent always fails, and cancellation requests do nothing. text:
To write CSV needs less code than to read CSV. The writer writes most fields with no change. If a field contains a comma, a quote or a line break, the writer puts the field in quotes. It also writes each quote in the field two times. The program below writes six records with this rule, and six more records without the rule. Then it reads the two files with the reader from Read CSV. It compares each field with the field that it wrote. title: Input
description: The game latches presses one time in each frame and gives each press to exactly one tick. A held key must not cross the board.
headings: Why the fields are booleans and not key states
A frame that needs no ticks
What the platform layer does not do
text: The simulation runs at a fixed 120 Hz. The window runs at the rate of the display. The two rates do not divide evenly. Thus a rendered frame can need zero ticks, one tick, or three ticks from the simulation. A press must get to exactly one of these ticks: If the game drops a press, the game ignores the player. If the game gives a press to more than one tick, one tap moves the player across three lanes. poll runs one time in each rendered frame, before the tick loop. take gives the latched presses to one tick and clears them. Why the fields are booleans and not key states IsKeyPressed is true on the frame when a key goes down. It is false while the key stays down. The game needs that behaviour. If the player holds D, the player must move one lane. The player must not slide across the board at a hundred lanes each second. The simulation states this rule in its own type: A test checks the rule: A frame that needs no ticks If a frame makes no ticks, nothing calls take. The latch keeps its presses for the next frame. Thus the game remembers a tap between two ticks, and does not lose it. If a frame makes three ticks, the first tick gets the press. The other two ticks get nothing. This works because take clears the latch. Touch The same poll reads the mouse. It divides the window into a left half and a right half. A tap on the left half steers left. A tap on the right half steers right. A tap on either half is also the confirm that starts a run. A phone needs only these controls. title: Parse Strings at Compile Time
description: Parse a route pattern during compilation, and make a struct type for its parameters.
text: A string that the compiler knows is data that comptime code can read. A comptime function can split it, check it and change it into a type. This chapter parses a web route such as /users/:user/posts/:post. A segment that starts with : is a parameter. The result of the parse is two things: A Params struct with one field for each parameter. A match function that reads a path and fills a Params. All of the parse happens during compilation. At runtime, only the match remains. Split the pattern fn segments(comptime pattern: []const u8) [segmentCount(pattern)][]const u8 { var result: [segmentCount(pattern)][]const u8 = undefined; var it = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, pattern, '/'); for (&result) segment segment. = it.next().?; return result; } std.mem.tokenizeScalar is the same function that a program uses at runtime. Comptime code can call it because it does not allocate memory and does not do I/O. Comptime code has no allocator, thus the function cannot return a list that grows. It returns an array, and the array needs a length in its type. segmentCount calculates that length: it runs the same tokenizer and counts the segments. The pattern is comptime-known, thus the count is comptime-known too. paramCount and paramNames use the same method. They count the segments that start with :, then they copy the names. Make the type pub const Params = @Struct(.auto, null, &names, &@splat([]const u8), &@splat(.{})); Each parameter becomes a field of type []const u8. @splat makes an array with the same value in each item, with the length that @Struct needs. title: Serve Many Clients
description: One handler for each connection through Io, thus the same source runs with threads and without threads.
headings: The handler does not know about sockets
A Group so nothing outlives the scope
A handler cannot return an error
Shared state still needs a lock
Why the replies print in order
text: If a server handles one connection at a time, one slow client can stop the server. There are two usual solutions, and each solution has a cost: One thread for each connection. Each thread costs a stack, and the server cannot scale past some thousands of threads. A single-threaded event loop. The loop can scale, but each function that you write must use callbacks. Zig uses neither of these two solutions. This page runs the Zig solution in your browser, on a target that has no threads. The handler does not know about sockets const Connection = struct { request: []const u8, reply: [64]u8 = undefined, reply len: usize = 0, }; The struct has no transport, by design. handle reads bytes and writes bytes. It does not know where the bytes came from. Thus this page runs without a network below it. If you put a std.Io.net.Server in front of the same function, you get the TCP round trip. Write protocol code for Reader and Writer, not for a socket. Then the tests are fast, and the browser can run the example. io.async, not Thread.spawn var group: std.Io.Group = .init; for (&conns) conn { group.async(io, handle, .{ conn, &counter, &mutex, io }); } try group.await(io); The Io implementation decides what "async" means. std.Io.Threaded runs the tasks on a thread pool. This page runs on the single-threaded WASI implementation, which runs the tasks inline. The source does not change. For this reason, you cannot run the Threads page here, but you can run this page. title: Migrations as Data
description: The schema history as an append-only list, and a pure plan that applies it.
headings: Pure functions make the edge cases cheap
Append-only is a social contract, not a technical one
text: Database migrations are easiest to test as data. The history is an append-only list of {version, up, down} entries. A pure function, plan(current, target), returns the steps to run. A separate loop runs the plan. Thus you can test each case of the planner without a database. The problem Schemas change after they ship. Most mature ORMs handle this in the same way: Each change is a versioned migration with an up and a down. The list is append-only. The database records its current version. The design question is the location of the logic. The code that calculates what to run often becomes mixed with the code that runs it. Then you cannot test anything without a database. The pattern 1. The history is data: an ordered array of {version, up, down}. Do not edit an entry after a release, because the database of a user already ran it. 2. The planner is a pure function. plan(current, target) returns the steps to run, in order. An upgrade walks forward. A downgrade walks the affected range, with the newest entry first. 3. A separate, simple loop runs the plan. That loop belongs to the repo. Pure functions make the edge cases cheap The four tests cover the cases that go wrong in real systems: The new, empty database. The partial upgrade. The rollback, in reverse order. Forward order corrupts the database. The no-op. Each test is an assertion about a function from two integers to a slice. The tests need no fixtures, containers or cleanup. If the planner and the executor are one function, each of those tests needs a live database, and programmers never write most of them. title: Exit the Process
description: exit stops the process. It does not return from your program.
headings: cleanExit, and why it does nothing in Debug
text: The snippet writes two lines and registers two defer statements. Only one line comes out. What exit skips defer std.debug.print("this defer never runs\n", .{}); defer out.flush() catch {}; try out.writeAll("second line, still sitting in the buffer\n"); std.process.exit(0); std.process.exit is noreturn. It never returns to the caller, so no code between the call and the end of main runs. No defer runs at any depth of the stack, no errdefer runs, and the program flushes nothing. Look at the lost line. Those bytes were in a buffer in the memory of your process. The operating system never received the bytes, and then the process ended. Output often disappears in this way from a program that "definitely printed it". The second defer above is the one that flushes. It looks like it protects the output. But it never runs, so it protects nothing. When main returns normally, every defer runs. Thus an error return from main and exit(1) are not the same: An error return unwinds the stack and runs the cleanup. exit(1) stops the process immediately. The status that you leave exit takes a u8. Zero means success, and you decide the meaning of each other value. This is the same one-bit protocol that the parent sees as Term in Spawn a Process. When main returns an error, Zig sets a nonzero status for you. In debug builds, Zig also prints the error name with a stack trace. For a tool, that is the correct default.
