title: Undo
description: Keep only the changed rectangle. Undo and redo are one swap, two stacks are an array and an index, and a memory failure costs an undo step, not the stroke.
headings: A copy of the full picture is expensive
Undo and redo are one swap
A new action removes the future
When the memory is not sufficient
Explain before you read the answer
text: People expect one Undo to remove one action. One action is one stroke or one fill. It is not one dab, and it is not one pointer sample. Thus the history saves data one time for each action, immediately before the action changes a layer. The question is which data to save. A copy of the full picture is expensive The simplest answer is a copy of each layer. At 640 by 400 with two layers, one copy is 2 × 640 × 400 × 4 = 2,048,000 bytes. Eight undo steps need 16,384,000 bytes, about 15.6 MiB. That is much memory for a short line in one corner. Most of each copy is pixels that the action did not touch. Save only the changes Each action in this program knows the rectangle that it touches: A stroke gets the rectangle from the dirty rectangle of the stroke buffer. A fill knows the bounds of the area that it found. Thus the history copies that rectangle, from that one layer, immediately before the action changes it. A stroke 100 pixels wide and 60 pixels high saves 100 × 60 × 4 = 24,000 bytes. That is about 1% of a full copy. Undo and redo are one swap To undo, put the saved pixels back into the layer. But redo needs the pixels that the action made. If undo puts the old pixels back with a copy, the new pixels are lost. Thus undo does not copy. It swaps : the saved pixels go into the layer, and the current pixels of the layer go into the entry. Now the entry holds the newer pixels. Redo is the same swap again. One function does the two jobs. Thus undo and redo cannot become different. Two stacks in one array The usual design has two stacks: Undo removes an entry from the past stack a

title: Testing
description: The assertions other than expect, and the allocator that finds leaks.
headings: expect tells you nothing, and the others tell you what failed
How zig test finds and runs tests
Tests are documentation that is always current
text: Zig tests are test blocks, and zig test runs them. std.testing supplies the assertions, for example expectEqual and expectError. It also supplies std.testing.allocator, which fails a test that leaks memory. expect tells you nothing, and the others tell you what failed When try std.testing.expect(a == b) fails, it says "expected true, found false". Then you must add print statements. The typed assertions put the values into the failure message: Assertion Reports on failure --- --- expectEqual(expected, actual) both values expectEqualStrings both strings and the first differing byte expectEqualSlices(T, ...) both slices and the diverging index expectError(err, expr) which error, or that none was returned By convention, the expected value comes first. expectEqual gets its type from that first argument. For this reason, @as(?u8, null) sometimes needs the cast: the cast tells the comparison the type of null. Assert the error paths too Bugs hide in failure paths that have no tests. With expectError, "this input is rejected" becomes a normal assertion. You can check it as easily as the success case. A parser test must check the digit that the parser accepts, and also the character that it refuses. Floats need a tolerance Never compare calculated floats with ==. Use one of these assertions: expectApproxEqAbs takes an absolute tolerance, for values near a known magnitude. expectApproxEqRel takes a relative tolerance. std.math.floatEps(f64) is the natural limit for "as close as the type permits." expectEqualDeep for structures Take two structs that hold slices. expectEqual on these s

title: Emit an Executable
description: How to build without a build.zig.
headings: You will use zig run most
text: For a single file, you do not need a build script: zig build-exe main.zig an executable zig build-lib main.zig a static library zig build-obj main.zig an object file zig run main.zig build and run in one step zig test main.zig build and run its tests Useful flags Flag Effect --- --- -O optimisation mode -target cross-compile --name output name -femit-bin= where to write the binary -fstrip drop debug info -fsingle-threaded assume no threads You will use zig run most The only difference between run and build-exe is the location of the binary: zig run foo.zig │ ├── compile ├── binary into the cache └── execute it zig build-exe foo.zig │ └── compile │ ▼ ./foo build-exe puts an artifact in your working directory. You can then run the artifact, ship it or link it. run puts the same artifact in the cache and runs it immediately. Thus there is nothing to delete after the run, and nothing to add to .gitignore. For a program of a few hundred lines or fewer, zig run main.zig is sufficient, and there is no build step to remember. Put the arguments for the program after --: zig run main.zig -- --verbose input.txt The cache is content-addressed. If nothing changed, a second zig run does not compile again. Thus zig run is fast enough to use as a script interpreter. You can work on a tool in a single file this way for a long time. zig test works in the same way, and it does not need a main. title: Cross-compilation
description: All targets are available when you install Zig.
text: In Zig, cross-compilation is not a special mode. Zig includes the libc sources for the targets that it supports. The compiler that made hello.exe is the same binary that you use for a native build. The Linux computer has no Windows SDK, no MinGW and no Wine. Change the triple to aarch64-linux-musl. Then file reports a statically linked ARM64 ELF. title: Zig Build
description: The build system is a Zig program.
headings: Why a program and not a configuration file
Steps are a graph, not a list
text: build.zig is not a configuration file. build.zig is a Zig program that makes a graph of steps. Then zig build runs the steps in the graph. const std = @import("std"); pub fn build(b: std.Build) void { const target = b.standardTargetOptions(.{}); const optimize = b.standardOptimizeOption(.{}); const exe = b.addExecutable(.{ .name = "myapp", .root module = b.createModule(.{ .root source file = b.path("src/main.zig"), .target = target, .optimize = optimize, }), }); b.installArtifact(exe); const run = b.addRunArtifact(exe); const run step = b.step("run", "Run the app"); run step.dependOn(&run.step); } The module comes first addExecutable takes a root module. It does not take a source file directly. Older examples give .root source file, .target and .optimize directly to addExecutable. Zig removed that form. Make the module first. Steps and options zig build the default step zig build run a step you declared zig build --help lists your steps and options zig build -Dtarget=wasm32-wasi -Doptimize=ReleaseSmall b.option(...) declares your own flags. Your flags then show in the --help output. Why a program and not a configuration file Many people say that a build script must be declarative. But each declarative build system adds a way to run ordinary code, and the difficult parts of the build go into that code. For example, Make runs shell commands, and CMake has its own language. Zig lets you write the build in Zig from the start. Thus all that you know about Zig applies in build.zig. You can use loops, functions and a switch on the target. The build of this site is an example. The

title: Dependencies
description: How to declare, fetch and connect a package with build.zig.zon.
text: The Zig build system includes a package manager. There is no separate tool, and there is no central registry. A dependency is a URL and a hash. Zig fetches the dependency into a global cache and verifies the hash when the files arrive. Two files work together: build.zig.zon declares the packages that you depend on. build.zig gets each package and connects its modules to your artifacts. The path of a dependency build.zig.zon │ │ declares ▼ Dependency │ │ downloaded, hash checked ▼ Global Zig cache │ │ requested by ▼ build.zig │ ▼ executable / module The two files answer two different questions: build.zig.zon answers what do I depend on? build.zig answers where must the build use that dependency? The two files are separate. Thus, on each computer, a checkout and zig build give the same set of dependencies. The manifest records what you depend on. The build script connects each dependency to your code. You cannot edit one file into a state where the other file disagrees and nothing tells you. If build.zig uses a name that the manifest does not declare, the result is an error, not an empty module. build.zig.zon The manifest is a ZON literal. ZON is Zig Object Notation, and it has the same syntax as a Zig struct literal. A minimal manifest: .{ .name = .myproject, .version = "0.1.0", .fingerprint = 0x1234567890abcdef, // generated once by zig init .dependencies = .{ .mecha = .{ .url = "https://github.com/Hejsil/mecha/archive/ .tar.gz", .hash = "mecha-0.9.0-...", }, }, .paths = .{ "build.zig", "build.zig.zon", "src", }, } You rarely write the .url and .hash pair manually. headings: What to write in a doc comment
Only pub declarations are in the output
text: Zig makes HTML documentation from doc comments. zig build-lib src/root.zig -femit-docs zig build docs if your build.zig declares it The comment forms Syntax Attaches to --- --- /// the declaration that follows //! the file or module that contains it (must be at the top) // ordinary comment, not documentation //! Only pub declarations are in the output. If a /// comment is in a position where it cannot attach to a declaration, the result is a compile error, not a warning. Thus, if a doc comment becomes separate from its declaration, the compiler tells you. The output The generator does one thing. It copies the signature from the source and puts your /// text below the signature. Source /// Adds two integers. pub fn add(a: i32, b: i32) i32 { ... } │ │ zig build-lib -femit-docs ▼ Generated page add(a: i32, b: i32) i32 Adds two integers. The signature is already on the page. The generator makes the signature from the code, thus the signature is always correct. If your comment repeats the signature, the comment can become incorrect, and the generated signature above it stays correct. title: Merge Intervals
description: A sort by start for one pass, the nested interval that shortens a run without @max, and a sweep that counts open intervals.
headings: Sort by start, then make one pass
Put the events in the correct order
Half-open intervals change the overlap count
Merge and sweep answer different questions
text: The example below has eleven intervals. The problem is to combine the intervals that overlap. The input has three special cases: Some intervals are fully inside [1, 20]. [3, 5] ends where [5, 8] starts. [40, 40] holds only one coordinate. If the intervals are in random order, it is difficult to know which intervals can overlap. A sort by start position makes the problem much simpler. After the sort, the pass reads the intervals from left to right and keeps one merged interval open at a time. For each new interval, the pass only has to check if the interval overlaps the current merged interval. The program sorts the intervals and shows each step of the merge. It also marks each coordinate that the intervals cover, and it uses these marks to check the result. Sort by start, then make one pass For each new interval, there are two cases: If the new interval starts before or at the end of the current merged interval, the two intervals overlap. The pass extends the current merged interval if necessary. If the new interval starts after the end of the current merged interval, there is a gap. The current merged interval is complete, and the pass starts a new merged interval. The program sorts the intervals by start position. Thus the pass never has to check an older merged interval again, because the starts only move forward. The sorted input is: sorted by start, the only preparation the pass needs start 1 3 4 5 12 13 18 24 26 33 40 end 20 5 7 8 15 17 21 26 29 36 40 The pass needs sorted starts only. title: A Batch Job Runner
description: Four workers, one batch, three kinds of shared state, and a measurement that says one thread did all of the work.
headings: Three kinds of state, three different answers
Claim work with one atomic add
The parser knows nothing about concurrency
The run is concurrent, the report is not
When this shape is the wrong one
text: Each other chapter here shows one primitive at a time. This chapter is a full program. A batch of order records goes in, four workers process the records, and a report comes out. Three of the records are malformed, each in a different way. A real batch runner cannot assume that its input is clean. The program has three items of state that the workers use. The program protects each item in a different way. Three kinds of state, three different answers The results are one slot for each record. Each worker writes only the slot of the record that it claimed. Thus two workers never write the same bytes, and the slots need no lock and no atomic. This is the cheapest way to share state, and the first way to try. The work index is a single number that each worker increments. It is one machine word, and one operation changes it. It does not have to agree with a different value. Thus an atomic is sufficient for the work index. The largest order in the batch is the third kind of state. The struct has two fields that must agree with each other. One is a value that belongs to an index. The other is an index that belongs to a value. Atomic operations cannot keep that pair consistent. The end of Atomics explains why. Thus the pair needs a mutex, and the pair is the only item in the program that needs one. Claim work with one atomic add Each worker runs the same function, and the workers compete for records. fetchAdd returns the value from before the addition. Thus each worker gets an index that no other worker can get. That is how the program gives work to the workers. When the returned i

title: Directories
description: Create a tree of directories, list one level, walk all levels, rename a directory and delete the full tree.
text: A directory is a list of names. Each name points to a file or to a different directory. The program below makes a small project tree and lists the tree in two ways. Then it renames part of the tree and deletes all of the tree. Create a tree createDirPath(io, "project/src/util") creates project, then project/src, then project/src/util. The function skips each directory that exists already. A shell does the same with mkdir -p. createDir creates exactly one directory, and the parent directory must exist already. The two functions are also different when the directory exists already. createDir again: PathAlreadyExists createDirPath again: ok createDir reports an error. createDirPath succeeds, because the path that the program asked for exists. To make sure that a directory exists before you write into it, use createDirPath. When the directory must be new, use createDir. This is the same as .exclusive = true for a file. List one level Dir.cwd() is not open for a listing. Its doc comment says that iteration over Dir.cwd() is illegal behaviour. Thus first open the directory that you want with .iterate = true, then list that directory. dir.iterate() returns an iterator. it.next(io) returns one entry at a time, or null at the end. Each entry has a name and a kind. file README.md directory docs directory src The filesystem decides the order of the entries. The order is not alphabetical, and it is not the order in which the program created the files. The order can be different on two computers. It can also be different between two runs on the same computer, after a program adds and de

title: Difficulty You Can Prove
description: Row spacing from what is physically possible, a bot that proves that the course is solvable, and a reaction time model for playability.
headings: Calculate the spacing, do not adjust it by hand
text: The course generator puts down rows of blocks. The rows must become more difficult, and they must stay possible. A mistake here does not look like a bug. Each row still has an open lane and the game still runs, but nobody can survive the course. The only sign is that people stop their play. The spacing has a minimum Between the arrival of one row and the next row, the player can have to cross the full board. That costs two lane changes. Also, the player cannot start while the current row is level with the player. A move to the side into a block next to you is a crash. The smallest spacing that a player can still survive is the sum of these two times. The second term becomes smaller when the game becomes faster, because a faster row is next to you for less time. The first term does not change with the speed. Calculate the spacing, do not adjust it by hand The first version had two constants that a person selected: an easy spacing and a hard spacing. The game interpolated between them. This method worked. But it had three numbers that had to agree, and nothing in the code said so. If you changed the lane change time, the hard spacing became impossible without an error. Now the code calculates the spacing from the minimum, and the spacing decays toward the minimum. The decay never gets to the minimum, and this fixes a second problem. The earlier curve got to its most difficult setting at sixty seconds and then stayed there. A sufficiently good player never lost. One named constant now holds the margin above the impossible spacing. Prove it with play All of this is still an arg

title: Know the Limits
description: What comptime code cannot do, what to use instead, and what comptime costs.
headings: One copy for each set of arguments
text: Comptime code is usual Zig, but it runs inside the compiler. The compiler has no program, no operating system and no heap for that code. Thus some functions that work at runtime do not work during compilation. This chapter gives the limits, and the tool to use for each one. No runtime allocator An ArrayList needs an allocator, and an allocator asks the operating system for memory. During compilation, there is no operating system to ask: The error points inside the standard library, at the place where the allocator asks for memory. The notes called at comptime from here lead back to the append call. Use these tools instead: An array with a length that a comptime function calculates. Parse Strings at Compile Time uses this method. A comptime var of type []const u8, extended with ++. The program joins the color names with ++: 2. names: red, green, blue, saffron (25 bytes) Each ++ makes a new comptime string, with a length that the compiler knows. No I/O, except @embedFile Comptime code cannot open a file, read the clock or call the network. A build that reads the clock would give a different binary each time. @embedFile("colors.txt") is the exception. The compiler reads the file and makes its bytes a string constant. The path is relative to the source file. The compiler notes the file as an input, thus a change to the file starts a new build. The program parses the file during compilation: const colors = std.StaticStringMap(u24).initComptime(parseColors(colors txt)); parseColors splits the lines and parses each hex value. A line without =, or with a bad hex value, stops the bu

title: Failure Is Ordinary
description: The end of a stream is not an error, and a truncated message can look like a good message.
headings: The call that does not invent a delimiter
What to do for each error
text: On a network, failure is normal. A client can stop in the middle of a request, and a computer can stop. Also, each connection ends when it succeeds. These events will occur. The important question is if your code can see the difference between them. The clean close clean close: read "complete", then EndOfStream (expected: the client is done) EndOfStream after a complete message is the normal end of a successful conversation. If you make it a failure, you log an error for each client that operates correctly. Then the log has no value. The truncated message truncated: Exclusive returned "truncat" and no error The client sent "truncat" and then stopped. The client did not send a newline. But takeDelimiterExclusive returned the bytes as a message, with success. The result has no error and no flag to check. This is not a bug in the standard library. The documentation says: End-of-stream is treated equivalent to a delimiter, unless it would result in a length 0 return value, in which case error.EndOfStream is returned instead. That behaviour is correct for a text file, because the last line of a text file often has no newline at the end. The behaviour is wrong for a socket. On a socket, the absence of the delimiter is the only sign that the sender did not complete the message. If your protocol does an action on the data that it reads, this default does an action on half of a request. The call that does not invent a delimiter truncated: Inclusive returned EndOfStream, so the 7 buffered bytes get discarded takeDelimiterInclusive returns the delimiter as a part of the slice. title: The Repo
description: The composition root, and the fake driver that lets you test the full ORM.
headings: RecordingDriver is the test suite of the ORM
text: The Repo is the one stateful object in an Ecto-style ORM. It is also the only part that talks to the database. In Zig, it is Repo(Driver), and the driver is a comptime parameter. Thus a test can give it a driver that records the SQL and does not run it. The problem Each part so far (schema, statements, dialects, plans) is pure. At some point, the library must talk to a real database, and that point decides if you can test the library. If database calls are in all parts of the code, each test needs Postgres. If the calls are behind one seam, you can test the full ORM against a fake. The Ecto answer is the Repo, which holds the connection. Each operation goes through the Repo. This page builds the skeleton of the Repo. The pattern 1. Repo(Driver) is a type function, as all other parts of this library are. The driver is a comptime parameter with a structural contract: an exec function that takes SQL. 2. The methods of the Repo combine the pure parts (the derived SQL of a Table) with one effect (driver.exec). 3. The test driver records the SQL and does not run it. The assertions read the log: the SQL that the database gets, and the order of that SQL. RecordingDriver is the test suite of the ORM RecordingDriver is thirteen lines. With it, you can test each feature of the library (inserts, transactions, migrations). Each test has one form: "for these calls, exactly this SQL, in exactly this order". These tests check the behavior of your library, and the database is not part of them. A thin layer of integration tests against real SQLite and Postgres then tests the drivers. No othe

title: Fill
description: A flood fill finds its area a small number of pixels at a time. A queue and a visited map do this in fixed memory. Recursion uses all of the stack.
headings: The fill finds the region a small number of pixels at a time
Recursion is short, but it is the wrong answer
A queue and a visited map
Why the queue never needs to grow
Four neighbours, and the soft edge
Explain before you read the answer
text: The Fill tool paints a full area in one action. You click one pixel. Each pixel that has the same colour and connects to that pixel changes to the new colour. The fill stops at all other colours. That set of pixels is the region . The work is to find the region. The fill finds the region a small number of pixels at a time The fill cannot know the shape of the region before it starts. It knows only the first pixel. The neighbours of the first pixel that have the same colour are also in the region. Their neighbours with the same colour are in the region too, and so on. Thus each pixel that the fill accepts can give more pixels to examine. Recursion is short, but it is the wrong answer The shortest code is a function that fills one pixel and then calls itself on the four neighbours of that pixel. The code is short, but it is incorrect for a paint program. Each call waits for the calls that it makes, thus the calls nest. A fill of an empty 640 by 400 layer nests 256,000 calls deep. Each call needs some stack space. The stack of a thread is usually 8 MiB or less, and in a browser it is much less. The program stops before the fill is complete. A queue and a visited map Instead, the code keeps a list of the pixels that it must examine. This list is a queue , and the code takes pixels from the front: 1. Put the clicked pixel in the queue. 2. Take the next pixel from the queue. 3. Examine each of the four neighbours of that pixel. If a neighbour has the target colour and it has no mark, put a mark on it and add it to the queue. 4. Do step 2 again until the queue is empty. The marks

title: ABI
description: extern and packed, for layouts with a guarantee.
text: To pass a struct from Zig to C, declare it as extern struct. An extern struct uses the field order and padding of the C ABI. A packed struct gives exact bits with no padding, for registers and wire formats. A plain Zig struct makes no layout promise . The compiler can put the fields in a different order and add padding in any way that it prefers. This freedom is a feature, because it lets the optimiser pack the fields. But you cannot give a plain struct to C. The three layouts Declaration Layout Use for --- --- --- struct unspecified ordinary Zig code extern struct C ABI: declaration order, C padding C interop packed struct exact bits, no padding, integer-backed wire formats, registers const CPoint = extern struct { x: i32, y: i32 }; // offsets 0 and 4 const Flags = packed struct { a: bool, b: bool, rest: u6 }; // exactly 8 bits A packed struct converts to and from its backing integer with @bitCast. Thus a packed struct is the natural way to describe hardware registers and protocol headers. What "ABI" means The application binary interface is a set of agreements. Two pieces of code that are compiled separately need these agreements to call each other: The position of the fields of a struct. The registers that hold each argument. The side that cleans the stack. The form of a name in the symbol table. The source language does not specify these items. The platform decides them. The two sides must agree before they meet, because at that time no type information remains to check. Because nothing remains to check, a mistake here makes no noise. An incorrect field offset is not a

title: C Primitive Types
description: Types whose width follows the target's C ABI.
headings: What C guarantees, and what it does not
Keep the C types at the boundary
text: In Zig, a C int is c int and a C long is c long. The sizes of these types follow the C ABI of the target. Use them at the C boundary, because long is 8 bytes on 64-bit Linux and 4 bytes on Windows. Zig has these C types: c char, c short, c int, c long and c longlong. An unsigned type for each of these types except c char. There is no c uchar. c longdouble. The C ABI of the target sets the size of each type. Why not use i32 A C long does not have one size. If code uses i64 for a C long, the code is correct on one platform and wrong on a different platform. Nothing tells you about the error. A bug of this type appears only after a port. c int and i32 are different types , also when they have the same size. Thus the compiler does not let you use one type for the other by accident. What C guarantees, and what it does not C does not specify the size of its integer types. C specifies minimum ranges and an order of sizes. The platform sets the actual widths, and a document called the ABI records them. For this reason, the table below has three answers and not one: C type 64-bit Linux/macOS 64-bit Windows wasm32 --- --- --- --- int 4 4 4 long 8 4 4 long long 8 8 8 size t 8 8 4 pointer 8 8 4 long causes the most problems, because the two most common desktop platforms do not agree about its size. c long gives the correct size on all targets that Zig supports. c char has a second problem in addition to the width. The platform also decides if c char is signed or unsigned, and the answer is different on x86 Linux and ARM Linux. Zig also models this difference. For this reason, c char is

title: C Pointers
description: [*c]T: the pointer type translate-c emits, and why to convert it at the boundary.
headings: A C pointer has no guarantees
Read the header, not the signature
text: Zig's C pointer type is [ c]T. A [ c]T can be null, has no length and has no bounds checks. Convert it to a slice or a T at the C boundary. Do not use it in the rest of the program. [ c]T is Zig's model of C's T . The main reason for the type is that translate-c can then convert headers automatically. A C pointer has no guarantees Property T []T [ c]T --- --- --- --- can be null no no yes carries a length n/a yes no bounds checked n/a yes no indexable no yes yes coerces freely no no yes The last row is the dangerous row. A [ c]T converts to and from the safe pointer types, and the compiler does not complain. At a C boundary, this conversion is convenient. In all other places, the conversion causes damage. The conversion removes the guarantees that the rest of the language depends on, and nothing tells you. Why the type is necessary A C header cannot tell the translator which of the three things a T is. Look at void process(int data, size t n). A human reads the two parameters together, and decides that data is an array of n items. Look at int out. A human reads the name, and decides that out is one item that the function writes through. But the declaration itself is the same in the two examples. Thus translate-c cannot select a type. [ c]T is the type that means "any one of these three things". Each safe pointer type would be a guess. A wrong guess causes more damage than no guess. Read the header, not the signature Thus at a C boundary, your task is to decide what the C function really promises. Then write that promise as a Zig type. Ask four questions. Usually, the docume

title: Import C
description: translate-c, and calling C without bindings.
headings: Tell the build where to look
What translates and what does not
Why the snippets here have no Run button
text: Zig reads C headers directly. You do not need a binding generator, and you do not maintain an intermediate .zig file. The change is the place where Zig reads the header. Before, a builtin in your source read the header. Now a step in your build reads the header. @cImport is gone If you come from an older tutorial, this line does not compile: // Removed from the language. Every tutorial written before 2026 shows this. const c = @cImport({ @cDefine(" GNU SOURCE", {}); @cInclude("stdio.h"); @cInclude("string.h"); }); On current Zig, the line fails with error: invalid builtin function: '@cImport'. @cInclude and @cDefine are also removed. Headers now come from b.addTranslateC, which makes an ordinary Zig module. Import the module by the name that you gave to it: All declarations of the header are still members of c. The difference is that the source file does not name a header now. The build names the header. The translate step takes one C file as its root. If a project needs several headers, write one header that includes them: // src/c.h include include // build.zig const translate = b.addTranslateC(.{ .root source file = b.path("src/c.h"), .target = target, .optimize = optimize, .link libc = true, }); translate.defineCMacro(" GNU SOURCE", null); defineCMacro replaces @cDefine. A null value means a macro without a value. Then translate.createModule() gives the module. Give that module to the code that needs it. The extra step has an advantage. The build now caches and configures a C again on each compile. Tell the build where to look There are three separate jobs, in three pla

title: What WebAssembly Is
description: A portable binary target for a sandboxed stack machine, and how Zig compiles to it.
headings: Only numbers go through a call
Three ways that Zig compiles to wasm
text: WebAssembly (wasm) is a binary instruction format for a stack machine. Wasm is a compile target , not a language. You write Zig, C or Rust, and the compiler emits a .wasm module. An engine (a browser, Node, wasmtime) loads that module and runs it in a sandbox at almost native speed. This site is an example. Each snippet that you read is Zig compiled to wasm32-wasi. The Run button gives that exact module to a WASI shim in your browser. Press the button below, and the code reports the target of its build. Module, instance, linear memory Three terms explain most of the model. A module is the compiled .wasm file. It contains code and a description of its imports and exports. A module does nothing alone, like a shared library that is not loaded. An instance is a module that an engine loaded and connected. The instantiation resolves the imports of the module, which are functions that the host supplies. It also gives the module its memory. You can instantiate the same module more than one time. Each instance has its own state. Linear memory is the heap of the instance. It is one flat, contiguous array of bytes, with addresses from zero, and the module and the host both see it. It starts at a number of 64 KiB pages and can grow. A Zig pointer inside a wasm module is only an offset into this array. The module cannot touch any other memory. Only numbers go through a call A call can carry only these types: i32, i64, f32 and f64. Later proposals added v128 for SIMD and reference types for host objects. But a JavaScript host still gives numbers. A call cannot give or return a string, a

title: Recipe: A WASI Command
description: Compile a Zig program to wasm and run it from a shell under any WASI runtime.
text: To run a Zig program as WebAssembly outside the browser, do these steps: 1. Build the program with zig build-exe -target wasm32-wasi. 2. Run the .wasm under a WASI runtime, for example wasmtime, wasmer or the node:wasi module of Node. The program itself needs no code that is specific to wasm. The problem You have a Zig program with a main. You want a single .wasm that runs the same on Linux, macOS and Windows, without a new compilation. WASI makes this possible. WASI is the system interface for a wasm command. The command calls WASI for the OS operations (here, stdout) that pure wasm cannot do. The plan 1. Write an ordinary Zig program. Nothing in it is specific to wasm. 2. Build the program for wasm32-wasi. 3. Run the .wasm under a WASI runtime. The source is a normal program. It splits an embedded document and counts lines and words. It writes the totals to stdout through the Io instance that main receives. The code has no setup that is specific to wasm. Build the program zig build-exe wasi-command.zig -target wasm32-wasi -O ReleaseSmall This command emits wasi-command.wasm. -O ReleaseSmall is more important here than on a native build. The module is a file that you ship or fetch, and the debug build is approximately thirty times larger. For exactly this reason, the build.zig of this guide uses that mode by default. Run the program The module does not need a browser. Any WASI runtime runs it: wasmtime wasi-command.wasm lines: 3 words: 14 wasmer wasi-command.wasm same output node --experimental-wasi-unstable-preview1 run.mjs via node:wasi CI and the Run button on this page

title: Recipe: Call Zig from JavaScript
description: Build a reactor module with exported functions and call them by name from a host.
text: To call Zig from JavaScript, do these steps: 1. Mark the function export fn. 2. Build for wasm32-freestanding with -fno-entry and --export= . 3. After WebAssembly.instantiate returns, call the function as instance.exports. . The problem Usual uses are a hot loop, a parser, or math that is slow in the JavaScript engine. The module has no main. JavaScript instantiates the module one time, and then calls its functions when necessary. That is the reactor shape from the overview. The plan 1. Mark each function that the host must call with export fn. 2. Build for wasm32-freestanding with -fno-entry, and give the names of the exports. 3. Instantiate in JavaScript and call instance.exports. . Here, the Run button runs the test blocks of the file, because this guide verifies each snippet in that way. In real use, nothing calls these functions as Zig tests. The functions exist for calls from outside. The tests only prove that the functions return the values that the text below gives. Export the functions export fn does two things: It makes sure that dead-code elimination does not remove the function. It puts the function in the export table of the module, under its exact Zig name. There is no name mangling and no wrapper. add in Zig is add in the export table. The signatures use only i32 and u32/u64, and this is intentional. Those types map directly to the numeric types of wasm. Thus you do not have to think about marshalling at the boundary. fib returns a u64, and a JavaScript host receives a u64 as a BigInt. Build the reactor zig build-exe export-to-js.zig \ target wasm32-freestand

title: Recipe: Pass Data Across the Boundary
description: Move strings and buffers between JavaScript and wasm through shared linear memory.
headings: Why an offset and not a pointer
text: A string cannot go between JavaScript and a Zig wasm module as a value. Thus the string goes through the linear memory of the module: 1. The exported alloc function of the module returns an offset. 2. The host writes the bytes at that offset. 3. The host calls into the module with the offset and a length. The problem The last recipe gave numbers to the module, and a number fits in a wasm value. A string does not fit. A slice, a struct and a buffer do not fit either. Linear memory is the only place where both sides can see them. The two sides must agree on the meaning of the bytes there. The plan 1. Export an alloc function, so that the host can reserve space in linear memory. 2. Export the memory. The reactor build does this automatically. 3. The host writes bytes at the returned offset, then calls in with (offset, len). The host reads a result back from memory at an offset that the module reports. The test in the snippet is the script of the host, written in Zig. It does these steps: 1. Reserve space. 2. Copy bytes in. 3. Call sumBytes. 4. Change the bytes in place with upperInPlace. 5. Read the bytes back. A JavaScript host does the same steps through instance.exports and a typed-array view. The browser recipe shows how to build the module as a reactor and call it. This page covers the memory protocol itself. Why an offset and not a pointer Inside a wasm module, a Zig [ ]u8 is an offset into linear memory, counted from zero. It is not an address in the process of the host. When alloc returns [ ]u8, JavaScript sees a plain integer. The integer tells where in the shared arr

title: Recipe: A Freestanding Module
description: The smallest wasm target, with no WASI and no libc, and the memory builtins that replace them.
headings: When to select freestanding and not WASI
text: wasm32-freestanding is the smallest wasm target of Zig, with no WASI and no libc. The module has no main, no stdout, no files and no OS heap. Its host controls the module through exports. The problem You want the smallest possible module, with no dependency on a system interface. A JavaScript host or a native embedder controls the module. Thus the files and clocks of WASI only add weight that the module does not use. The plan 1. Write functions that do not need an OS: no files, no stdout, no main. 2. Supply your own memory, because no system allocator is available. 3. Build for wasm32-freestanding. The tests here run because the guide builds each snippet for wasm32-wasi to verify it. title: Recipe: Load wasm in the Browser
description: Fetch, instantiate, connect the imports and exports, and let a module call back into JavaScript.
text: To load a Zig wasm module in the browser, give fetch("module.wasm") and an imports object to WebAssembly.instantiateStreaming. Then call the functions on instance.exports. The module calls back into JavaScript through extern functions. The imports object supplies these functions by name. The problem You have a reactor module and a web page. This page shows all the parts together. The plan 1. fetch the .wasm, and give the stream to instantiateStreaming. 2. Give an imports object that supplies each function that the module imports. 3. Call the exports of the module, and let the module call your imports. This module imports and exports. It exports greet, and the page calls greet. title: The Monotonic Deque
description: The largest value in each window, from a deque with two ends that remove indices for two different reasons.
headings: Do not carry only the maximum
Scan again only when the maximum leaves
Keep useful indices in descending order
Remove by value at the back
Remove by position at the front
text: A window moves across an array one step at a time. At each step, one value enters from the right and one value leaves from the left. The problem is to find the largest value in each window. There are three cases: If the previous maximum is still inside the new window, the answer can stay the same. If the new value is larger, the new value becomes the new maximum. If the old maximum is the value that left, the answer is not known. This case is difficult. A monotonic deque solves the problem in one pass. The example below uses twelve values and a window size of four. Thus there are nine windows. The program prints the changes at the two ends of the deque at each step. Do not carry only the maximum A sliding sum is easy to update, because you can add the value that enters and subtract the value that leaves. A maximum does not work in the same way. If the largest value leaves the window, one stored number cannot give the next largest value. The stored number does not hold sufficient information. One correct solution is to scan each window again from the start. The cost is k comparisons for each window. A different method keeps the previous maximum and compares it with the new value. This method is faster, but it gives the wrong answer when the previous maximum leaves the window. title: When Things Go Wrong
description: What stat tells you, six file operations that fail and the error from each, messages for a person, and how to delete a half-written file.
text: Each chapter in this section handles some errors. This chapter looks at the errors together. A file operation can fail for reasons that the program does not control: A different program deleted the file. The path is incorrect. The disk is full. A different program changed something. Zig does not hide these failures. Each failure is an error value with a name. The return type of the function gives a list of all the errors that the function can return. The program below makes six operations fail intentionally. It prints the result of each operation. What is at a path dir.statFile(io, path, .{}) asks what is at a path. It does not open the path. notes.txt kind file, size 6 archive kind directory The result is a Stat: kind tells you if the path is a file, a directory, or a different thing, for example a symbolic link. size is the length of a file in bytes. For a directory, the size has no useful meaning. On Linux with ext4, the size is 4096. In the in-memory directory of the browser, the size is 0. Thus the program prints the size only for files. Stat also has mtime, the time of the last change to the file, and atime, the time of the last read. This program does not print these times, for two reasons: A real time is different on each run. Thus CI cannot compare it. The in-memory directory in your browser does not store times. Each time in that directory is 0. Six failures open a file that is not there: FileNotFound create a file in a missing dir: FileNotFound open a directory as a file: IsDir use a file as a directory: NotDir deleteFile on a directory: IsDir deleteFile on a mis

title: Recipe: Word Frequencies
description: Count occurrences with a hash map, then rank them with a sort.
headings: Why the program copies the keys
text: To count words in Zig, divide the text into words with std.mem.tokenizeAny. Count the words into a StringHashMapUnmanaged(u32) with getOrPut. Then copy the entries into an ArrayList, and sort the list with std.mem.sort. The problem You have a block of text, and you want the five most common words. These are the conditions: Upper case and lower case are the same. The program ignores punctuation. The order is stable, thus two runs always give the same order for words with equal counts. Log analysis, tag clouds and all types of "top N by count" reports use this shape. Be careful about one thing. A hash map is the correct tool to count, but a hash map has no order . To rank the words, you need a second structure. The plan 1. Tokenize. Use whitespace and punctuation as delimiters. tokenizeAny never gives an empty token. 2. Count with getOrPut. This function does one lookup for each word, not a get and then a put. 3. Rank. Sort a copy of the entries with a comparator. When two counts are equal, the comparator uses alphabetical order. Why the program copies the keys lowerString writes each word in lower case into the same buffer, which the program uses again for each word. If the map stores that slice as a key, all of the keys point to one buffer. Then the last word overwrites all of the keys. gpa.dupe gives each key its own bytes. The copy of the keys is the only ownership decision in this recipe, and the arena makes the copy cheap. The map, the list and the copied keys all have the same lifetime. Thus one arena state.deinit() frees all of them. No key needs its own free, and no

title: Sound Without Sound Files
description: Five effects that the game synthesises at startup from oscillators and envelopes, and waveform tests that run without an audio device.
text: This project has no audio files. The five effects are arithmetic. The game generates them when it starts. To record or license five short sounds would take less time than to write a synthesiser. But that choice also adds three costs: A folder of binary files that nobody can diff. A licence question for each file. An audio editor for each change. When the game generates the sounds, a sound changes when a number changes. One oscillator with an envelope Each layer has a frequency sweep, an amplitude envelope, and an optional low pass. The low pass removes the high hiss from noise. delay starts a layer later than the others. The arpeggios use delay, thus they need no sequencer code. The coin has two layers: a triangle, and a quieter sine one octave higher. The crash has six layers. The last three layers are the descending triad that plays over the game over screen: The six layers are one sound, and not two sounds. As two sounds, the thud would play at impact and the sting would play when the retry prompt appears. Then the code must record if the sting played yet, for a run that is already over. A layer can have a delay, thus the pause is in the waveform. The renderer The frequency sweep is exponential and not linear. Pitch is logarithmic. Thus a linear sweep sounds as if it becomes faster near the end. The renderer adds the layers together, then soft clips the sum with tanh. It does not clamp the sum. Layers on top of each other go past the limit, and a clamp cuts the peaks flat. You hear the flat peaks as distortion. The envelope, and the click The envelope is exactly zero at

title: UDP Datagrams
description: Bound sockets and discrete messages, without a connection.
headings: Why this program needs no threads
text: In Zig, a UDP socket comes from std.Io.net.IpAddress.bind with .mode = .dgram. There is no listen and no accept. Each send names its destination. Each receive returns the data and the address of the sender. The problem Some traffic does not need a connection: metrics, discovery pings, game state and sensor readings. The loss of one message is acceptable. The cost of the ordering and retransmission in TCP is not acceptable. For this traffic, use UDP. The API of UDP is very different from TCP, thus the "listen and accept" model does not apply. There is nothing to accept. A socket binds to an address, and messages arrive at any time. The plan 1. Call bind with .mode = .dgram, not listen. If you bind to port 0, the OS selects an ephemeral port and records it in socket.address. 2. Send with socket.send(io, &destination, bytes). Each message has a destination, because there is no connection to remember the destination. 3. Receive with socket.receive(io, &buffer). This function returns the data slice and the address of the sender. 4. To reply, send to that address. There is no connection for the answer, thus the reply is only one more send. Why this program needs no threads The snippet sends a message and reads it. Then it sends one more message and reads that message. All of this occurs on one thread. No code must wait when a datagram arrives, because the kernel keeps the datagrams on the bound socket until a program reads them. UDP works in this way: the sender and the receiver never meet. They only share an address. (The queue has a limit. When the queue is full, the kernel dro

title: Transactions and errdefer
description: COMMIT on success, ROLLBACK on each error path, enforced by four lines.
headings: Why the ROLLBACK discards its own error
text: In Zig, a transaction wrapper does these steps: 1. Run BEGIN. 2. Register an errdefer that runs ROLLBACK. 3. Run the work of the caller. 4. Run COMMIT. An error at any point after the errdefer, also in COMMIT, rolls the transaction back and returns the original error. The problem A transaction wrapper has one job: no path can leave the transaction open. Languages solve this problem with defer, context managers or RAII. The bugs are in the paths that a programmer forgot: the early return, the error between two statements, the failed COMMIT. The designers of Zig made errdefer for this case, and a library API is a good place to use it. The pattern This is the full contract: try r.driver.exec("BEGIN"); errdefer r.driver.exec("ROLLBACK") catch {}; try body.run(r); try r.driver.exec("COMMIT"); The errdefer covers each try after it. On success, the errdefer does not run. No path reaches the end of the function with the transaction open. You can verify that when you read four lines, and you do not have to examine each return. Why the ROLLBACK discards its own error The wrapper discards the error from the ROLLBACK on purpose. A real library must document this decision. The wrapper already returns with the error of the caller, and that error explains the problem. A second error, "and also the rollback failed", in place of the first error, hides the cause. A production library logs the rollback failure, but it still returns the original error. The callback shape body is anytype with a run method. In the snippet, it takes the place of a closure. The work of the caller runs inside the f

title: Save a PNG
description: The program flattens the picture onto white paper and writes it as a PNG. Each row gets the filter, of five, that makes its bytes smallest.
headings: Give the file to the browser
Explain before you read the answer
text: Save PNG in the studio writes the picture that you see: each visible layer over white paper. The Write a PNG chapter makes a PNG writer by hand: the signature, the chunks, a CRC on each chunk, and zlib compression. Read that chapter first. This chapter shows the changes for a real document. There are two changes. The writer takes an allocator, and it selects a filter for each row. Flatten the layers A PNG can store the transparency of the layers. But people expect to save the picture on the screen, with the white paper behind it. The screen buffer already holds exactly that picture. Thus the save starts from the screen buffer: writePng marks the full screen as stale and renders it first. Usually the engine draws again only the areas that changed. A saved file must not depend on the last areas that the engine drew. An allocator, not global variables The writer in the PNG chapter kept its buffers in global variables. That works for one fixed size of picture. A document can be of any size. Thus this writer takes an allocator and gets the memory that it needs: The state of the compressor, about 224 KB. This is too large for a small stack. The 64 KB window that the compressor needs. Two rows of pixels, and five filtered copies of a row. The compressed output, which grows while the writer writes it. Each allocation has a defer immediately below it. Thus the code frees each allocation on each path out of the function, and this is also true on the error paths. A filter for each row The PNG chapter tried two filters on the full picture and kept the smaller file. With Sub, a gradient

title: Recipe: Load a JSON Config
description: Use defaults for absent fields, validate wrong values, and return clear errors for the other problems.
headings: The errdefer is the important line
text: In Zig, std.json.parseFromSlice loads a JSON config into a struct. If the file does not have a field, and the field has a default value, the field keeps that default. Put checks such as a port range in a separate validate function, because the parser checks only types and field names. The problem Your program reads a JSON config file, and users edit the file by hand. Thus each type of failure will occur: fields that are not in the file values that the parser accepts but that have no correct meaning field names with spelling errors files that are not JSON For an absent field, the program must use a correct default. For a wrong value, the program must refuse the value with a specific error. The program must not crash, and it must not load only part of the config. The plan 1. Put the defaults on the struct. Give each field a default value. Then std.json.parseFromSlice sets only the fields that the input supplies. An empty {} is a complete and valid config. 2. Validate in a separate step. The parser checks the shape : the types and the field names. Your policy decides if port: 80 is acceptable. Thus that check goes in a validate function with named errors. 3. Use one load entry point to connect the two steps. The function uses errdefer. Thus, if a config parses but fails validation, the function frees the config, and the config does not leak. The five cases Partial input: host and port come from the file. workers and debug come from the defaults. This is the usual path. Empty input: {} gives the config with all defaults. If this case gives an error, a field does not have a defa

title: Recipe: A Custom JSON Serializer
description: Give a struct a jsonStringify method to rename fields and add computed fields.
headings: The hook, one field at a time
text: To control how Zig writes a struct as JSON, give the struct a jsonStringify method. The method controls the write stream with beginObject, objectField, write and endObject. Then you can rename a field or add a computed value, and you do not have to build strings. The problem The default JSON serializer writes your struct exactly as you declared it: the same field names, the same values, and nothing more. Often the wire format must be different. For example, the field is is admin in Zig but admin in the API. Or the response needs a value that you compute and do not store. You want that control. You do not want to join strings by hand, and you want to keep the checks that make the output valid. When the type declares pub fn jsonStringify, std.json.Stringify calls that function. It does not go through the fields itself. The plan 1. Define the struct as usual. 2. Add pub fn jsonStringify(self: T, jws: anytype) !void. jws is a pointer to the write stream. 3. Control the stream: call beginObject, then objectField(name) and write(value) for each field, then endObject. 4. Serialize with std.json.Stringify.value(x, .{}, writer). The serializer finds the hook automatically. The hook, one field at a time objectField("user id") writes the key. write(self.id) writes the value with the usual serialization. For a string, that includes the quotes and the escape characters. You give the name of each key yourself. Thus, to rename a field, type a different string: is admin becomes admin, and name becomes full name. The stream records the structure. You can forget an endObject, or write a valu

title: Recipe: A Binary Wire Format
description: Serialize a struct to explicit bytes and back, with safe checks.
headings: Why the buffer type does the bounds check
text: In Zig, write a binary wire format one field at a time with std.mem.writeInt. Read the format back with std.mem.readInt. Each call gives its endianness. The decoder checks a magic number first. Thus bad input returns an error, and the decoder does not return random values. The problem You must write a struct to a location outside your process, for example a file header, a network packet or a save format. Later, you must read the struct back, possibly on a different machine. A fast method is to copy the memory of the struct directly with std.mem.asBytes or @bitCast. Do not use this method. For a plain Zig struct, the field order and the padding are not specified. Also, the integers of the struct are in the byte order of the host . Thus the bytes can change when the compiler, the target or the optimizer changes. A wire format must specify each byte exactly. The plan 1. Specify the format on paper first. The format is a 4-byte magic, a 2-byte version and a 4-byte payload length, all big-endian. That is ten bytes, with no padding and only one meaning. 2. Encode one field at a time with std.mem.writeInt. This function takes the endianness as an argument. 3. Do not trust the input when you decode. Input from outside the process is untrusted. The magic check occurs first, and it returns an error value, not an assertion. Why the buffer type does the bounds check encode takes [encoded len]u8. That type is a pointer to an array of exactly ten bytes, not a slice. A buffer of the wrong size is a compile error . Inside the function, buf[0..4] is a sub-array with a size that is known at

title: Lost Datagrams
description: Loss, duplication and reordering, made on demand so that you can see them.
headings: Silence looks the same as no traffic
text: A network that carries UDP datagrams does three things to them. It loses some datagrams, it delivers some datagrams two times, and it delivers some datagrams in the wrong order. The problem UDP does not promise to deliver anything. The previous chapter sent datagrams over loopback. On loopback, datagrams always arrive, thus none of these failures occurred. It is difficult to learn how to handle failures that you never see. Thus this chapter makes the failures. The snippet is a channel that operates incorrectly by design. A seeded random generator controls the channel, thus each run has the same failures. The next two chapters send their traffic through the same type of channel, and they fix each problem in turn. The plan 1. Make a FlakyChannel with one method: put a datagram in, and see what comes out. Sometimes nothing comes out. Sometimes the datagram comes out two times. Sometimes an older datagram arrives late. 2. Send ten numbered datagrams through the channel. 3. Let the receiver count what arrived and name each failure. Silence looks the same as no traffic The channel dropped datagram 0, and the trace for datagram 0 is empty. The receiver does not see a gap at the position of datagram 0. The receiver sees nothing. The receiver also sees nothing before the traffic starts and between datagrams. Thus the receiver cannot see a loss at the time of the loss. After the run, this receiver can name the lost datagram. There are two reasons for this: The snippet numbered the datagrams. The snippet told the receiver that ten datagrams will arrive. A real receiver does not know t

title: Projects and Presets
description: A project file keeps the layers that a PNG merges. A preset keeps a brush. Other people can write both, thus the program examines both first.
headings: To open a file is to read bytes from an unknown source
A small file can ask for much memory
Explain before you read the answer
text: A PNG is for a completed picture that you share. It is a bad format for a picture that you will change again. A PNG is flat. When the program saves a PNG, it merges the layers into one image. When you open the PNG again, nothing tells which paint was on which layer. Thus the eraser cannot show the bottom layer again. Two layers and the size of the page can make the picture again. One merged PNG cannot. Thus the studio has two more types of file: Save project keeps each layer, and records which layers are visible. Save brush keeps the settings of a brush as a preset . A preset is a name and the numbers that control the brush. A preset holds no pixels. The project format Before the code, the top of the file that implements the format describes it, field by field: header, 16 bytes 0 magic 4 bytes "ZPNT" 4 version u16 1 6 width u32 10 height u32 14 layers u8 1 to 8 15 active u8 less than layers each layer 0 visible u8 0 or 1 1 size u32 bytes of compressed pixels that follow 5 pixels size bytes, zlib: width height premultiplied RGBA The Binary Files chapter makes a format in the same way. The magic bytes tell the type of the file. The version tells which edition of the format the file uses. Thus a later program can change the format and still identify an old file. The program compresses the pixels of each layer with zlib, the same compressor that the PNG writer uses. An empty layer of 640 by 400 is 1,024,000 bytes of zeros. After compression, it is about one kilobyte. To open a file is to read bytes from an unknown source To save is easy. The program wrote the data, and it trust

title: Recipe: JSON vs Binary, by Size
description: The same 100,000 records as JSON and as packed bytes, with exact measurements.
text: The program writes the same 100,000 records in two formats. With Zig's std.json.Stringify.value, the records take 4.62 times the bytes of a fixed 24-byte binary record that std.mem.writeInt writes. JSON repeats each field name, and it writes numbers as decimal text. The problem You must select a wire format for a stream of records. You want a concrete number, not a guess. JSON is readable and self-describing. A packed binary layout is compact. This recipe encodes the same 100,000 events in both formats and prints the exact byte counts. Thus you can compare measured numbers. The data comes from a seed. Thus the sizes are reproducible. You get the same numbers on each run, and for that reason this page can assert them. The plan 1. Make 100,000 events from a fixed PRNG seed. 2. Serialize the slice with std.json.Stringify.value, and measure the text. 3. Serialize each event as a fixed 24-byte little-endian record, and measure the bytes. 4. Divide. Why binary is smaller Here, JSON is 4.62 times larger, and the reasons come from the structure of the two formats: Each JSON record repeats its field names as text ("player id", "timestamp"). The binary form has no field names. Numbers become longer. A u32 is four bytes in binary, but in JSON it is up to ten decimal digits. A float becomes a decimal string, which is usually longer than its four raw bytes. The enum is one byte in binary. In JSON, it becomes "move" or "attack". JSON pays this cost because it is self-describing. The binary record is always 24 bytes, for all values. It contains an i64 timestamp, a u32 id, two f32 coordina

title: Recipe: A File-Backed To-Do Store
description: Records of fixed size on disk, updated in place by id with positional reads and writes.
headings: Why all records are the same size
text: When all records are the same size, a store on disk in Zig can update one record and not write the full file again. Record N is at (N - 1) @sizeOf(Record). readPositionalAll and writePositionalAll read and write at that offset. The problem You want to store a list of items on disk. You also want to update one item, and not write the full file again. With records of fixed size, a read or an update of one record is one positional operation, not a scan. Each database file with pages of fixed size uses the same idea. The plan 1. Define the record as an extern struct. Thus its byte layout is fixed and identical on each write. 2. To add a record, append it at the current end of the file. 3. Read or update record N at its fixed offset. 4. To update in place, read the slot, change a field, and write the slot again to the same offset. Why all records are the same size The record is an extern struct, which fixes its layout: an id, a done flag, a length byte and 64 bytes of text. The record is 72 bytes each time. The two extra bytes are alignment padding. They cause no problem, because the code computes each offset from @sizeOf. The size is constant. Thus the file is an array on disk. Item 3 is always at offset 2 72, and toggle goes directly to that offset. A format with records of different lengths, for example JSON lines, does not have this property. To find the start of record 3, you must read from the start of the file. Positional I/O, not seek Since Zig 0.16, the filesystem is behind the Io interface. For random access, use readPositionalAll and writePositionalAll. Each function

title: Recipe: Compress with zlib
description: Compress and decompress in one call each through the system zlib, linked from Zig.
headings: Give the header and the library separately
The size of the output buffer
Why the page does not show the size
text: Zig can compress a buffer with the system zlib. Link z, translate the zlib.h header, and call compressBound, compress2 and uncompress as usual C functions. The problem You must make a buffer smaller before you write it or send it. zlib is a library that each machine already has. This recipe compresses a buffer, decompresses it again and checks the result. The plan 1. Ask compressBound for the largest possible size of the output. Make the destination buffer that size. 2. compress2(dest, &destLen, src, srcLen, level) fills the buffer and changes destLen to the real size. Z OK means success. 3. uncompress does the opposite, into a buffer with the size of the original. 4. Compare the result with the input. Give the header and the library separately zlib shows that a header and a library can have different names. The library is z (you link it with -lz), but the header is zlib.h. The build.zig of this guide reads two markers from the snippet: //! link: z for the library and //! cinclude: zlib.h for the header. Then the build does these steps: 1. It makes a header that includes zlib.h. 2. It translates that header with a translate-c step. 3. It links z. 4. It gives the module to the snippet as c. For SQLite, the two names are the same. Thus SQLite needs only //! link: sqlite3. zlib needs both markers. The size of the output buffer On input that does not compress, compression can make a few more bytes than it read. Thus you cannot assume that the output fits in the size of the input. compressBound(srcLen) returns the worst case, and the program uses that size for the destination bu

title: Recipe: Catch Memory Leaks
description: Make the test suite prove that the code frees each allocation.
headings: The failure path is the path that leaks
Why this works in ReleaseFast too
text: Zig tests find memory leaks when the tests allocate through std.testing.allocator. To find leaks on error paths, use std.testing.FailingAllocator. This allocator makes a selected allocation return error.OutOfMemory. The problem With manual memory management, each alloc needs a free that matches it. The free must occur on each path, and also on the paths that occur only when a different operation fails. A careful read of the code does not work when the code becomes large. You want the test suite to fail, with a stack trace, immediately when a path leaks memory. If memory from std.testing.allocator is still allocated at the end of a test, the test fails . The allocator shows where the program allocated the memory that has no owner. The plan 1. Send all of the allocations in tests through std.testing.allocator. 2. Some init functions make more than one allocation. For each of these functions, test the failure in the middle with std.testing.FailingAllocator. This allocator succeeds N times. Then it returns error.OutOfMemory on purpose. 3. If many small allocations have the same lifetime, use an arena. Then the cleanup is one call, and not one free for each allocation. The failure path is the path that leaks Look at Buffers.init. The first alloc succeeds, and the second alloc can fail. On that path, the function returns an error, and the caller does not get the struct. Thus a has no owner. The errdefer gpa.free(a) runs on that error return and on no other path. title: Recipe: Print Any Struct
description: Comptime reflection builds a debug printer that works for all struct types.
text: Zig can print each struct without a function for each type. The code loops over @typeInfo with inline for at compile time. On current master, the fields come as the parallel arrays field names and field types, not as the old fields slice. The problem You want to show any struct for debugging or logging: the field names, the values, and the strings with quotes. You do not want to write a print function for each type. Also, you do not want reflection machinery at runtime. In most languages, this needs a reflection API and some overhead at runtime. The plan 1. Take the value as anytype, and get its type with @TypeOf. 2. Ask the compiler for the shape of the struct with @typeInfo. 3. Use inline for over the fields. The compiler unrolls the loop at compile time. Thus each iteration can use a different field type, and the generated code is a straight line of prints. The shape of @typeInfo changed If you used this API before, note the change. Before, @typeInfo(T).@"struct" had one fields slice of StructField structs, and each one had a name and a type. Current master divides that slice into parallel arrays: field names, field types and field attrs. Zig guarantees that the arrays have the same length. To use the names and the types together, write an inline for over two slices: inline for (info.field names, info.field types) name, Field { const v = @field(value, name); } A tutorial that shows .fields with field.name and field.type does not compile now. title: Sequence Numbers and Acks
description: One counter makes an invisible loss into a detected gap, and one reply gives the problem to the sender.
text: A sequence number on each message lets a receiver find loss and duplicates. A cumulative ack ("I have everything through N") tells the sender what to send again. The acks in TCP use the same design. The problem At the end of the previous chapter, the receiver could not see the difference between loss and silence. The fix costs one byte: put a number on each message. If a receiver expects 2 and gets 3, the receiver now knows that a message is lost. The network did not report the loss. If a receiver gets 4 two times, the receiver knows that the second 4 is a retry, not a new message. Detection is only half of the work. The receiver knows about the gap, but the sender has the lost message. Thus the receiver sends a report back. This report is an acknowledgement in the other direction. It tells the sender how much of the stream the receiver has. The reply gives the loss to the sender, and only the sender can fix the loss. The plan 1. Use the same channel that operates incorrectly, but with a script. The channel drops datagram 2 and duplicates datagram 4. Thus you can check each line of the output by hand. 2. Make a Watcher with one field: the next number that it expects. A number below that value is a duplicate. An equal number is in order. A number above that value is a gap, and the gap has exact edges. 3. Make a receiver that sends acks. It answers each arrival with "I have everything through N". Make a sender that reads these answers. One counter, three verdicts The Watcher is one u8 and a comparison. Detection with sequence numbers needs only these two things. Each result i

title: Recipe: Overflow Without Panics
description: Do arithmetic on values that can be too large, without undefined behavior and without a crash.
text: In safe builds, a plain + in Zig panics on overflow. To handle the overflow, select one of four explicit forms: std.math.add returns error.Overflow. + saturates. +% wraps. @addWithOverflow returns the result and a flag. The problem You add numbers that you do not control: user input, a file or a network peer. 200 + 100 is too large for a u8. In C, this overflow is undefined behavior for a signed type. For an unsigned type, the value wraps and no error occurs. In Zig, in safe builds, a plain + panics when the result is too large for the type. The panic is correct for a programming bug. It is wrong for input. The program must handle bad input, and it must not stop. The plan Select the operator that tells what overflow means for this value: You want Use On overflow --- --- --- an error to handle std.math.add(T, a, b) returns error.Overflow a value that stops at the limits a + b gives maxInt / minInt modular arithmetic a +% b wraps, by definition the flag and the bits @addWithOverflow(a, b) returns both Select a form std.math.add is correct at trust boundaries. The caller gets an error value and decides what "too large" means. For example, the caller can refuse the request, log the error or use a default value. Saturating (+ ) is correct for quantities where a value at the limit has a meaning: volume, progress, brightness. The result is not the true sum, but a stop at the limit is the behavior that you want. Wrapping (+%) is for domains that are modular: hashes, checksums, ring buffer indices and sequence numbers.
