title: Watercolour
description: Water and pigment on a grid of paper. They spread, the paper dries, and pigment settles into it. Fixed steps make each run the same on all computers.
headings: Read the old grid, write a new grid
The same run in all builds
Explain before you read the answer
text: Wet paint on wet paper does not stay where the brush put it. The water spreads into the paper around it, and the water carries the colour. Then the paper dries, and the colour stays where the water left it. The brushes in the previous chapters cannot do this. A brush decides each pixel one time, when the dab occurs. Watercolour continues to change after the brush moves away. Thus this is a separate experiment with its own state, and the experiment runs over time: A grid of paper The program divides the paper into cells, 80 across and 50 down. On the 640 by 400 page, each cell is 8 by 8 pixels. Each cell keeps three numbers: water : how wet the paper is, from 0 (dry) to 1 (fully wet). mobile : pigment that is still in the water. This pigment can move. deposited : pigment that is now in the paper. This pigment cannot move. The program stores a grid as one long array, row by row. Cell (x, y) is at y width + x. On a grid 80 wide, cell (3, 2) is number 2 × 80 + 3 = 163. 80 × 50 is 4,000 cells. One f32 field is 16,000 bytes, and all five fields are 80,000 bytes. The grid is coarse on purpose. The full simulation fits in a small cache, and it runs 30 times each second on a slow laptop. The picture on the page is these 4,000 cells, scaled up smoothly. The blur from the scaling gives the soft edge that watercolour must have. Neighbours Water spreads to the cells next to it: left, right, above and below. At the edge of the paper, some of those cells do not exist. The code examines the coordinates before it makes an index: If the code examined the index instead, that would be a bug. T

title: Recipe: The std.math Toolbox
description: Constants, trig, powers, roots, rounding, and a safe comparison of floats.
headings: pow takes a type, sqrt does not
text: The math functions of Zig are in std.math. Examples are std.math.sqrt, std.math.sin (which takes radians), std.math.pow(T, base, exp) and constants such as std.math.pi. Compare floats with std.math.approxEqAbs, not with ==. The problem You need a formula: a sine, a square root, or a change from degrees to radians. All of the functions are in std.math. Two details cause most first mistakes. Trig functions use radians, and pow needs its type as the first argument. This chapter is the short reference. The plan 1. Read constants such as std.math.pi directly from std.math. 2. Convert with std.math.degreesToRadians. Then call sin, cos and tan. 3. Use std.math.pow(T, base, exp) and std.math.sqrt. 4. Round with floor, ceil and round. Use hypot and clamp when you need them. 5. Compare floats with approxEqAbs, never with ==. Trig uses radians std.math.sin, cos and tan take radians, as the math library of almost each language does. degreesToRadians does the conversion. Thus sin(degreesToRadians(90)) is the clear way to get 1.0. The snippet prints 1.0000 and not 1 because of the {d:.4} format. At f32, the result is exactly one. Do not take that as a rule. For most angles of a whole number of degrees, the last bit of the f32 sine is different from the correctly rounded value. For that reason, the comparison below uses a tolerance. pow takes a type, sqrt does not std.math.pow(f32, 2.0, 8.0) takes the type as its first argument, because the function must select an algorithm for that type. std.math.sqrt gets all of the information from its operand. Thus sqrt(@as(f32, 64.0)) is sufficient.

title: Recipe: A SIMD Dot Product
description: Use @Vector to process four elements in each operation, with the tail too.
headings: The cast from slice to vector
text: A SIMD dot product in Zig multiplies chunks of @Vector(4, i32) with plain and +=. Then @reduce(.Add, acc) adds the lanes together, and a scalar loop does the elements that remain. The problem You have two arrays of numbers, and you want their dot product. The scalar loop is slow in your profile. Modern CPUs (and wasm) have SIMD registers that do one operation on several values at the same time. Zig gives you these registers through @Vector, in a portable way, with the usual operators. Thus the vector code looks like the scalar code. Errors usually occur at the two ends: the change from slice data to vector operands the tail, when the length is not a multiple of the lane count The plan 1. Define a vector type. @Vector(4, i32) has four i32 lanes. 2. Loop over the slice in steps of one full vector. xs[i..][0..Lanes]. takes four contiguous elements as an array. The array coerces to a vector. 3. Multiply and accumulate with plain and +=. These operators work on each lane at the same time. 4. After the loop, add the lanes together with @reduce(.Add, acc). Then do the zero to three elements that remain with a scalar loop. The cast from slice to vector xs[i..][0..Lanes] is a common pattern. The first slice moves the start. The second slice has a length that is known at comptime. Thus its type is a pointer to an array, const [4]i32. The dereference with . gives the array by value. An array coerces to a vector of the same length and element type. This needs no @memcpy and no unsafe cast. In safe builds, Zig checks the bounds. The tail is necessary With ten elements and four lanes, tw

title: Retransmission and the Window
description: A timeout recovers the messages that the network lost, and a window keeps traffic in motion during the recovery.
text: Retransmission sends a message again when its ack does not arrive before a timeout. A sliding window keeps many messages in flight, thus one loss does not stop the stream. Together with sequence numbers and cumulative acks, these two methods are the core mechanism of TCP. The problem The sender now knows which messages got no confirmation. The sender must still recover these messages. Something must decide when to stop the wait for an ack and send the message again. The data cannot make that decision. Silence does not tell how long it will continue, thus the sender can only use the clock. The sender waits a fixed time, then it sends again. That fixes the delivery, but it causes a speed problem. If a sender sends one message and waits for its ack, the sender spends most of its time in the wait. The fix is a window: many messages in flight at the same time, each with its own timer. In this snippet, time is a counter that has the name tick. It is not a real clock. The tick counter makes each run the same. The round trip of the ack also costs no time. Thus the only delay in the trace comes from the timeout policy. The plan 1. The scripted network drops transmissions by position: the 2nd and 4th data transmission, and the 4th ack. A retry is a new transmission, thus the network can also drop a retry. 2. The receiver is the receiver from the previous chapter, with one change. It records what arrived and answers with a cumulative ack. It also keeps the arrivals that are out of order. 3. The sender records base (all messages below it have a confirmation) and next. It also records w

title: Recipe: Scan Bytes with SIMD
description: The five-step pattern that changes a loop of one byte at a time into a scan as wide as a register.
headings: Why not let the compiler do it
text: A SIMD byte scan in Zig loads the bytes for a full vector at one time and compares each lane in one operation. Then @bitCast changes the bool vector from the comparison to an integer, and @ctz finds the first match. The pattern has five steps: splat, load, compare, extract, tail. The problem A parser that reads a JSON string uses most of its time in a loop such as this one: while (i The mask is an integer Step 4 changes the comparison into an answer. @bitCast packs a @Vector(16, bool) into a u16, with lane 0 in the lowest bit. After that, each question about the lanes is a question about an integer, and one instruction answers it: Question Answer --- --- did a lane match? hits != 0 where is the first match? @ctz(hits) how many matched? @popCount(hits) On x86, the name of this operation is movemask. The snippet uses @ctz to find the first special byte, and @popCount to count the quotes. Both scans use the same steps 1 to 3. They are different only at step 4. The mask type is @Int(.unsigned, lanes). On current master, this builtin replaces std.meta.Int. Two needles in one pass The scan looks for " or \. Each needle has its own splat and its own compare. An integer merges the two masks. A third needle costs one more compare, not one more pass over the data. Scalar code pays one branch for each needle, for each byte. The vector loop pays nothing more for each byte, and it has one branch for each 16 bytes. Targets without SIMD suggestVectorLength asks the target how many lanes its registers hold. title: Recipe: Vector Algebra
description: Dot, length, normalize and cross on @Vector, written as math and not as loops.
headings: The length is exactly one by chance
text: Vector math on the @Vector(3, f32) type of Zig uses the usual operators. The dot product is @reduce(.Add, a b), and normalization divides by @splat(len). Only the cross product must use specific lanes by index. The problem You do 3D work (graphics, physics, a game), and you need the four basic operations: dot product, length, normalization and cross product. As scalar loops, these operations are hard to read, and it is easy to make small errors in them. With @Vector, the code looks like the math that it implements, and the compiler emits SIMD. Errors usually occur in two steps: the change from a vector to one number the change from one number to a vector The plan 1. Select a vector type. @Vector(3, f32) has three f32 lanes. 2. Dot product: multiply each lane by the same lane of the other vector, then add the lanes together. 3. Length is sqrt(dot(v, v)). It uses the dot function again. 4. Normalization divides each lane by the length, in one operation. 5. Cross is the exception. It uses specific lanes. Thus you cannot write it for all widths, as you can write the other operations. @reduce changes lanes to a scalar a b multiplies element by element, and the result is a vector. For a dot product, you also need the horizontal step: add lane 0, lane 1 and lane 2 into one number. That step is @reduce(.Add, product). The same builtin does .Min, .Max, .Mul and the bitwise reductions. Thus it is the general way to change a vector into a scalar. The body of dot uses only @reduce and . title: Recipe: Keep the Last N Items
description: A generic ring buffer with a fixed capacity, built with a type function.
text: In Zig, a ring buffer can be a type function: fn LastN(comptime T: type, comptime capacity: usize) type. The function returns a struct that holds a fixed [capacity]T array. When the buffer is full, a push writes over the oldest item. No code allocates memory. The problem You want the N most recent items. Some examples: the last log lines for an error report the last sensor readings for a moving average the recent commands for an undo stack The storage must have a limit. Old entries must go away automatically, and if possible, no code allocates. This is a ring buffer. A ring buffer is also a good first example of Zig generics: a function that takes types and comptime values, and returns a type. The plan 1. Write LastN, and return a struct from it. The capacity becomes part of the type. Thus the array can be on the stack. 2. Keep two fields of state. head is the next slot to write. len increases to the capacity and then stays there. 3. push writes at head and moves head forward, modulo the capacity. When the buffer is full, push writes over the oldest entry. This overwrite is intentional. 4. get(i) gets items with the oldest first. It calculates the start position from head and len. The type function in detail LastN([]const u8, 4) and LastN(f32, 3) are two different concrete types. The compiler makes them at compile time. The generic code needs no boxing, no interface and no cost at runtime. Each instance compiles as if you wrote it by hand. const Self = @This() gives a name to the anonymous struct. title: Recipe: Set Operations on the Cheap
description: A static bit set does membership, intersection and union with one instruction each.
headings: Why a bit set is better than a hash set here
text: In Zig, std.bit set.Static(n) keeps a set of small integers as bits. Thus union and intersection are bitwise operations, and no code allocates memory. std.bit set.Static(24) keeps the hours of a day in one u24. The problem You need sets of small integers, and set arithmetic on these sets. Some examples: the hours when two calendars are both free the seats, of 64, that people use the permissions that two roles share A hash set can do this work. But a hash set allocates memory and follows pointers. Also, with a hash set, the intersection of two sets is a loop with lookups. Sometimes the possible members are few and known, for example hours 0 to 23 or seats 0 to 63. Then a bit set does the same work with one integer and some bitwise operations. The plan 1. Select the size of the universe at compile time: std.bit set.Static(24) for the hours of a day. At 24 bits, the full set is one u24. This recipe does not use an allocator. 2. Start from the empty constant, and set the members. 3. Combine sets with intersectWith and unionWith, which return new sets. The functions setIntersection and setUnion do the same operations in place. 4. Get information with isSet, count and iterator. What changed in the API Older material makes these sets with initEmpty() and initFull(). Current master does not have those methods. Now the type has the declaration constants empty and full. Use them with the .empty syntax, which looks like an enum literal: var hours: std.bit set.Static(24) = .empty; The containers of the standard library use the same pattern: .empty replaces the init functions. title: Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union)
description: Groups that merge when edges arrive. A merge moves one root in a parent array, and a find follows links to the root.
headings: See a tree become a chain
Do not compare parents instead of roots
Do not link the nodes instead of their roots
Do not use a recursive find on a long chain
text: Think of ten nodes with no connections between them. Edges arrive one at a time. After each edge, the problem asks how many separate groups there are. The problem also asks for each edge that joins two nodes in the same group. Such an edge closes a cycle. Union-find answers the two questions. Another name for union-find is disjoint set union, or DSU. Union-find has two operations: find gives the name of the group that a node is in. unite merges two groups into one group. The program below gives ten edges to ten nodes and solves the problem in three ways. For each way, the program prints the cost. Read the example input 10 nodes and 10 edges parsed from the input 0-1 2-3 1-3 4-5 6-7 5-7 0-2 8-9 2-6 7-1 The first line of the input has the node count. Each line after the first line is one edge. If you know all of the edges before the first question, a breadth-first search can also count the groups. Use union-find when edges continue to arrive and the questions occur between the edges. Relabel a whole group The first method gives each node a label. Two nodes are in the same group when they have the same label. This check costs one comparison. The cost is in the merge. title: Recipe: Reproducible Randomness
description: Seeded generators make random worlds, tests and replays repeatable.
headings: Do not use a PRNG for secrets
text: For repeatable randomness in Zig, make a generator from a fixed seed with std.Random.DefaultPrng.init(42). Give prng.random() to the code that needs it. On the same Zig version, the same seed gives the same output on all platforms. The problem Your program makes something random: a game map, test data or a shuffled playlist. Then a bug report comes. You need the exact map that the user saw, not a new random map. Or a test fails one time in fifty runs, and you need that run again. In each of these cases, the randomness must come from a seed that you control. Zig has no hidden global generator. Thus the code always gives the generator explicitly. The plan 1. Make a deterministic generator from a seed. 2. Give its std.Random interface to the code that needs randomness. That code cannot see a difference between a seeded generator and a generator with a new seed. 3. Store or log the seed. When you use the seed again, you get again all of the data that came from the seed. Give the std.Random interface generateCave takes std.Random, not a concrete generator. In production, you can make the seed from the clock or from entropy. In a test or a replay, you give a fixed seed. The code that makes the cave is the same in both cases. title: Project: Units of Measure
description: A number type that carries its unit. Metres times metres is an area, and metres plus seconds does not compile.
headings: A unit is a list of powers
The same unit is the same type
text: A program that calculates with physical values must keep the units correct. A value in metres plus a value in seconds has no meaning, but two f64 values add without a complaint. This project puts the unit into the type. The compiler then checks each calculation, and a wrong unit stops the build. At runtime, each value is one f64 and nothing more. The project uses these chapters: Know What the Compiler Knows, for a struct value as a comptime parameter. Reject Bad Input with @compileError, for the message. A unit is a list of powers const Dim = struct { m: i8 = 0, s: i8 = 0, kg: i8 = 0, }; Each physical unit in this program is a product of three base units. Dim keeps the power of each one: Metres is .{ .m = 1 }. Metres per second is .{ .m = 1, .s = -1 }. Newtons, the unit of force, is .{ .kg = 1, .m = 1, .s = -2 }. To multiply two units, add their powers. To divide, subtract the powers. Dim.mul and Dim.div do this. They are usual functions, and the compiler runs them. A type for each unit fn Quantity(comptime dim: Dim) type { return struct { value: f64, ... }; } const Metres = Quantity(.{ .m = 1 }); const Seconds = Quantity(.{ .s = 1 }); A comptime parameter can be a struct value, not only a type. Each different Dim makes a different type. headings: Status is data, not an error

title: Recipe: Split Work Across Threads
description: Divide a slice among threads with no locks and one join.
headings: Why the program needs no locks
text: To divide work among threads in Zig, give each std.Thread.spawn worker its own chunk of the slice and its own output slot. Then join all of the threads and add the slots. Current master does not have std.Thread.Pool. The problem You have a large slice and a computation for each element, and one core does all of the work. The usual solution is to give each thread a chunk. The usual problem in practice is shared data. When threads write to common state, you need locks. Locks cause contention and can cause a deadlock. This recipe gets parallel work with no locks. The threads share no data. The plan 1. Divide the slice into one chunk for each worker. Use ceiling division, thus the last chunk gets the remainder. 2. Give each thread its own input chunk and its own output slot. No two threads use the same data. Thus no shared mutable state needs protection. 3. join each thread. Then combine the slots on the main thread. Why the program needs no locks Exactly one thread writes slot w. The main thread reads the slot only after join returns. join is the synchronization point. It guarantees that the writes of the joined thread are visible to the thread that called join. The pattern works for each workload of the map type: 1. Divide the inputs. 2. Give each worker a private output. 3. Merge the outputs after the join. The alternative is that each thread adds to one shared total. That needs a mutex or an atomic on the hot path. Private slots move that cost to one merge loop at the end. What replaced the pool Older tutorials use std.Thread.Pool with a WaitGroup. Current master has neithe

title: Recipe: An Atomic Work Index
description: Dynamic load balancing with fetchAdd, without locks or chunks.
headings: Why fetchAdd cannot give one job to two threads
When threads claim more indices than there are jobs
text: An atomic work index in Zig is a shared std.atomic.Value(usize). Each thread increments it with fetchAdd(1, .monotonic) to claim its next job. A thread that completes its work early claims the next job, and no lock is necessary. The problem Static chunks (one part of the slice for each thread) balance the load only when all items have the same cost. Item 7 can take a hundred times longer than item 8. Then the thread with the chunk of item 7 completes last, and the other threads have no work. You want each thread to get the next job when it is free, as workers take tickets from a dispenser. A mutex around a next job counter works, but the counter is the full critical section. Atomics do the same work without a lock. The plan 1. Share two atomics. next is the index of the next job that no thread claimed. total is the result so far. 2. Each worker runs a loop. It claims an index, and stops when the index is past the end. If the index is not past the end, the worker processes the job and adds the result to total with another fetchAdd. 3. Spawn the workers, join them, and read the total. Why fetchAdd cannot give one job to two threads fetchAdd is one indivisible read-modify-write. It returns the old value and stores the incremented value. No other thread can run between the read and the write. Two threads in a race on the same counter always get two different indices. That guarantee is the main reason to use an atomic here, more than speed. The absence of a lock is an extra benefit. Both atomics use .monotonic ordering, because each atomic is independent. No thread reads total b

title: Recipe: A Producer/Consumer Queue
description: std.Io.Queue as a bounded channel, with close() as the shutdown protocol.
text: A producer/consumer queue in Zig is std.Io.Queue(T). Workers block on getOne. After the producer calls close, the workers get the items that remain, and then they get error.Closed. The problem One part of your program finds work. A different part does the work. The usual solution is a queue between the two parts. Versions that people write by hand usually get extra parts: a mutex, a condition variable and a "no more work" flag. They also often get a subtle bug: at shutdown, workers wait forever. On current Zig master, std.Io.Queue(T) does all of this. It is a bounded, thread-safe channel. It has a put and a get that block, and a close protocol. The plan 1. Make a std.Io.Queue(u64) on a fixed buffer that you supply. The length of the buffer is the capacity of the queue. If a producer is more items ahead than the capacity, the producer blocks until the workers take more items. The name of this behavior is backpressure. 2. Spawn workers that loop on getOne. getOne blocks until an item arrives. 3. Produce the items, then call close. The workers get the items that remain. Then getOne returns error.Closed, and each worker stops its loop. 4. join the workers. Close is the shutdown protocol Shutdown is the usual place where worker queues fail. Usual solutions are a sentinel value for each worker, or a flag and a broadcast. It is easy to make an error in each of these. close makes shutdown part of the contract of the queue: 1. A put after close fails. 2. The queue still delivers the items that it already has. 3. Only then does a get return error.Closed. Thus the worker loop is two l

title: Recipe: Struct Memory Layout
description: Read the size, alignment and field offsets that a struct really gets, and control them.
headings: The default layout changes the order of fields
align(N) increases the alignment of the full struct
text: In Zig, @sizeOf, @alignOf and @offsetOf report the real size, alignment and field offsets of a struct. A plain struct can change the order of its fields. Use extern struct to match C, and use packed struct for exact bits. The problem You must know how a struct is in memory: the size of the struct the position of each field if you can give the struct to C or to hardware Do not guess from the field types. The default layout can change the order of the fields and add padding. The plan 1. Examine a type with @sizeOf, @alignOf and @offsetOf. 2. Put a field on a specified boundary with align(N). 3. Use packed struct for fields at the bit level with no padding. Then use @bitCast to change the struct to an integer. 4. Use extern struct when the layout must match the C ABI. The default layout changes the order of fields The declaration of Padded is a: u8, b: u64, c: u32. A C programmer expects this layout: a at offset 0, seven bytes of padding, b at 8 and c at 16. The total is 24 bytes. The default layout of Zig is not specified, and the current compiler uses that freedom. The compiler puts b at 0, c at 8 and a at 12. The total is 16 bytes. With the largest field first, the padding decreases from eleven bytes to three bytes. These numbers are specific to this compiler and this target. Do not depend on the field order of an auto struct. If a byte offset is important, read it with @offsetOf, or use a layout that guarantees the order. align(N) increases the alignment of the full struct Aligned puts a on a 16-byte boundary. The alignment of a field cannot decrease the alignment of the s

title: Recipe: SQLite From Zig
description: Open a database, create a table, insert with a prepared statement, and query, through the C API.
text: Zig calls the C API of SQLite directly. A translate-c build step changes sqlite3.h into a module, and the program imports that module as @import("c"). The program links sqlite3. Zig removed @cImport, thus older examples that use it do not compile now. The problem You want a real database from Zig, and SQLite is the usual first database. SQLite is a C library with no server. Thus you need only a header and a linked library. Zig calls C directly, thus you do not have to install a binding layer. The work is to learn the open/prepare/bind/step/finalize shape of SQLite, and to change its integer return codes into Zig errors. The plan 1. Import the C API. On current Zig, this is a translate-c step in the build, imported as @import("c"). It is not the old @cImport (see below). 2. Call sqlite3 open(":memory:", &db). With an in-memory database, the example is deterministic, and it leaves no file. 3. Use sqlite3 exec for statements with no results, for example CREATE TABLE. 4. For inserts, call sqlite3 prepare v2 one time. Then bind, step and reset for each row. 5. Step a SELECT, and read the columns until the step returns SQLITE DONE. Zig removed that builtin. Now headers come through a step of the build system, b.addTranslateC. This step makes a usual Zig module that you import by name. title: Recipe: A Redis RESP Round Trip
description: Use the RESP protocol of Redis over a socket, with a small server and client in one process.
headings: Read lines: be careful with the delimiter
text:
A Redis command in RESP is and the argument count. Then each argument follows as $, its byte length and its bytes. Each line ends in 
. A Zig program can write and parse that format directly, with no client library. The problem Redis uses RESP, a small text protocol over TCP. You do not need a client library to communicate with Redis. A command is an array of strings, each with its length before it. A reply is one line with a tag. This recipe implements a small part of both ends, sufficient to run SET and GET. Thus you can see the exact bytes that go over the wire. The recipe does not depend on a redis-server that runs. It runs a small RESP server in the same process, as the TCP recipe does. CI runs the full exchange and compares the output. Thus CI verifies the protocol code, but no external database is necessary. The plan 1. Encode a command as RESP. Write for the argument count. Then, for each argument, write $ and the bytes. End each line with 
. 2. On the server, parse that array. Send SET and GET to a StringHashMap, and reply in RESP. 3. On the client, send a command. Decode the one-line reply by its first byte: + simple string, - error, : integer, $ bulk string. The wire format SET framework zig goes out as 3
$3
SET
$9
framework
$3
zig
. A RESP command contains only these parts: a count, then each argument as a byte length and the bytes. The length is explicit. Thus the parser never has to guess where a value ends. A value can contain any byte,

title: Take or Skip: The 0/1 Knapsack
description: All subsets, the take-or-skip recursion, the table that stops repeats, the walk back to the items, and the one-row version with its loop direction.
headings: Fill the table from the bottom up
Use one row instead of a table
text: A bag holds 10 kilograms, and there are five items. Each item has a weight and a value. The problem is to get the most value that fits in the bag. Each item goes into the bag one time or not at all. You cannot cut an item in half, and you cannot take two copies of an item. The "0/1" in the name means exactly this rule. The program below solves the same problem in five ways. It prints the work that each method does. The problem The input is the capacity, then a row of weights, then a row of values. 5 items, a bag that holds 10 item 1 2 3 4 5 weight 5 4 6 3 2 value 10 40 30 50 15 Item 4 is light and has a high value. Thus item 4 is an easy choice. For the other items, the best choice is not easy to see: Items 2 and 3 together weigh exactly 10, and their value is 70. Items 2, 4 and 5 weigh 9, and their value is 105. You need a method that checks all of the options, but does not make a list of each option. Try all subsets The certain method is to try all of the subsets. Each item is in the subset or not in it. Thus one bit for each item is sufficient to keep a subset. When mask counts from 0 to 2^n - 1, it gets to each subset exactly one time. For each mask, the function adds the weights and the values. It keeps the best subset that fits. every subset of 5 items 32 subsets tried, best is items 2 4 5, weight 9, value 105 Five items give 32 subsets. Twenty items give 1,048,576. Each new item doubles the work. Thus this method is useful only as a check on small inputs. The program keeps this method for that check. Each faster method below must give the same answer. title: Recipe: The PostgreSQL Wire Protocol
description: Use the Postgres protocol directly, and frame a startup handshake and a query by hand.
headings: The handshake is a stream, not a call
text: A Zig program can use the PostgreSQL wire protocol with no driver. After the startup message, each message has three parts: a one-byte type, a big-endian Int32 length that counts itself, and the payload. The problem A Postgres driver is mostly a codec for one TCP protocol. When you see that protocol without a driver, you see the real cost of a query, and the cause of a hang. This recipe implements a part of both ends, sufficient to complete a startup handshake and run one query. Thus the exact bytes are on the page. The other database recipes run a mock backend in the same process, and this recipe does too. Thus CI runs the full exchange and compares the output, without a postgres that runs. The framing is the real protocol. Only the authentication and the query engine are stubs. The plan 1. All of the integers are big-endian. Write one putInt and one getInt, and use them everywhere. 2. Send a StartupMessage. It has no type byte, only a length and a list of parameters that ends in a null. 3. Read the reply stream of the backend until ReadyForQuery (Z). Decode each message by its type byte. 4. Send a Query (Q). Then read RowDescription (T), DataRow (D), CommandComplete (C) and the next ReadyForQuery. Two message shapes After the first message, each Postgres message has the same frame: 1. a one-byte type 2. an Int32 length that counts itself but not the type byte 3. length - 4 bytes of payload sendMsg and readMsg encode exactly that frame. Thus the other code works only with payloads. The startup message is the one exception. It is older than the type-byte convention. Thus it

title: Project: Parse Arguments from a Struct
description: The fields of a struct are the options. The compiler makes the parser and the help text.
headings: Match an argument to a field
text: A command-line program declares its options in one place and parses them in another. When you add an option, you must change both places, and the help text too. If you forget one, the three disagree. In this project, a struct is the only declaration. The compiler reads the fields of the struct and makes the parser and the help text from them. A new field is a new option, with no other change. The project uses Read a Type for the fields and their defaults. Command-Line Arguments shows how a real program gets its arguments. This page uses a fixed list of strings, so that the program can run in your browser. The options are a struct const Options = struct { port: u16 = 8080, host: []const u8 = "localhost", verbose: bool = false, level: Level = .info, name: []const u8, }; The parser uses these rules: The name of a field is the name of an option: port is --port. A bool field is a flag. --verbose sets it to true, and it takes no value. Each other field takes the next argument as its value. A field with a default is optional. A field without a default must get a value from an argument. The help text options: port host verbose level name (required) help walks the fields during compilation and joins the lines with ++. For an enum field, it lists the tag names from @typeInfo. The main function prints the text with comptime help(Options), thus the binary contains the finished text. Match an argument to a field inline for (info.field names, info.field types, 0..) name, F, f { if (std.mem.eql(u8, key, name)) { known = true; seen[f] = true; if (F == bool) { @field(result, name) = true; }

title: The WebSocket Handshake
description: An HTTP request asks to upgrade, std.http.Server answers 101, and the checks that std leaves to your code.
headings: What std checks, and what it does not
text:
HTTP is request and response. The client asks, the server answers, and the server cannot speak first. A chat, a live score or a game needs messages in both directions at any time. WebSocket gives a TCP connection to the two sides for that purpose, and it starts as an ordinary HTTP request. The client sends a GET with an Upgrade: websocket header. The server answers 101 Switching Protocols. After the empty line at the end of that answer, the connection carries WebSocket frames, not HTTP. This chapter is about the handshake. WebSocket Frames is about the frames. The program below plays both sides in memory. The server is std.http.Server, the same type as in An HTTP Round Trip. The request client sends: GET /chat HTTP/1.1
 Host: example.com
 Upgrade: websocket
 Connection: Upgrade
 Sec-WebSocket-Key: dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==
 Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13
 
 Four headers make this request an upgrade request: Upgrade: websocket names the protocol that the client wants. Connection: Upgrade tells each proxy on the path that the Upgrade header is for this connection. Sec-WebSocket-Key is 16 random bytes in base64. The client makes a new key for each connection. Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13 is the version from RFC 6455. No other version is in use. The key is not a secret and it is not security. The key lets the client check that the server read this request and understood it. The answer The server appends a fixed GUID to the key. RFC 6455 defines the GUID. Then the server computes the SHA-1 of the result and encodes the 20 bytes in base64. The key in the program is th

title: A Contest Template
description: The one program in the section that reads real stdin, and three problems that a judge finds and a browser never shows.
headings: Write one time, at the end
Choose integer widths from the limits
text: Each other chapter in this section parses its input from a const string. A judge does not give you a string. A judge gives you standard input, and it compares your standard output with the correct output. This program is the shape around each solution in the section. The program reads real stdin. Thus it cannot run in your browser, because the WASI sandbox has no standard input. CI builds the program for the host. Then CI gives it a file as input and compares the output, in the same way as a judge. The problem The problem is small on purpose. Thus you can look at the template and not at the problem. The input has this format: The first number is the number of test cases. Each test case is a count n, then n integers. For each case, print the sum of the integers and the largest integer. CI gives the program this input: 3 4 3 -1 4 1 3 1000000000 1000000000 1000000000 5 5 -2 -9 -1 -3 The output must be the same as this text, byte for byte: 7 4 3000000000 1000000000 20 -1 Look at the second test case. Its three numbers are on two lines. A judge can do this. The problem statement tells you the tokens and their order. It does not tell you the line of each token. Read tokens, not lines The other chapters read a line with takeDelimiter and split the line. That method works when you write the input yourself. On a judge, a reader that expects three numbers on one line fails on the second test case above. Thus the template reads one integer at a time. title: A Framebuffer Is an Array
description: Row-major layout, top-left origin, packed pixels, and a putPixel that clips.
text: This section uses no graphics library. Code that you can read sets each pixel. Between the code and an image, there is only a block of numbers and a decision about how to interpret the numbers. The decision has three parts: Row-major. Pixel (x, y) is at y width + x. A row is contiguous, and the next row starts immediately after it. Top-left origin. y = 0 is the top row, and y increases downward. Almost all display APIs use this rule. It is upside down from the rule that you learned in maths, and you will probably make this mistake at least one time. One value per pixel. These chapters use a u32 that holds 0x00RRGGBB, because X11 and Wayland want this format in a client buffer. When you write full u32 values, the byte order is also correct without more work. On a little-endian computer, the value is in memory as B, G, R, X. Why the buffer is global 640 480 4 is 1.2 MB. The default thread stack is 8 MB on Linux and 1 MB on Windows. On some embedded targets, the stack is smaller. A full-size image in a local variable can work on one computer and overflow the stack on a different computer. Make the image global, or allocate it on the heap. undefined is safe here only because drawGradient writes each cell before the program reads a cell. A scene that fills only part of the buffer must start from a known colour. If it does not, the image contains the old data that was in memory. Two arithmetic errors const r: u8 = @intCast((x 255) / (width - 1)); Multiply before you divide. (x / (width - 1)) 255 is zero in all columns but the last, because integer division truncates. title: Project: A Typed Event Bus
description: Handlers are plain functions. The bus reads their parameter types and connects each one to its event during compilation.
headings: Read the payload type of a handler
text: An event bus delivers each event to the functions that want it. In many languages, a handler registers with a string name, and the bus calls it at runtime with an untyped value. A misspelled name or a wrong type shows only when the event arrives. In this project, a handler is a plain function, and its parameter type says which event it wants. The bus reads the parameter types during compilation. Thus a handler for an event that does not exist stops the build. The project uses three earlier chapters: Read a Type, to read the parameter types of a function. Dispatch with Comptime, for inline else. Reject Bad Input with @compileError, for the message. Events and handlers const Event = union(enum) { click: Click, key: Key, resize: Resize, }; fn logClick(out: Writer, c: Click) !void { ... } fn countKey(out: Writer, k: Key) !void { ... } fn quitOnEscape(out: Writer, k: Key) !void { ... } const UiBus = Bus(Event, .{ logClick, countKey, quitOnEscape }); Each variant of Event has its own payload type. Each handler takes a writer and one payload type. The list of handlers is a tuple of functions, and it is a comptime argument to Bus. Read the payload type of a handler fn Payload(comptime handler: anytype) type { const info = @typeInfo(@TypeOf(handler)).@"fn"; if (info.param types.len != 2) @compileError("a handler takes ( Writer, payload)"); return info.param types[1].?; } The type of a function is a usual type, and @typeInfo describes it. param types is a list of the parameter types. Each item is optional, because a parameter of a generic function has no fixed type. Here, the .? stop

title: WebSocket Frames
description: The two header bytes as packed structs, the three length forms, the client mask, and the frames that std.http.Server refuses.
headings: What std reads, and what it refuses
text: After the handshake, the connection carries frames. A frame is a length-prefixed message, as in Three Ways to Frame, with a header of two to fourteen bytes. The header tells the receiver four things: the type of the frame: text, binary, ping, pong or close if the frame is the last part of a message the length of the payload if the sender masked the payload, and with which mask The program writes frames with std, decodes a header, masks a client frame by hand, and gives eight frames to the reader of std.http.Server. Two bytes of header The first byte holds the fin bit, three reserved bits and a 4-bit opcode. The second byte holds the mask bit and a 7-bit length. std declares each byte as a packed struct(u8): WebSocket.Header0 and WebSocket.Header1 in std.http.Server. The program reads the layout of the two structs with @bitOffsetOf and prints it: the header structs in std, field=bits, bit 0 first: Header0: opcode=0-3 rsv3=4 rsv2=5 rsv1=6 fin=7 Header1: payload len=0-6 mask=7 Zig puts the first field of a packed struct in the lowest bits. RFC 6455 draws the frame with the highest bit first. Thus the fields in std are in the reverse order of the diagram in the RFC: opcode is the first field in Zig, and the RFC draws it last in the byte. A @bitCast turns a byte into the struct, and the program prints the fields: the first two bytes, 81 85: byte 0 = 10000001: fin=true rsv=0 opcode=text byte 1 = 10000101: mask=true length=5 Three length forms The length field has 7 bits, thus it holds 0 to 127. The values 0 to 125 are the length. The value 126 means that a 16-bit length follows.

title: Write an Image File
description: PPM, the image format that you can write without a library, and the one strict rule that is easy to break.
headings: Format the header from the constants
When to use a different format
text:
A buffer is useful as a picture when you can look at it. PPM is the shortest way to save a buffer: a short text header, then the pixel bytes. The format has nothing more, and it needs no library. PPM is part of the Netpbm family. The family has six formats, on two axes: what a pixel is, and whether the data is text or binary. ASCII Binary A pixel is --- --- --- --- PBM (bitmap) P1 P4 one bit, black or white PGM (graymap) P2 P5 one gray sample PPM (pixmap) P3 P6 three samples: R, G, B Write P6. P3 holds the same pixels as decimal numbers in text. P3 is larger and slower. But if you want to read your own image in an editor, it is useful to make a P3 file one time. The header P6
64 32
255
 The header has four fields, then the data: the magic, the width, the height, and the maxval (the largest value that a sample can have). Any mix of spaces, tabs and newlines can separate the fields. Thus P6 64 32 255 is as valid as the form above. Then there is one strict rule: Exactly one whitespace byte follows the maxval. All the bytes after that single byte are pixel data. If you write "255

", each pixel moves by one byte. The image shows diagonal noise. No parser can find the mistake, because 0x0A is a legal pixel value. At the end, the snippet below decodes a file with exactly this defect, so that you can see what the reader gets. The pixel data The pixels go from left to right and from top to bottom. There is no padding, no alignment and no row header. Each pixel is three samples in the order R, G, B. The maxval sets the size of a sample: A maxval below 256 gives one byte for eac

title: Write a PNG
description: A signature, three chunks and a CRC on each chunk. The writer filters the pixels, then compresses them with the zlib in the standard library.
headings: A filter can also make the file larger
What this writer does not do
Explain before you read the answer
text: A PPM file is easy to write, but it is large. The 64 by 32 test picture of this section is 6157 bytes as a PPM. As a PNG, the picture is 680 bytes, and all image viewers and browsers open it. A PNG needs two things in addition to the pixels: zlib compression and a CRC-32 checksum. The Zig standard library has both. Thus a PNG writer is about a hundred lines. The two pictures under the output are the two PNG files that the program wrote. Your browser decoded the files with its own PNG decoder. No code from this site decoded those files. The shape of the file A PNG is an 8-byte signature and then a list of chunks. signature 89 50 4E 47 0D 0A 1A 0A IHDR width, height, and what kind of pixels IDAT the pixels, compressed IEND nothing, it marks the end The signature is the same in all PNG files. 50 4E 47 is the text PNG. The other bytes find a file that a text copy damaged: A tool that converts line endings changes 0D 0A. A tool that removes the top bit changes 89. In both cases, a reader refuses the file at the first eight bytes. A chunk All chunks have the same four parts: length 4 bytes, big-endian, the size of the data only type 4 letters, like IHDR data length bytes crc 4 bytes, CRC-32 of the type and the data The CRC covers the type and the data. It does not cover the length. All numbers in a PNG are big-endian. Thus each call to writeInt gets .big. std.hash.Crc32 is the same CRC-32 that zip and Ethernet use. Call init, then call update as many times as necessary, then call final. The header chunk IHDR is always 13 bytes, and it must be the first chunk. Colour type 2 means

title: Lines
description: Bresenham's algorithm: one add and one compare per pixel, integers only.
headings: What this version does not do
text: A line between two pixels is a question about rounding. Almost everywhere, the ideal line goes between pixel centres. At each step, the algorithm must decide on which side to put the pixel. The obvious answer is to calculate y = y0 + slope (x - x0) and round the result. This method works, but it costs a float multiply and a rounding for each pixel. On long lines, the result drifts, because the error accumulates. Bresenham's algorithm asks the same question with an integer error term. The algorithm updates the error term by addition. It does not drift, because it never rounds a value. The error term err records how far the ideal line is from the pixel that the loop plotted last. The code scales the value, so that it stays a whole number. At each step, the major axis always advances. The minor axis advances only when the accumulated error shows that the line is a full pixel behind. The scale factor of two comes from the comparison of 2 err with dx and dy. With this factor, the comparison uses a half-pixel threshold, and the code does not divide. The form in the snippet keeps dy negative: const dx: i32 = @intCast(@abs(x1 - x0)); const dy: i32 = -@as(i32, @intCast(@abs(y1 - y0))); When dy is negative, the eight cases (four quadrants, shallow and steep) become one loop. Many textbooks swap the endpoints, or swap x and y for steep lines. Then they need two loops that are almost the same. This version needs neither change. The two tests are intentionally not an if/else: if (e2 = dy) { err += dy; x += sx; } if (e2 <= dx) { err += dx; y += sy; } On an exact diagonal, the two tests a

title: Circles
description: Compare squared distances, loop over the bounding box, and let putPixel clip.
headings: An outline is the same test two times
What the circles do not have
text: A point is inside a circle when the distance from the point to the centre is not more than the radius: sqrt(dx dx + dy dy) The bounding box The simple version scans the full buffer to fill one circle. At 64x32, the scan does 2048 tests for a shape of about 150 pixels. At 640x480, a circle of radius 100 costs 307,200 tests to fill 31,000 pixels. A better version loops y and x over [centre - r, centre + r]. This version tests (2r+1)^2 pixels. The snippet prints this count next to the count for the simple version. The change is only three lines, because putPixel clips. When a circle is near an edge, its bounding box goes outside the buffer, and fillCircle does not check for this. To show this, the last circle in the snippet goes past two sides of the buffer at the same time. If the clipping is not in one place, each shape routine needs its own @min/@max against the buffer size. Then, at some time, one of those routines will be wrong. An outline is the same test two times if (d2 inner) putPixel(...); The pixels inside the outer radius and outside the inner radius make a band. The band needs no new algorithm and no special case, and the thickness is a parameter. The midpoint circle algorithm draws a one-pixel outline faster. It calculates only one octant and mirrors the octant eight ways. It is the circle version of Bresenham, and you should read it one time. But if you want to fill a shape, the squared-distance test is simpler, and the compiler can vectorize it. What the circles do not have The edge is hard: a pixel is in or out, with no value between. title: Alpha Blending
description: Source-over compositing in integers, the reason for the /255, and the reason that order is still important.
headings: sRGB bytes are not linear light
text: Each chapter before this one draws a shape on top of the old pixels. A later write replaces an earlier write. This method is the painter's algorithm, and it is sufficient for opaque shapes. When the shape on top is not opaque, use blending instead. The standard operator is source over destination . It operates on one channel at a time: out = (src a + dst (255 - a)) / 255 At a = 255, the output is the source. At a = 0, the output does not change. Between these two values, the output is a weighted average. The sum of the weights is exactly one. Thus the blend alone never makes the result brighter or darker. Do not skip the division A division by 256 with a shift is faster than a division by 255. But the error is visible: (255 a) 8 // a = 255 gives 254, not 255 The output above shows both columns. An opaque white composite gives 254. For this reason, much older blending code cannot make pure white. The error increases each time that you blend onto the same pixel again. The expression (s + d + 127) / 255 rounds to the nearest value. The cost is one division, and the compiler usually changes that division into a multiply and a shift. If you want a fast version that is also correct, the usual method is: const t = @as(u32, src) a + 128; const blended: u8 = @intCast((t + (t 8)) 8); This version is exact for all 8-bit inputs. Use it only when a profile shows that the division is important. Read, blend, write The only change in structure from putPixel is that the destination is now an input: const i = uy width + ux; pixels[i] = blend(color, pixels[i], a); With this one change, the dr

title: Linear Light
description: A stored byte is not an amount of light. Decode, mix, encode, with both tables built by the compiler.
headings: What linear light does not fix
Explain before you read the answer
text: For the colour halfway between black and white, most code writes 128. The value 128 is half of 255. But when a screen shows 128, the screen gives about 22% of the light that it gives for 255. The bytes in an image are not amounts of light. The bytes are an encoding of the light. Thus decode the bytes to light, mix the light, and then encode the result again. The worked example The program finds the colour halfway from black to white in two ways: Mix the bytes: (0 + 255) / 2 is 128, after the program rounds the result. Mix the light: the average of 0% light and 100% light is 50%. When the program encodes 50% light again, the result is byte 188. The output shows both values. The values 128 and 188 are very different. The change from red to green shows the same problem in colour: A mix of the bytes gives 128 128 0, a dark olive. A mix of the light gives 188 188 0, a yellow. The third and fourth bands of the picture show these two ramps. Why images store encoded bytes The human eye does not see light linearly. In a dark area, a person sees a small change much more easily than the same change in a bright area. For this reason, the sRGB encoding gives more of its 256 values to dark tones. Thus the steps between bytes look approximately equal to a person. For the same reason, the first band in the picture looks even, and the second band looks mostly pale. The second band has equal steps of light, and to the human eye most of those steps look bright. Thus there are two different tasks: To store or show a colour, use the encoded bytes. To add or average light, use linear values. Ble

title: Rasterize Triangles
description: Edge functions tell inside from outside, and the same three numbers interpolate values across the face.
headings: Barycentric coordinates at no extra cost
Shared edges, and the top-left rule
Why an incremental loop is faster
text: The triangle is the primitive that a GPU actually draws. All other shapes become triangles before they arrive at the rasterizer. A quad that you draw also becomes triangles. Three vertices are always coplanar and always convex. For this reason, the inside test is fast enough to run for each pixel. The test is one function, and the rasterizer calls it three times: fn edge(a: Point, b: Point, p: Point) i32 { return (b.x - a.x) (p.y - a.y) - (b.y - a.y) (p.x - a.x); } The function calculates the 2D cross product of b - a and p - a. The result is two times the signed area of the triangle (a, b, p). The sign of the result tells you on which side of the line ab the point p is. The magnitude of the result is exactly the barycentric weight that interpolation needs. Thus a rasterizer calculates the value one time and uses it two times. Inside is three signs A point is inside the triangle when all three edge functions have the same sign. The snippet first makes the winding the same for all triangles. Then "the same sign" means "all values are zero or more", and the second case is not necessary: if (edge(v0, v1, v2) = 0, the rasterizer draws the pixel two times. With 0, the rasterizer leaves a gap. When the code uses blending, a pixel drawn two times is visible. A gap is always visible. The solution is a rule that decides the tie only from the edge. The rule does not look at the triangle that the code draws. For a top edge or a left edge, zero counts as inside. For other edges, zero does not count as inside. This rule is the top-left rule , and all hardware rasterizers use it. This sn

title: Antialiasing
description: Coverage is alpha. Do the inside test sixteen times for each pixel, and the jagged edges disappear.
text: A pixel is not a point. A pixel is a small square of the image. The edge of a shape usually crosses the square. Usually the square is not fully outside or fully inside the shape. A test at only the centre of the pixel gives a yes-or-no answer. But the real answer is a fraction. The staircase on each hard edge is this rounding error, and you can see it. Do the same test at sixteen points inside the pixel. Then the answer is a count from 0 to 16. This count is the coverage , and the coverage is exactly the alpha value for the composite. The two circles have the same radius and the same colour: The left circle uses the hard test from Circles. The right circle tests a 4x4 grid of samples in each pixel. It blends by the fraction of samples that passed. The table in the output goes across the edge of the right circle on one row. A pixel that is half covered gets alpha 127. The arithmetic stays integer The sub-positions are at the centres of a 4x4 grid inside the pixel. Thus the sub-positions are at odd multiples of half a sub-pixel. The code multiplies each coordinate by 2 samples, and then the sub-positions are whole numbers. Thus the distance test is the same comparison of squared integers as before: const scale = samples 2; const px = x scale + 2 sx + 1; The + 1 is the offset of half a sub-pixel. Without the + 1, the samples are at the corners. Then the full edge moves by half a sub-pixel, which is one eighth of a pixel here. This error is small and always in the same direction. When two antialiased shapes must touch, you can see the error. The cost The code does sixteen insid

title: Per-Pixel Transforms
description: Brightness, contrast, threshold and invert are all one table lookup, and brightness needs Zig's saturating add.
text: All the chapters before this one draw into an empty buffer. The other chapters of this section read a buffer that already has a picture in it. Then they write a changed picture back. The simplest type of filter reads exactly one pixel to make one pixel. Brightness, contrast, invert, threshold, gamma and all colour curves are point operations. Point operations share a useful property: An 8-bit channel has only 256 possible inputs. Thus there are only 256 possible answers. Calculate the answers one time into an array. Then the filter is an array index. const Lut = [256]u8; fn apply(buf: []u32, lut: Lut) void { for (buf) p { const c = canvas.channels(p. ); p. = canvas.rgb(lut[c.r], lut[c.g], lut[c.b]); } } This loop runs all filters of this type. Brightness and threshold use the same code. The only difference is 256 bytes of data. Brightness needs a saturating add Brightness adds a constant. For a u8 with the value 250, an add of 10 has three possible meanings, and Zig makes you select one: value + 10 // illegal behaviour: traps in a safe build value +% 10 // wraps: 250 + 10 = 4 value + 10 // saturates: 250 + 10 = 255 Only the third operator is correct here: The second operator is the bug that puts black spots in a brightened sky. The second operator is the default in C. In C, an unsigned overflow wraps by definition, and no warning occurs. The first operator asks for the true sum, 260. A u8 cannot hold 260, thus no u8 value is a correct result. A safe build stops the program. + and - are operators of the language. They compile to a single instruction on each target that has s

title: Convolution
description: Blur, sharpen and Sobel are one loop with different numbers in it. The two bugs are always the border and the buffer.
headings: The kernel is a type, not a struct field
Sobel, and what the sign means
text: A point operation reads one pixel. A convolution reads a neighbourhood. The steps are: 1. Move a small matrix over the image. 2. Multiply each weight by the pixel under it. 3. Add the products. 4. Divide the sum. Blur, sharpen, emboss and edge detection all use this loop. Only the numbers in the matrix are different. The kernel is a type, not a struct field fn Kernel(comptime side: usize) type { comptime std.debug.assert(side % 2 == 1); return struct { weights: [side side]i32, divisor: i32, const radius: i32 = @intCast(side / 2); }; } Kernel(3) and Kernel(5) are different types. Inside the convolution loop, the side length is a compile-time constant. Thus the compiler knows the bounds, and the inner loops unroll. Also, you cannot give a 5x5 kernel to code that expects a 3x3 kernel. A runtime side: usize field also compiles, but it loses both of these advantages. Comptime explains type functions in general. Here the advantage is easy to see. The comptime std.debug.assert runs at compile time. An even side length is a compile error, not a runtime panic. The reason is that a kernel with no centre pixel has no meaningful answer. The divisor is necessary The sum of the gaussian weights is 16, and the divisor is 16. Thus the image keeps its initial brightness. If the sum of the weights is not equal to the divisor, the kernel changes the brightness of the full image. Sometimes you want this result. Usually it is a bug, and you see the bug three filters later. Two useful special cases: The sharpen weights have a sum of 1, with a divisor of 1. Flat areas do not change, because the n

title: Colour Matrices
description: Grayscale, sepia and saturation are one 3x3 matrix. A chain of these matrices multiplies into one matrix before the program changes the image.
headings: Saturation is a line through grey
The rows of sepia do not sum to 256
text: Grayscale, sepia, saturation, hue rotation and channel swaps look like different filters. They are one filter with different constants: a 3x3 matrix that multiplies the channel vector. [ R' ] [ a b c ] [ R ] [ G' ] = [ d e f ] [ G ] [ B' ] [ g h i ] [ B ] When the filters have this form, you can multiply them together. A chain of four colour filters becomes one matrix. The program calculates that matrix before it changes the image, and then it makes one pass over the image. Write grayscale as a matrix Put the luma weights in all three rows: const luma matrix: Matrix = .{ 77, 150, 29, 77, 150, 29, 77, 150, 29, }; Each output channel becomes the same weighted average, and the result is grayscale. The entries use a scale of 256, and the multiply divides by 256 at the end. Thus all of the arithmetic stays in integers. Floats add precision, but the last cast to u8 removes that precision. Floats also need a conversion at each end. Saturation is a line through grey out = luma + s (in - luma) The value of s controls the result: At s = 0, the result is grayscale. At s = 1, the result is the original. Above 1, the result continues in the same direction, away from grey. As a matrix, saturation is a blend of the luma matrix and the identity: fn saturation(s: i32) Matrix { var m: Matrix = undefined; for (&m, identity, luma matrix) out, i, l { out. = @divTrunc(s i + (scale - s) l, scale); } return m; } Saturation is a matrix and not a special case. Thus it composes with the other matrices. The output shows that saturation changes chroma and does not change brightness: luma under saturati

title: Histograms and Levels
description: Count what the image contains, and get the correction table from the counts. Auto-levels, equalization, and why to apply them to luma.
headings: Equalization: the table is the distribution
Apply it to brightness, not to channels
text: The tables in per-pixel transforms were constants: you selected a contrast factor and made a table from it. The tables on this page come from a measurement. Count the number of pixels at each luma value. The correction that the image needs comes directly from the counts. fn histogram(src: []const u32) [256]u32 { var hist: [256]u32 = @splat(0); for (src) p hist[canvas.luma(p)] += 1; return hist; } The function uses 256 counters and one pass. The analysis needs nothing more. All of the other results on this page come from these counts. Read the shape Most of the histogram of the test picture is in the low third: The background ramp is between 13 and 68. The block and the discs are three separate spikes at higher values. No pixel has a value from 80 to 95 or from 112 to 143. The picture uses approximately half of the range that it has. This shape is the numeric meaning of "the image looks flat". Levels and equalization each correct this shape in a different way. Levels: measure the ends The simple correction stretches the range of the image to fill 0 to 255. The only question is where the image really starts and stops. The answer is not the first and the last bin that is not empty: const black = percentile(hist, total, 10); // 1% const white = percentile(hist, total, 990); // 99% The program clips a fraction at each end first, and this is intentional. Without the clip, one hot pixel at 255 or one dead pixel at 0 sets the full range. Then the stretch does nothing. All auto-levels implementations clip, and the fraction is the only setting. The result is the contrast table from p

title: A WebSocket Client
description: A client that std does not have. It checks the handshake, masks each frame, puts fragments together, answers a ping, and closes correctly.
headings: What this client does not do
text: std.http.Client has no WebSocket support. Thus a Zig program that connects to a WebSocket server needs its own client. The client is about 170 lines. It has five tasks: 1. Send the upgrade request with a random key, and check the answer. 2. Mask each frame with a new random mask. 3. Put a message in fragments together. 4. Answer each ping with a pong, also in the middle of a message. 5. Complete the close handshake. The client reads from a std.Io.Reader and writes to a std.Io.Writer. It never sees a socket. Thus the program below runs in your browser: it plays the server in memory with std.http.Server, and you can see the bytes in each direction. A WebSocket Server on a Socket imports this file and uses the same client over a real TCP connection. The handshake The key is 16 random bytes in base64. The client keeps the key, because it needs the key again to check the answer. The program makes the random numbers with std.Random.DefaultPrng and a fixed seed. Thus the key is the same on each run, and CI can compare the output. A real client takes the seed from io.random, as the server chapter does. The RFC requires a key and masks that a script cannot predict. The request and the answer are split into two functions, because a server must read the request before it answers. Over a socket, call the two functions one after the other. finishHandshake reads the head line by line with takeDelimiterInclusive. After the empty line, the next byte in the reader is the first byte of the first frame. The reader can hold frames that came in the same TCP packet as the answer, and the client

title: Median and Rank Filters
description: A convolution cannot ignore a value. Sort the neighbourhood, and one function is a denoiser, an eroder or a dilator. The index decides which.
headings: Why the median is better than the blur on this noise
Why the median keeps the edge
The next filters in the family
text: A convolution is a weighted sum. Each pixel under the kernel adds something to the result. No weight has the meaning "this value is wrong, ignore it". A family of filters, the rank filters, does not have this limit. Sort the neighbourhood, and then select a pixel by its position. One function, three filters fn rankFilter(dst: []u32, src: []const u32, comptime rank: usize) void Sort the nine pixels of a 3x3 window by brightness, and take the pixel at rank: Rank 4 is the median. Rank 0 is the minimum, which is erosion. Rank 8 is the maximum, which is dilation. Basic morphology and the standard denoiser are the same loop with a different index. The choice is comptime. Thus each rank compiles to its own specialised function, and the inner loop has no branch for the rank. The output checks the morphology at the end. The block has 153 pixels that are brighter than 200. Erosion decreases this number to 105, and dilation increases it to 209. Thus bright regions shrink or grow by one pixel at the boundary. Erosion followed by dilation is opening, and dilation followed by erosion is closing. These operations remove small specks and do not change the size of large shapes. Why the median is better than the blur on this noise Salt and pepper noise replaces a pixel fully with black or white. The corrupted value has no relation to the old value. A weighted average gives a bad result in this case: black white mean luma error vs clean noisy: 54 75 9.03 gaussian: 0 0 11.80 median: 0 2 1.59 If you read only the first two columns, the gaussian looks perfect. Not one pure black or pure white pi

title: Scale and Resample
description: Nearest, bilinear and box filters, the half-pixel bug, and why a downscale without a filter makes fine detail into a solid bar.
headings: The mapping, and the bug in it
A downscale is a different problem
text: Each of the earlier filters kept the grid that it got: one output pixel for one input pixel, at the same position. A change in size breaks this rule. The output pixels do not align with the input pixels. Thus you must decide the colour at a position between pixels. The mapping, and the bug in it An output pixel covers a range of the input. The point to sample is the centre of that range: src = (dst + 0.5) scale - 0.5 The two halves are both necessary: dst + 0.5 moves from the index of the output pixel to its centre. - 0.5 moves from the centre in the input back to the index. If you remove the two halves, you get src = dst scale. This formula aligns the centres of the first pixels in the two grids, and not the corners of the images. The result moves by 0.5 (1 - scale) source pixels. The snippet upscales four pixels to eight, with and without the correction: 4 pixels - 8, source luma 0 0 255 255 bilinear, centres correct: 0 0 0 0 63 191 255 255 bilinear, half-pixel bug (note the shift): 0 0 0 0 127 255 255 255 The correct version puts a symmetric ramp of two samples across the edge. The version with the bug puts a ramp of one sample. The full image is half an output pixel to the left of its correct position. On a 2x upscale, this offset is visible, and it is a common resampling bug. The bug is easy to write and difficult to see in one image. When you blend the result with the original, the bug is immediately clear. The code uses fixed point and not floats. If a resampler rounds differently on two machines, it makes different files. A difference of one in the last bit is suffi

title: Bitmap Text
description: A glyph is a small rectangle of bits. To draw text, copy those bits.
text: The earlier chapters drew shapes from maths: a line from an equation, a circle from a radius. Text is different. No formula gives the letter G, so the program must store the shape. The oldest method to store the shape is the simplest method that works. A glyph is a small rectangle of bits, with one bit per pixel, on or off. To draw a character, the program reads each bit. Where the bit is a one, the program sets a pixel. The program What just happened Each glyph is seven bytes. Each row uses five bits, and there are seven rows. The source writes the rows in binary, so you can see the shape. Look at Z in the code, and you can read the letter from the ones. The program skipped the zeroes. It did not draw them. That one if lets text compose with other drawings. A glyph has no background of its own, so it draws over the pixels that are already there. If the program fills the zeroes with a background colour, each character is in an opaque box. This mistake is immediately visible. The pen moved by a fixed amount. The step is always six columns per character. A font of this type is a monospaced font, and for this reason terminal output aligns in columns. A proportional font stores an advance width for each glyph. That one change is most of the difference between this program and a text engine. With that change, the width of a string is a sum and not a multiplication. The full font is 49 bytes. There are seven glyphs at seven bytes each. For this reason, machines with only kilobytes of memory used this method. A bootloader or an embedded display still uses this method. Check yourse

title: Sprites and Transparency
description: A copy of a rectangle is easy. The important feature is the decision about which pixels not to copy.
text: A sprite is a small image that a program copies onto a larger image. The copy is a nested loop, and you can write it in a minute. A sprite is different from a rectangle because of one part: the part that decides which pixels to skip. Without that part, each sprite is a box. Then a spaceship moves a square of background with it. The program What just happened The background shows through the corners. Inside the bounding box of the sprite, you can see the checkerboard at each pixel where the sprite has the transparent value. The program drew 18 of the 35 pixels and skipped 17. The program prints these counts, so you can see the ratio: almost half of a sprite is usually empty. Transparency is one comparison. The program uses a key colour : one value that means "skip". Each 8-bit and 16-bit console used this method. The reason is that a per-pixel alpha channel costs one byte per pixel, and those machines did not have that memory. The method has one well-known disadvantage: the artwork cannot use the key colour. For this reason, much sprite art of that time did not use one specific shade of magenta. The program clipped the third copy. The program drew the third copy partly off the right edge, and the loop skipped the cells outside the canvas. No extra code does the clipping. The clipping comes from the bounds check. The program stores the sprite one time and draws it three times. The program does not make a copy of the sprite data in memory. A sprite is data, and a loop draws it. Thus the second and third copies cost only the loop. Check yourself Key-colour transparency is binar

title: A Scene Graph
description: Position each thing relative to its parent. When the parent moves, everything below the parent moves with it.
headings: What a real scene graph stores
text: To draw one sprite, you must know where the sprite goes. To draw fifty sprites that belong together, you must know where all fifty go. When the group moves, all fifty numbers must stay correct. A scene graph solves this problem. Do not store where each thing is. Store where each thing is relative to its parent , and calculate the rest. An arm is always at "shoulder plus two", and the shoulder can go to any position. The program What just happened Two lines changed and four shapes moved. nodes[0] went from (4, 3) to (26, 5). The program did not change other items in the array. The head and the two arms followed the body, because no child knew its position on the canvas. The transform is an addition. Each node draws at the position of its parent plus its own offset. Then the node gives that total to its children. The walk adds one time for each level, and the total grows as the walk goes down the tree. The layout engine uses the same downward walk for the same reason. The position of a child depends on its parent. The position of a parent does not depend on its child. The order in the array is not the order in the tree. The program stores the nodes in a flat array and links them by index. The order of the siblings sets the order of the paint. This is the painter's algorithm again: a later sibling covers an earlier sibling. What a real scene graph stores Two integers only let a node move. A full scene graph stores a matrix for each node, usually 3x3 for 2D. With a matrix, a node can also rotate and scale. To combine a parent with a child, the walk multiplies two matrices. It d

title: A Bar Chart
description: One division changes numbers into pixels. If the division is wrong, the chart misleads the reader.
headings: The lie that a bar chart can tell
text: In this section, a chart is the first drawing where the programmer does not select the shape. The data sets the height of each bar. Thus a function changes a number into a height in pixels, and charts go wrong in that function. The function is one division. The difficult part is to select the value to divide by. The program What just happened Each bar is value rows / max. The largest value is the denominator, thus the largest bar fills the plot exactly. This scale is not the only possible scale, and the choice has a result. You cannot compare two charts that use this scale, because each chart used a different scale and did not tell you. The integer division truncates, and the table shows the truncation. 12 of 40 over 14 rows is 4.2, and the program draws 4. Each bar is up to one row shorter than the correct height, and never taller. You cannot see this bias in the picture. If a chart has only a small number of pixels for each bar, the bias can show small differences incorrectly. The program draws the axis, and also the scale. 40 is at the top and 0 is at the bottom. Without these labels, the picture shows a shape and makes no claim. The reader cannot tell if the tallest bar is 40 or 40,000. The reader also cannot tell if the baseline is zero. The lie that a bar chart can tell If the vertical axis starts at a value other than zero, the bars are not proportional to their values. A bar that is two times as tall as another bar does not mean two times the value. The reader can see this problem only in the axis labels. A quick look at a chart does not read the labels.
