title: A Canvas Is a View
description: Four fields, not a slice. Each routine draws inside a region, and the routine does not know that the canvas is a region.
headings: The stride gives what the width cannot give
A rectangle is not a slice
text: Until now, each drawing routine in this section assumed that it owned the full buffer. The type says so. There is one width, and the width is a constant. The pixel at the end of a row is immediately before the pixel at the start of the next row. Frequently you want to draw into a region of the buffer instead. Examples are a panel inside a window, a cell inside a chart, or a widget inside a toolbar. The region has its own origin and its own edges, and these are different from the origin and the edges of the buffer. You have two choices: Give an offset and a clip rectangle to each routine, and apply them in each routine. Change the value that each routine gets. The program What just happened The bar is 40 pixels wide inside a panel that is 26 pixels wide. The bar stops at the edge of the panel. The program does not change the panel next to it. Neither rect nor the caller refers to the position of the panel to get this result. The three sub-canvases share one buffer and one stride with the root. The table at the end shows this in four rows. width is different for each region. stride is 60 for all of them, and also for the region two levels deep. All of the canvases address the same memory, and the shape of that memory did not change. The child does not know its position. Canvas has no x and no y. A sub-canvas is its pixels, its size, and the distance between its rows. A drawing routine needs nothing more. The canvas stores no parent coordinate, thus no routine can forget to add a parent coordinate. The dump of the right panel copied nothing. The second picture is the same memo

title: Texture Mapping
description: The triangle already interpolates. Point the triangle at a second image, and it interpolates coordinates into that image, not colours.
headings: The seam is not a bug in the rasteriser
Why a texture is not a canvas
text: At the end of the triangles chapter, the triangle had three barycentric weights. That chapter also showed that the weights interpolate each value that you attach to the corners. That chapter attached colours. Attach a pair of coordinates into a different image instead, and the result is a textured triangle. No line of the rasteriser changes. The program What just happened The interpolation uses the same three weights. The program calculates w0, w1 and w2 exactly as it did for Gouraud shading. The only change is the values that the weights multiply: const u = w0 a.u + w1 b.u + w2 c.u; const v = w0 a.v + w1 b.v + w2 c.v; The coordinates go from 0 to 1, not from 0 to 8. The texture is a square of 8 by 8 pixels, and only sample refers to that size. With normalized coordinates, the same four corners address a texture of 16 pixels or of 4096 pixels. The geometry does not know which texture it has. A coordinate past 1 is not an error. The square on the right asks for coordinates up to 2. Wrapping changes that range into two copies of the image in each direction. A clamp would stretch the edge texels into a smear. The two choices are both reasonable, and you must tell the sampler which one to use. The trapezoid has a seam. Look along its diagonal. The program draws a shape with four corners as two triangles, and each triangle gets its own affine interpolation. When the shape is not a parallelogram, the two maps do not agree along the edge that they share. The seam is not a bug in the rasteriser The seam comes from a limit of an affine map. The three corners of a triangle set a line

title: Transforms
description: To move, turn and resize a shape is one operation. To combine them is a multiply, and you cannot select its order freely.
headings: The purpose of the bottom row
text: The scene graph stored two integers for each node, and that chapter gave the limit: two integers only let a node move. A full scene graph stores a matrix. Thus a node can also turn and change its size. To combine a parent with a child, the walk then multiplies two matrices. This chapter builds that matrix. The program What just happened Six numbers cover all cases. A move, a turn, a scale and a shear are four ways to fill the same six slots. A routine that applies a transform does not know which of the four it got. The order changes the answer. The two arrows in the first picture come from the same quarter turn and the same offset, combined in the two possible orders. The rotation is about the origin. Thus, if the move occurs first, the turn also turns the offset. The shape goes a quarter circle to a different position. The picture shows that matrix multiplication is not commutative. A turn about a point is three transforms. No rotate function takes a centre. Do these three steps: 1. Move the pivot to the origin. 2. Turn. 3. Move the pivot back. The three steps combine into one matrix, and that matrix costs the same as one rotation. The arrows with the numbers 1, 2 and 3 move around the +, but the program has no code for an orbit. Each arrow is this matrix with a different angle. The program never changes the shape. shape is one const array of seven points. The program draws it eight times in the three pictures. Each difference is in the matrix. Read a composition In practice, transforms are difficult because the usual notation is in the reverse order of the operations. Wit

title: Onto the Screen
description: The same buffer, given to X11 through translate-c, and what changes on Wayland.
text: A file write goes in one direction: you make bytes, and then the work is complete. A window needs messages in the two directions. The display server decides when you can paint, asks if your program is still alive, and reports input. If your program does not do its part of this exchange, the window stays blank, freezes, or the server kills it. Three things are different from Write an Image File. The pixels are wider. X11 and Wayland both want 32 bits per pixel, not 24. On a little-endian computer, both want a u32 that holds 0x00RRGGBB. In memory, this value is B, G, R, X. When you write full u32 values, the byte order is correct without more work. For this reason, the framebuffer in this section uses 32 bits from the first chapter. Two programs can share the buffer. A file write is a copy. To put pixels on screen, a copy is not always necessary. Wayland's wl shm gives the compositor a file descriptor for the same pages that you drew into, and no copy occurs. X11's XPutImage copies the pixels to the server. The MIT-SHM extension exists to prevent that copy. One drawing is not sufficient. The server tells you when to paint, and it asks again later. Xlib, the short version Open a display, create a window and map it. Then answer the events. Xlib needs much less setup code than Wayland. It still runs on all Linux desktops, also under XWayland on a Wayland desktop. When you write your own version, four details in that code are important. @cImport does not exist now. title: A WebSocket Server on a Socket
description: std.http.Server upgrades a real TCP connection and echoes messages. The server answers pings, closes correctly, and refuses a message that is too big.
headings: The size of the buffer is the limit
Ping and close are your work
The log comes from the server thread
text: The last three chapters used buffers in memory. This chapter uses a real TCP connection on loopback. The server is std.http.Server with its WebSocket support. The client is the client from A WebSocket Client. The program imports that file with @import("websocket-client.zig"). The client runs here without a change. It reads from the reader of a TCP stream in place of a fixed buffer. That is the purpose of the rule of this section: parse from a Reader, never from a socket. The program makes two connections. The first sends a text, a ping and a long text, and then closes normally. The second sends a message that is too big for the server. connection 1: got text "hello" got pong "beat" got text, 400 bytes got close 1000 connection 2: got close 1009 One connection The function has three parts: 1. receiveHead reads the HTTP request, as in An HTTP Round Trip. 2. upgradeRequested and respondWebSocket do the handshake. A request with no key gets a 400. An ordinary request gets an ordinary answer. 3. The loop reads messages with readSmallMessage and answers each one. The handshake chapter also checks the version header. This server does not, to keep the function short. The size of the buffer is the limit readSmallMessage returns the payload as a slice of the buffer of the reader. Thus the whole frame must fit in that buffer, and max message is the largest message that the server accepts. Here it is 512 bytes. The 400-byte text fits.
